Uniqueness: a $C_tL^2$ weak solution has continuous Fourier coefficients whose distributional derivatives are the displayed continuous right-hand sides; for each coefficient $z(t)$ and its continuous right-hand side $g(t)$, subtract the classical primitive $G(t)=\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$. On every compact real interval, each real and imaginary component of the continuous $g$ is Riemann integrable by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. The oriented primitive $G$ is therefore $C^1$, with $G'=g$ by [[thm-ftc-first-part]], componentwise and for either sign of $t$. Under the already declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the $C^1$ regular-distribution compatibility clause of [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]] gives $\partial_tu_G=u_g$. Subtracting this from the actual weak coefficient equation $\partial_tu_z=u_g$ proves that $z-G$ has zero distributional derivative. [[thm-a-distribution-with-zero-derivatives-on-a-connected-open-set-is-constant]] on $\mathbb R$ makes this regular distribution constant; continuity makes the equality pointwise. Thus each coefficient is a classical solution of the displayed finite-dimensional ODE, and global ODE uniqueness with its given initial value identifies it. Product completeness then identifies the fields. Energy conservation passes to the limit in norm. Countable Choice covers the Fourier, Fubini, Hilbert-space and regular-distribution supplier contracts; the finite-dimensional modal equations require no extra choice premise.

items.title: Newtonian potential of smooth compact data is smooth and solves the Poisson equation pointwise
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be any scalar parameter and let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ and let $$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)}{4\pi|x-y|}\,dy .$$ Then $Nf\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $-\Delta Nf=f$ pointwise, and for every multi-index $\alpha$ the spatial derivative satisfies $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$. In particular, for smooth compactly supported $\rho$ the field $E=-\varepsilon_0^{-1}\nabla N\rho$ is smooth. The statement is about the explicit integral transform of compactly supported smooth data and does not assume smoothness of the kernel at the pole; the distributional identity $-\Delta Nf=f$ is the one supplied by the Newtonian-potential theorem ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]), upgraded here from a distributional to a pointwise identity for smooth data.
items.strategy: Substitute $z=x-y$: $Nf(x)=\int\Phi(z)f(x-z)\,dz$ with $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. On a compact set of $x$ the derivatives $D^\alpha f(x-z)$ vanish outside a common bounded $z$-set and are bounded there, so every parameter derivative has an integrable bound $C|\Phi|$ on that set; differentiation under the integral sign ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]], applied coordinatewise) gives $D^\alpha Nf(x)=\int\Phi(z)D^\alpha f(x-z)\,dz$ and continuity of the result, hence $C^\infty$. The distributional identity $-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f$ is the cited Newtonian-potential theorem ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]). Since both sides are smooth functions (the right side is $f$, the left side is a smooth representative by the first part), the distributional equality is a pointwise equality by localization against compactly supported nonnegative smooth tests. The derivative identity $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$ is the parameter-differentiation formula just proved, and the final smoothness claim for $E$ follows by linearity. Countable Choice is inherited from the exact Statement of [[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]] and its regular-distribution interface; it is explicitly assumed here, not silently removed by the smooth upgrade.

items.title: Unique solution of a symmetric coercive variational problem on a Hilbert space
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice, or the Axiom of Choice as declared ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-complete-metric-space]]), let $a:H\times H\to\mathbb R$ be a symmetric bounded bilinear form ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]]) with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$ for all $v\in H$ and some $\alpha>0$, and let $\ell:H\to\mathbb R$ be a bounded linear functional with dual norm $\|\ell\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]). Then there is exactly one $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=\ell(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\|u\|\le\|\ell\|/\alpha$. No Lax-Milgram theorem, Zorn-type argument or unproved minimiser existence is invoked: the proof minimises the explicit functional $J(v)=\tfrac12a(v,v)-\ell(v)$.
items.strategy: The functional $J(v)=\tfrac12a(v,v)-\ell(v)$ is bounded below by $\tfrac\alpha2\|v\|^2-\|\ell\|\|v\|$ and tends to $+\infty$ as $\|v\|\to\infty$. Choose a minimising sequence $v_n$ with $J(v_n)\to m=\inf J$; the choice of the sequence uses Countable Choice as declared ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The parallelogram law ([[thm-parallelogram-law]]) gives $J((v_n+v_k)/2)=[J(v_n)+J(v_k)]/2-a(v_n-v_k,v_n-v_k)/8$, so $\alpha\|v_n-v_k\|^2/8\le[J(v_n)+J(v_k)]/2-m\to0$: the sequence is Cauchy, and completeness of the Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-complete-metric-space]]) gives $v_n\to u$ in norm, with $J(u)=m$ by continuity of the bounded form and functional ([[def-bounded-bilinear-map]]). For fixed $v$ the real quadratic $s\mapsto J(u+sv)$ has a minimum at $s=0$, so its linear coefficient $a(u,v)-\ell(v)$ vanishes; conversely any such $u$ satisfies $J(u+v)-J(u)=\tfrac12a(v,v)\ge0$. Uniqueness: for two solutions test the difference with itself to get $\alpha\|u_1-u_2\|^2\le0$. Testing the equation at $v=u$ gives $\alpha\|u\|^2\le\|\ell\|\|u\|$, hence the estimate.

items.title: Thin closed current: divergence-free distribution and convergence of its mollified Biot-Savart fields
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ be a closed embedded $C^2$ curve parametrized by arc length and let $I\in\mathbb R$ be a constant and $\mu_0>0$. Define the vector-valued distribution $$j(\psi)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3).$$ The test space is [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. Then $\operatorname{div}j=0$ in the distributional sense ([[def-distributional-derivative]]). For any family of nonnegative smooth radial kernels $\eta_\varepsilon$ of integral one supported in $B_\varepsilon(0)$, $\varepsilon>0$ (including the usual rescalings $\eta_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-3}\eta(x/\varepsilon)$ of a chosen unit-mass radial kernel supported in $B_1(0)$), the mollified fields $j_\varepsilon=j*\eta_\varepsilon$ are smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, and their Biot-Savart fields converge, with every derivative uniformly on any compact $K$ disjoint from $\gamma$, to $$B(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))}{|x-\gamma(s)|^3}\,ds .$$ In addition, assigning arbitrary finite values on the curve gives a representative $B\in L^1_{\rm loc}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, smooth off the curve, with $\operatorname{div}T_B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}T_B=\mu_0j$ globally. The first identity is tested on scalar $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and the second on vector $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$. If the curve lies in $B_a(0)$, then $|B(x)|\le\mu_0|I|L/[4\pi(|x|-a)^2]$ for $|x|>a$, so $B$ decays at infinity. The distributional assertions are proved globally and do not follow merely from convergence away from the curve. For the circle $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ and a point $z e_3$ on its axis the value is $B_z=\mu_0Ia^2/[2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}]$. Nothing is asserted about the divergent line self-energy or about fields on the curve itself.
items.strategy:
First, for every scalar compact smooth test $\varphi$, $\langle\operatorname{div}j,\varphi\rangle=-I\int_0^L(d/ds)\varphi(\gamma(s))ds=0$ by [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and periodicity. The order-zero bound $|j(\psi)|\le|I|L\|\psi\|_\infty$ makes $j$ a compactly supported vector distribution by [[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]. Write the mollification explicitly as $j_\varepsilon(x)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))ds$. Compact parameter differentiation proves smoothness and support in the compact epsilon-neighbourhood of the curve; $\operatorname{div}j_\varepsilon=-I\int_0^L(d/ds)\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))ds=0$. These statements include $I=0$.

For the global field, put $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$ with finite pole value and $A(x)=\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\Phi(x-\gamma(s))ds$. On a bounded observation set $Q$ and for $y$ on the compact curve, $Q-y$ lies in one fixed ball $B_R$. Polar integration gives $\int_{B_R}|\Phi|=R^2/2$ and $\int_{B_R}|\nabla\Phi|=R$. Tonelli followed by the integral triangle inequality therefore bounds $\int_Q|A|$ by $\mu_0|I|LR^2/2$ and the absolute integral defining $B$ by $\mu_0|I|LR$. The curve is Lebesgue-null: a length-L unit-speed curve is covered by at most $1+L/h$ balls of radius $2h$ from an equally spaced parameter partition, with total volume $O(Lh^2+h^3)\to0$. The finite cover estimate uses [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]] and [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]; arbitrary finite assignments on the null curve remain measurable by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]. Reset exceptional curve values finitely. The explicit off-curve formula is smooth by compact differentiation; measurable kernels and Tonelli give the globally locally integrable representative.

Establish $\partial_jT_\Phi=T_{-z_j/(4\pi|z|^3)}$ directly: integrate by parts on $\{\delta<|z|<R\}$ containing a scalar test support; the outer term vanishes and the inner boundary term is bounded by $\|\varphi\|_\infty\delta$, since $\Phi=1/(4\pi\delta)$ and the sphere area is $4\pi\delta^2$. The integrals of $|\Phi|$ and $|\nabla\Phi|$ on the omitted ball tend to zero by the displayed polar bounds, proving the first-derivative distribution identity. Translation and absolutely integrable Fubini now give $\operatorname{curl}T_A=T_B$, with the stated cross-product sign.

For a scalar test $\varphi$, let $H(y)=\int\Phi(z)\varphi(z+y)dz$. Every derivative can be passed to the smooth test on a common bounded z-set, so $H$ is smooth near the compact curve. Then $\langle\operatorname{div}T_A,\varphi\rangle=-\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\nabla H(\gamma(s))ds=-\mu_0I\int_0^L(d/ds)H(\gamma(s))ds=0$. The translated identity of [[thm-minus-laplacian-of-the-fundamental-solution-is-dirac]] similarly gives, componentwise, $\langle-\Delta T_A,\psi\rangle=\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))ds=\mu_0j(\psi)$. All interchanges are absolutely integrable by the uniform kernel bound times a finite test-derivative norm. Constant-coefficient distributional derivatives commute because mixed derivatives of smooth tests commute. Componentwise alternating-symbol cancellation thus yields $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}T_A=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}T_A=\nabla\operatorname{div}T_A-\Delta T_A=\mu_0j$. This proves the global identities for $T_B$ without any unsupported limit through the wire. Since $B$ is smooth off the curve and $j$ vanishes there, the distributional identities imply the pointwise $\operatorname{div}B=\operatorname{curl}B=0$ there by regular-distribution injectivity and continuity.

For away-from-curve convergence, write the Biot-Savart field of $j_\varepsilon$ by Fubini as the loop integral additionally averaged over $u$ against $\eta_\varepsilon(u)$. Absolute integrability follows from the same local kernel estimate and compact source support. For a compact $K$ disjoint from the curve and $d=\operatorname{dist}(K,\gamma)>0$, the kernel and each specified x-derivative are smooth and uniformly continuous on the enlarged compact difference set for $|u|\le d/2$. Each derivative error is bounded by $\mu_0|I|L/(4\pi)$ times that derivative's uniform modulus at epsilon, since the averaging kernel is nonnegative with integral one. This tends to zero by [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], and compact differentiation under the integral follows from [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]. For $|x|>a$, $|x-\gamma(s)|\ge|x|-a$ gives the stated far bound. For a circle at an axis point, the numerator integrates to $2\pi a^2e_3$ and the denominator is $(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}$, giving the original formula. No value of the singular line integral on the curve, finite self-energy or force product is asserted. Countable Choice enters through the exact polar, surface, fundamental-solution and regular-distribution interfaces; no stronger axiom is used. The convergence proof uses only nonnegativity, unit mass and support in $B_\varepsilon$; no fixed-shape dependence on epsilon is required. The usual rescaled unit-ball kernel is a special case, not a narrowing of the permitted family. In the first-derivative excision, present each spherical boundary by the same six signed-maximal-coordinate regular graph faces; their finite seam arcs have zero surface measure. This checks the precise finite-face hypothesis of the cited divergence theorem.

references.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
references.locator: Full242-page source, printed pp.32-36 (PDF38-42), read for normalized kernel, first derivative, local integrability and distributional point-source interpretation. The curve-measure argument and global derivative pairings are supplied explicitly here, rather than claimed as a theorem stated in this source.

references.title: David Tong, Electromagnetism
references.locator: Printed pp.49-51, integral vector potential and thin-wire Biot-Savart formula. Read relevant sections of available full236-page source; global locally integrable proof is the explicit local argument here.

items.title: The gradient norm dominates the H-one norm on zero-boundary Sobolev space
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice as declared by the Sobolev completeness theorem ([[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ be bounded and open, and write $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with $H_0^1(\Omega):=W_0^{1,2}(\Omega)$ the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ in the $W^{1,2}$ norm ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). Then $H^1(\Omega)$ and its closed subspace $H_0^1(\Omega)$ are complete, the quadratic integral norm is a Hilbert norm (its coordinate $L^2$ inner products satisfy the parallelogram law), and $$\|v\|_{L^2}^2\le(2L)^2\,\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2}^2\le(2L)^2\,\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}^2\qquad\text{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega). $$ In particular the gradient seminorm is equivalent to the full $H^1$ norm on $H_0^1$, and the argument needs neither a smooth domain nor a general boundary-trace theorem.
items.strategy: For $v\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ extend $v$ by zero to the box $(-L,L)^3$ (legitimate because $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$). Along each coordinate line the Newton-Leibniz formula ([[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]) gives $v(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\int_{-L}^{x_1}\partial_1v(s,x_2,x_3)\,ds$; Cauchy-Schwarz for $L^2$ ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) gives $|v|^2\le2L\int_{-L}^{L}|\partial_1v|^2ds$, and integrating in the other coordinates and then in $x_1$ over a length-$2L$ interval gives $\|v\|_2^2\le(2L)^2\|\partial_1v\|_2^2$, hence the displayed squared inequality with $(2L)^2$ and the nonsquared bound $\|v\|_2\le2L\|\nabla v\|_2$. Approximation in the $W^{1,2}$ norm (the definition of $H_0^1$ as a closure, [[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) passes both the inequality and the equivalences to all of $H_0^1$ by continuity of the $L^2$ norm; completeness is the Sobolev completeness theorem ([[thm-sobolev-spaces-are-banach-spaces]]) restricted to the closed subspace, and the Hilbert-norm claim follows because the $W^{1,2}$ quadratic norm is induced by the coordinate $L^2$ inner products, which satisfy the parallelogram law.

items.title: The L-two Dirichlet resolvent and smooth zero-boundary test density
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let `Omega` be a bounded `C∞` domain in `R3`, in the graph sense of `def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts`; connectedness is unnecessary. Write `H^m(Omega)=W^{m,2}(Omega;R)` with the multi-index integral norm and `H0^1(Omega)` for the `H1` closure of `Cc∞(Omega)`. For every real `f in L2(Omega)` there is a unique `u in H0^1(Omega) ∩ H2(Omega)` satisfying

$$\int_\Omega(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+uv)=\int_\Omega fv\quad(v\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

It satisfies `(1−Delta)u=f` distributionally and almost everywhere as an `L2` identity, and

$$\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad \|u\|_{H^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$

Moreover `D={phi in C∞(closure Omega): phi|boundary Omega=0}` is dense in `H2(Omega) ∩ H0^1(Omega)` in the `H2` norm: every such `w` has `phi_j in D` with `phi_j→w` in `H2`. Here smoothness on the closure means restriction of a smooth function in a neighbourhood of the closure, equivalently the smooth chart representatives used below. In particular, `grad phi_j→grad w` in the graph norm of `H(curl) ∩ H(div)`, with zero curl and `div grad w=Delta w`; every `grad phi_j` is smooth and PEC since its tangential derivatives vanish at the boundary. For precision, let `X_Omega` be the graph-norm closure of smooth vector fields on a neighbourhood of the closure with `nu cross v=0` on the boundary, where `nu` is the outward Euclidean unit normal. The ambient graph space consists of real `L2` vector fields whose distributional `div v=sum_i partial_i v_i` and `curl v=(partial_2 v_3-partial_3 v_2, partial_3 v_1-partial_1 v_3, partial_1 v_2-partial_2 v_1)` lie in `L2`; its norm squared is `||v||2^2+||curl v||2^2+||div v||2^2`. Thus `grad w` belongs to this explicitly defined `X_Omega`, the same completion used by the later cavity item. No equality with every maximal trace realisation is asserted.

No smoothness of `f`, no classical boundary value for general `u`, and no general nonsmooth-domain, Neumann, interface, or variable-coefficient claim is included. Zero boundary condition means membership in `H0^1`; the published trace theorem identifies its trace as zero.
items.strategy:
1. **Variational existence and its sharp H1 bound.** B1 supplies completeness and the Hilbert structure of `H0^1`. Equip it with the full quadratic `H1` norm and set `a(w,v)=integral(grad w·grad v+wv)`. Cauchy–Schwarz on the four-component `L2` tuple makes this a bounded symmetric form, and `a(v,v)=||v||H1²`, so the coercivity constant is exactly one. The functional `ell(v)=integral fv` has norm at most `||f||2` because `||v||2≤||v||H1`. Apply B2's explicit minimizing-sequence solver, with its declared Countable Choice covered by AC, to obtain the unique weak `H0^1` solution and `||u||H1≤||f||2`. Testing against compactly supported smooth functions gives the distributional equation. No Lax–Milgram result or unproved minimizer theorem is substituted. None of B1's numerical Poincaré constants is used.

2. **Charts and admissible tangential tests.** Cover the compact closure by finitely many interior patches and smooth graph patches. Shrink each patch twice, with compact support away from its artificial sides, and choose cutoffs equal to one on the inner patches. A graph flattening followed, if needed, by reversal of the last coordinate sends the domain side to `t>0`; smooth charts and inverse bounds through order two give bounded local `H1` and `H2` changes of variables. With `y=Phi(x)`, `J=|det D(Phi^{-1})|`, `U=u∘Phi^{-1}`, the local weak equation is

$$\int A_{ij}\partial_jU\partial_iV+cUV=\int FV,\qquad A=J(D\Phi)(D\Phi)^{\mathsf T},\quad c=J,\quad F=J(f\circ\Phi^{-1}).$$

All coefficients and first derivatives are bounded on the chosen patch, `A` is symmetric and uniformly positive, and `||F||2≤C||f||2` locally. The change-of-variables formula and weak chain rule justify these identities. A localized flattened `U` lies in `H0^1` of the half-space: take the sequence of `Cc∞(Omega)` functions defining the original `H0^1` membership, multiply by the patch cutoff, and pull back. These are smooth compactly supported functions on the open half-space and converge in `H1`; their supports need not have a uniform distance from its boundary. Hence tangential translations and smooth cutoffs preserve this closure. For `k=1,2`, `w_h=delta_h^k U` and `V=−delta_{−h}^k(eta² w_h)` are admissible tests, pulled back and extended by zero outside the chart. Use a larger preliminary localization equal to one on the quotient neighbourhood, so its cutoff never changes the original equation on the test support. Interior patches allow all three quotient directions. No normal quotient crosses the boundary.

3. **The L2-data estimate, with no differentiated datum.** Put `S=F−cU`, only in `L2`. Discrete integration by parts and the quotient product rule give the principal term

$$\int\eta^2 A_{ij}(y+he_k)\partial_jw_h\partial_iw_h\ge\alpha\|\eta\nabla w_h\|_2^2.$$

The exact remaining principal terms are `integral eta²(delta_h Aij)∂jU ∂iw_h` and `integral [Aij(y+h)∂jw_h+(delta_h Aij)∂jU](∂i eta²) w_h`. Thus their absolute sum is at most

$$C\bigl(\|U\|_{H^1}+\|w_h\|_2\bigr)\|\eta\nabla w_h\|_2+C\|U\|_{H^1}\|w_h\|_2.$$

Here `||delta_h A||infinity≤||∂k A||infinity`, and the published directional increment estimate yields `||w_h||2≤C||U||H1` on the required enlarged quotient neighbourhood. The undifferentiated right side obeys

$$\left|\int S\,\delta_{-h}^k(\eta^2w_h)\right|\le C\|S\|_2\bigl(\|\eta\nabla w_h\|_2+\|w_h\|_2\bigr),$$

because the same increment bound applies to `eta²w_h` in that direction. Cauchy–Schwarz and Young's inequality absorb half the principal gradient square and give, uniformly for all sufficiently small nonzero `h`,

$$\|\eta\nabla\delta_h^kU\|_2\le C(\|F\|_2+\|U\|_{H^1}).$$

This estimates the actual `L2` datum, not its difference quotient; no `delta_h F` or derivative of `f` is present. The published tangential-test lemma supplies the exact commutator identity, but this explicit estimate is still part of the new proof.

4. **Weak mixed derivatives and corrected normal recovery.** On a smaller patch where `eta=1`, for every compactly supported smooth test `psi`, discrete integration by parts gives `integral delta_h^k(∂jU) psi = −integral ∂jU delta_{−h}^k psi`, whose limit is `−integral ∂jU ∂k psi`. The uniform bound in step 3 makes this distribution a bounded functional in the `L2` norm on tests. Extend it continuously to the closed `L2` subspace generated by those tests, which is Hilbert by `L2` completeness; Riesz gives an `L2` representing function with the same bound. This represents `∂k∂j U` distributionally. No weakly convergent subsequence, reflexivity theorem, or asserted density of tests in the whole `L2` space is required. Thus boundary patches have every second derivative with at least one tangential index; weak derivatives commute by testing smooth functions. The divergence-form equation gives the missing normal derivative with the signs

$$A_{33}\partial_{33}U=cU-F-\sum_{(i,j)\ne(3,3)}A_{ij}\partial_{ij}U-\sum_{i,j}(\partial_iA_{ij})\partial_jU.$$

Every term on the right is in `L2` and `A33≥alpha>0`, so division yields `∂33U in L2` and its bound. This follows distributionally before making the almost-everywhere identification. Interior patches already have all second derivatives. Return through the bounded `H2` chart maps, sum the finitely many inner-patch estimates, and obtain `||u||H2≤C(||f||2+||u||H1)≤C_Omega||f||2`. The equation now holds in `L2`. Uniqueness in `H0^1∩H2` is already uniqueness in the larger variational space.

5. **Zero-trace H2 density: prerequisites and flat gluing.** This step applies to every `w in H2∩H0^1`, not just the resolvent. Use a finite smooth ambient partition with one interior part and boundary parts compactly contained in graph charts. Multiplication and flattening preserve `H2`; a boundary part gives a compactly supported `W in H2(H)` with flat trace zero by chart compatibility and bounded trace continuity (or by the `H0^1` approximating sequence from step 2). Its support is separated from the chart's artificial edges. To justify the reflection, first obtain unrestricted smooth `H2` approximants of `W` on the half-space from the published `k=2,p=2` half-space extension, multiplication by a fixed compact cutoff equal to one on its support, and whole-space mollification. They converge in `H2`, so traces of the functions and their first derivatives converge in `L2` by the published `H1` flat trace bound. For any `zeta in Cc∞(R2)` and tangential `k`, their classical boundary integration by parts gives `integral T(∂kW) zeta = −integral TW ∂k zeta = 0`. Hence `T(∂kW)=0` as a distribution and almost everywhere; uniqueness of regular distributions follows directly from mollification/test pairings. This proves the needed tangential trace identity, rather than assuming it.

Define the odd reflection `W_o(y,t)=W(y,t)` for `t>0`, `−W(y,−t)` for `t<0`. A piecewise `H1` function whose two traces agree is globally `H1`: prove this by testing each half against a compact smooth ambient test, using smooth half-space approximation, one-variable integration and Fubini; the sole interface contribution is the difference of its two traces and hence cancels. Apply this gluing calculation first to `W_o` (both traces zero), then to its first derivatives. The tangential derivatives are odd reflections of `∂kW`, with both traces zero by the preceding argument. The normal derivative is the even reflection of `∂tW`, with identical traces on both sides; its trace need not vanish. Thus `W_o in H2(R3)`, and each derivative has the indicated reflected `L2` class; its `H2` norm is `sqrt(2)||W||H2`. No delta layer occurs. Even reflection of `W`, or zero extension in `H2`, would generally fail and is not used.

6. **Mollification, localization, and the actual cavity norm.** Choose a real compactly supported mass-one mollifier invariant under `t→−t`, for example a radial one, and convolve `W_o`. The mollifications converge in `H2(R3)` because weak derivatives commute with convolution and the `L2` approximate identity converges for each of the finitely many derivatives. They remain odd, so vanish exactly at `t=0`. Multiply by a fixed smooth cutoff in the flattened ambient chart equal to one near the support of `W_o`, with support separated from the artificial edges. This preserves boundary vanishing and convergence. For all sufficiently small radii the cutoff may also be chosen even in `t`, although only zero values at `t=0` are needed after multiplication. Pull back through the smooth chart and extend by zero outside its artificial support to get globally smooth functions on a neighbourhood of the closure with zero physical boundary value. Approximate the interior part by compactly supported smooth functions using legitimate compact-support zero extension and mollification, with radii smaller than its distance from the physical boundary. Add the finitely many parts, choosing radii tending to zero (AC covers sequence choices), to obtain `phi_j→w` in `H2` with `phi_j|boundary=0`. Each lies in `H0^1` by the published zero-trace kernel theorem. Finally `curl grad phi_j=0`, `div grad phi_j=Delta phi_j`, and `n×grad phi_j=0`, the last identity following by differentiating the identically zero smooth boundary restriction. Therefore

$$\|\nabla\phi_j-\nabla w\|_2+\|\operatorname{curl}(\nabla\phi_j-\nabla w)\|_2+\|\operatorname{div}(\nabla\phi_j-\nabla w)\|_2\longrightarrow0.$$

The curls vanish distributionally by commutation of weak derivatives, which is a direct test-function calculation. This is exactly convergence in G3's graph norm, giving `grad w in X` without a maximal-trace-density assumption.

items.title: Dispersion relations for a finitely subtracted analytic response
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$ be an integer, let $\omega_0\in\mathbb R$, and let $\chi$ be holomorphic on the upper half-plane and continuous on its closure, of class $C^1$ on its real boundary away from $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$ in $\mathbb C$, and satisfying $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ outside a compact set ([[def-complex-domain]]). Let $P(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)(z-\omega_0)^j/j!$ be the Taylor polynomial at $\omega_0$ and $f(z)=[\chi(z)-P(z)]/(z-\omega_0)^n$, with the removable value at $\omega_0$. Assume the boundary restriction of $f$ is class $C^1$ (the local holomorphy supplies this at $\omega_0$). Then for real $\omega$,

$$\operatorname{Re}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Re}P(\omega)+\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi,$$

$$\operatorname{Im}\chi(\omega)=\operatorname{Im}P(\omega)-\frac{(\omega-\omega_0)^n}{\pi}\operatorname{PV}\!\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\operatorname{Re}f(\xi)}{\xi-\omega}\,d\xi.$$

At $\omega=\omega_0$ the formula is read as the stated Taylor value. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is also valid with $P=0$, $f=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and the factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ for all $\omega$; at $\omega_0$ use the same principal-value formula rather than a Taylor-value convention. For the separate constitutive polynomial branch assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]), fix integers $d\ge1$, $m\ge0$, let $A_0,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ (real scalars when $d=1$), and let $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ satisfy all hypotheses of [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]]. On histories $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^d$ of class $C^m$ with $E^{(j)}$ bounded for $0\le j\le m$, the response $\sum_{j=0}^mA_jE^{(j)}+K*E$ is causal, and its transfer function in the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z):=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared polynomial $Q$ leaves the proved entrywise dispersion formulas for $\chi_K$; this branch does not require holomorphic continuation through a real subtraction point. The Taylor-subtracted formulas above apply to the total response when its additional local-holomorphy, growth and boundary hypotheses are satisfied; $Q$ need not equal its Taylor polynomial $P$. General passivity and storage remain separate model conditions.
items.strategy:
[[thm-taylor-expansion-holomorphic-function]] on a complex neighborhood of $\omega_0$ shows that $\chi-P$ has a zero of order at least $n$, so division gives the holomorphic removable continuation of $f$ there. Elsewhere in $H$ its denominator is nonzero. Continuity of $\chi$ on $\overline H$ and the removable continuation make $f$ continuous on $\overline H$; its real restriction is $C^1$ by hypothesis. The growth bound on $\chi$ and the degree of $P$ give $f(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly in $\overline H$ at infinity. For completeness the boundary contour step is valid for any scalar $f$ holomorphic on $H:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>0\}$, continuous on $\overline H$, with $C^1$ real boundary restriction and $f(z)=O(1/|z|)$ uniformly on $\overline H$ at infinity. Fix $\omega\in\mathbb R$, $R>|\omega|+2$ and $0<\eta<1$. Use the real intervals from $\omega-R$ to $\omega-\eta$ and $\omega+\eta$ to $\omega+R$, a clockwise upper semicircle of radius $\eta$ about $\omega$, and the counterclockwise large upper semicircle of radius $R$ about $\omega$. For $\delta>0$ apply [[cor-cauchy-theorem-for-null-homotopic-loops]] to $f(z+i\delta)/(z-\omega)$ on $D_\delta:=\{\operatorname{Im}z>-\delta/2\}\setminus\{\omega-iv:v\ge0\}$. This open domain is star-shaped about any point $\omega+iA$, $A>0$, so the contour is null-homotopic there and the integrand is holomorphic. All contour pieces lie in $D_\delta$; no analytic extension of $f$ across the real boundary is assumed. On each fixed contour, continuity on a compact closed-half-plane neighborhood gives $f(z+i\delta)\to f(z)$ uniformly as $\delta\downarrow0$ by [[thm-heine-cantor-metric]], and [[thm-uniform-limit-interchanges-complex-line-integrals]] transfers the zero contour identity to $f(z)/(z-\omega)$. The large arc has $|z-\omega|=R$, $|z|\ge R-|\omega|$ and length $\pi R$, hence its contribution is $O(1/R)$. Parametrizing the clockwise small arc by $z=\omega+\eta e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta$ decreasing from $\pi$ to $0$ gives $-i\pi f(\omega)+o(1)$. Locally the divided difference $[f(\xi)-f(\omega)]/(\xi-\omega)$ is bounded because the boundary is $C^1$; the constant term cancels under the symmetric indentation. The tails are absolutely integrable by $f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)=O(|\xi|^{-2})$. First $\eta\downarrow0$, then $R\to\infty$ therefore gives $\operatorname{PV}\int_{\mathbb R}f(\xi)/(\xi-\omega)d\xi=i\pi f(\omega)$ and the two real/imaginary formulas. Apply that boundary-contour argument to $f$, multiply both formulas by the real factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^n$, and add the complex polynomial $P$. At $\omega_0$ the factor vanishes and the removable Taylor identity gives the asserted Taylor value. The imaginary numerator subtracts the full complex $P$; it cannot be omitted.
For the distinct constitutive branch, multiplication by $(-i\omega)^j$ is the derivative multiplier on the stipulated monochromatic histories, so the transfer polynomial is exactly $Q$. Derivatives at a time are determined by a history agreeing on its whole past, including its endpoint, and the convolution is causal; hence their finite sum is causal on histories with the stated bounded continuous derivatives. The residual $\chi-Q=\chi_K$ satisfies [[lem-em-integrable-causal-dispersion]] entrywise. Without that lemma's AC and integrability conditions a merely integrable causal kernel still gives a bounded upper-half-plane holomorphic response, but does not automatically supply these principal values or Taylor continuation. The stated additional analytic assumptions, not causality alone, govern the Taylor branch.

items.title: Weak Dirichlet existence for a prescribed lift and uniformly elliptic coefficient
items.statement:
Let $\Omega\subseteq(-L,L)^3$ be bounded and open, let $\varepsilon$ be a measurable symmetric real $3	imes3$ matrix field on $\Omega$ with $\alpha|\xi|^2\le\xi\cdot\varepsilon(x)\xi\le eta|\xi|^2$ for a.e. $x$ and all $\xi\in\mathbb R^3$, $0<\alpha\le eta<\infty$, let $G\in H^1(\Omega)$ be a specified lift, and let $F\in(H_0^1(\Omega))^*$ be bounded. Then there is exactly one $u\in G+H_0^1(\Omega)$ with $$\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla u=F(v)\qquad	ext{for every }v\in H_0^1(\Omega),$$ where $H_0^1=W_0^{1,2}$ carries the gradient norm. For $F(v)=\int_\Omegaho v$ with $ho\in L^2(\Omega)$ this is the weak Poisson solution $-\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon
abla u)=ho$, with the homogeneous boundary datum represented by membership of $H_0^1$ rather than by an unproved classical trace. No boundary datum outside the specified lift class is assumed attainable; classical boundary regularity, general Neumann lifts and transmission regularity remain later obligations.
items.strategy:
On $H_0^1$ the gradient norm is equivalent to the full $H^1$ norm and $H_0^1$ is complete ([[lem-em-zero-boundary-coercivity]]). Put $a(w,v)=\int_\Omega
abla v\cdot\varepsilon
abla w$ and $\ell(v)=F(v)-a(G,v)$ for $v,w\in H_0^1$. The coefficient bounds and Cauchy-Schwarz ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) make $a$ a bounded symmetric bilinear form with $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|
abla v\|_2^2$, and $\ell$ is bounded because $F$ is bounded and $a(G,\cdot)$ is controlled by $ eta\|
abla G\|_2\|
abla\cdot\|_2$. The symmetric coercive variational solver ([[lem-em-symmetric-coercive-variational-solver]]) gives a unique $w$ with $a(w,v)=\ell(v)$ for all $v$, and $u=G+w$ solves the stated problem; testing with compactly supported smooth $v$ gives the distributional equation by the weak first-derivative identity. For $F(v)=\intho v$ with $ho\in L^2$, the bound $|F(v)|\le\|ho\|_2\|v\|_2\le2L\|ho\|_2\|
abla v\|_2$ ([[lem-em-zero-boundary-coercivity]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) makes $F$ bounded, so the existence conclusion applies. Across finitely many material interfaces the weak equation encodes flux continuity where one-sided classical traces exist, by integration by parts on each side.

items.title: Magnetic dipole expansion with an explicit uniform remainder
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu_0>0$ be any scalar parameter and let $J\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$ and $\operatorname{supp}J\subset B_a(0)$, $a>0$, and put $m=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Then for $r=|x|\ge2a$ the vector potential and magnetic field $$A(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad B=\operatorname{curl}A,$$ satisfy, uniformly in $n=x/r$, $$A=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m\times x}{r^3}+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1}{r^3}\Bigr),\qquad B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3n(m\cdot n)-m}{r^3}+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1}{r^4}\Bigr).$$ The constants in the $O$ terms are absolute (the second follows by differentiating the first, not by differentiating an unspecified remainder), and $\|J\|_1=\int|J|$.
items.strategy: Integrating $\operatorname{div}(y_iJ)=J_i$ over $\mathbb R^3$ and using the vanishing of the integral of a divergence of a compactly supported $C^1$ field ([[lem-integral-of-a-divergence-of-an-l-one-c-one-field-vanishes]]) gives $\int J_i=0$; integrating $\operatorname{div}(y_iy_jJ)=y_jJ_i+y_iJ_j$ gives antisymmetry of $M_{ij}=\int y_jJ_i$, and with the definition of $m$ one has $M_{ij}=-\varepsilon_{ijk}m_k$ and hence $Mx=m\times x$. Writing $|x-y|^{-1}=r^{-1}+(x\cdot y)/r^3+\text{remainder}$ with the following explicit twice-FTC integral identity (not by interpreting a Peano remainder quantitatively): for $h(t)=|x-ty|^{-1}$, [[thm-ftc-second-part]] twice gives $h(1)=h(0)+h'(0)+\int_0^1(1-t)h''(t)dt$, the integral remainder is $\int_0^1(1-s)y_jy_k\,\partial_j\partial_k|x-sy|^{-1}ds$, whose Hessian is $O(r^{-3})$ and whose spatial derivative is $O(r^{-4})$ with absolute constants because $|x-sy|\ge r/2$ on the support; the modulus-of-integral bound ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) against $J$ gives the $A$ estimate and its differentiated estimate. Finally the curl computation $\operatorname{curl}(m\times x/r^3)=3x(m\cdot x)/r^5-m/r^3$ follows by component differentiation of the cross product ([[lem-the-divergence-and-curl-of-a-cross-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), the first term being the Coulomb-dipole expression of the cited remainder lemma ([[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]]). All current moment cancellations invoke [[lem-integral-of-a-divergence-of-an-l-one-c-one-field-vanishes]] with compact smooth fields $y_iJ$ and $y_iy_jJ$, whose fields and divergences are integrable; Countable Choice is inherited by that supplier and the Lebesgue measure interfaces. For the differentiated remainder, $D_x^\alpha D^2|x-ty|^{-1}$ for $|\alpha|\le1$ is bounded by an absolute constant times $r^{-3-|\alpha|}$ uniformly in $t\in[0,1]$, $|y|\le a$ and $r\ge2a$ because $|x-ty|\ge r/2$. On a small x-neighbourhood retain a positive lower bound and differentiate this explicit compact-t integral by uniformly bounded difference quotients; the compact y-integral then has integrable majorant $C|y|^2|J(y)|r^{-4}$. This proves the differentiated field remainder independently of any unspecified O term.

items.title: Outgoing source Helmholtz field: fundamental solution, Fraunhofer and Fresnel error terms
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. For $k>0$ define $G_k(x)=e^{ik|x|}/(4\pi|x|)$ off the origin, a locally integrable complex function. Then

$$(-\Delta-k^2)G_k=\delta_0$$

distributionally: for every $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, $T_{G_k}(\psi)=\int G_k\psi$, $\delta_0(\psi)=\psi(0)$, and $\langle\partial_iT,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_i\psi\rangle$ ([[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); thus the displayed identity means $\int G_k(-\Delta-k^2)\psi=\psi(0)$. For $a>0$ and a finite complex measure $\alpha$ supported in the closed ball $\overline{B_a(0)}$, the field $u=G_k*\alpha$ is smooth outside the support, solves $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ there and is outgoing: for $x=rn$, $r\ge2a$,

$$u(rn)=\frac{e^{ikr}}{4\pi r}\int e^{-ikn\cdot y}\,d\alpha(y)+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}}{r}\Bigl[\frac{a}{r}+\frac{ka^2}{r}\Bigr]\Bigr)$$

uniformly in direction, and $r(\partial_ru-iku)=O(r^{-1})$ uniformly. For a planar aperture $y=(y_1,y_2,0)$ with observation $x=(\xi_1,\xi_2,z)$, $z>0$, $|\xi|\le b$, $0\le b$ and $(a+b)/z<1$, the Fresnel approximation replaces $R=|x-y|$ by $z+|\xi-y|^2/(2z)$ and $1/R$ by $1/z$ with phase error $O(k(a+b)^4/z^3)$ and relative amplitude error $O((a+b)^2/z^2)$, hence absolute field error $O(\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}z^{-1}[(a+b)^2/z^2+k(a+b)^4/z^3])$. Aperture data are an explicitly specified scalar source, not asserted to be the unknown exact Maxwell boundary traces, and no uniqueness or existence for arbitrary obstacle boundary data is claimed.
items.strategy: For radial $f(r)$ one has $\Delta f=f''+2f'/r$ by direct coordinate differentiation of $\partial_ir=x_i/r$ ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]), and inserting $f=G_k$ gives $(\Delta+k^2)f=0$ for $r>0$. For the distributional identity excise a ball $B_\delta$ inside a compact test integration; the second Green identity ([[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]) on the excised domain cancels the $k^2$ terms and leaves the inner flux, where $G_k=1/(4\pi\delta)+O(1)$ and $\partial_rG_k=-1/(4\pi\delta^2)+O(1)$: the derivative-test boundary term is $O(\delta)$ and the leading unit flux multiplies $\psi(0)$, while the local $k^2G_k$ integral is $O(\delta^2)$; the limit is $\delta_0$ with the displayed sign. Off-support smoothness and all derivatives follow from the positive separation of compact observation and source sets, with differentiation under the source integral. For the Fraunhofer error write $R=|rn-y|$ and use the norm expansion of the cited dipole-remainder technique ([[lem-em-coulomb-dipole-remainder]]): $|R-r+n\cdot y|\le Ca^2/r$ and $|r/R-1|\le Ca/r$; the exponential difference is bounded by $C r^{-1}(a/r+ka^2/r)$ via $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$, and integrating against the total variation of $\alpha$ with the integral triangle inequality ([[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]]) gives the displayed error; the outgoing relation follows from $\partial_rR=1+O(a^2/r^2)$ and $R^{-2}=O(r^{-2})$. The Fresnel estimate is the Taylor expansion of the norm with explicit remainder on the compact small-$s$ region $s=|\xi-y|^2/z^2$, using $|e^{i\theta}-1|\le|\theta|$. Countable Choice is inherited by the actually used Green, surface/regular-distribution and/or harmonic-boundary supplier interfaces. The supplier updates do not alter the local source, trace or modal class used here. To make the cited norm-remainder TECHNIQUE an actual calculation, for h(s)=|x-sy| one has $h'(0)=-n\cdot y$ and $h''(s)=|y|^2/|x-sy|-((x-sy)\cdot y)^2/|x-sy|^3$, whose modulus is at most $2a^2/(r-a)$ when |y|<=a and r>=2a. The finite Riemann FTC remainder therefore gives |R-r+n dot y|<=Ca²/r; the same lower bound yields |r/R-1|<=Ca/r. Thus this is proved directly, not falsely deduced from a supplier statement about the inverse kernel integral. For integration against a finite COMPLEX measure alpha, the estimate |integral h d alpha|<=sup|h| times ||alpha||TV follows first for finite simple functions from the defining total variation, then for bounded continuous kernels by uniform finite-simple approximation of their range. Every off-support parameter derivative is continuous and uniformly bounded on compact observation/source products, so uniform difference quotients through this finite-measure bound prove all derivatives without an unprovided complex-measure dominated-convergence premise. Finally $\partial_r R=1+O(a²/r²)$ in the explicit radial derivative formula gives the claimed outgoing O(r^-1) estimate after multiplication by r. For the Fresnel remainder, write s=|xi-y|²/z²; on any prescribed small-angle range (a+b)/z<=eta0<1, twice-FTC gives |sqrt(1+s)-1-s/2|<=s²/8 and |(1+s)^(-1/2)-1|<=s/2. Combined with |exp(i theta)-1|<=|theta| these yield exactly the original phase, relative amplitude and absolute field error bounds, uniformly on that declared range. The finite-total-variation branch and every original exterior/approximation claim are retained.

items.title: Spherical harmonics: orthogonal decomposition, complete basis and addition theorem
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $P_l$ denote the real vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $l$ on $\mathbb R^3$, $H_l=\ker(\Delta:P_l\to P_{l-2})$ with $P_k=\{0\}$ for $k<0$, and let spherical harmonics of degree $l$ be the restrictions of $H_l$ to $S^2$, with unnormalised surface measure $d\Omega$ of total mass $4\pi$. Then $P_l=H_l\oplus|x|^2P_{l-2}$, $\dim H_l=2l+1$, harmonics of distinct degree are orthogonal in $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$, and the union over $l$ of the spaces of spherical harmonics admits a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). For any real orthonormal basis $Y_{lm}$, $m=1,\dots,2l+1$, of degree-$l$ harmonics the addition theorem holds: $$\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}Y_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')=\frac{2l+1}{4\pi}P_l(n\cdot n'),$$ where $P_l$ is the Legendre polynomial of the convergent zonal kernel lemma ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]). The Laplacian is the Euclidean one ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]). This supplies the harmonic decomposition, orthogonality, completeness and exact addition kernel; it does not assert higher boundary regularity. The purely polynomial decomposition and finite dimension identities use no Choice; the surface/L2/completeness claims retain the stated Countable Choice.
items.strategy: For homogeneous $Q$ of degree $l-2j$, Euler's identity $x\cdot\nabla Q=(l-2j)Q$ gives $\Delta(r^{2j}Q)=2j(2l-2j+1)r^{2j-2}Q+r^{2j}\Delta Q$; the ansatz $H=\sum_ja_jr^{2j}\Delta^jP$ with $a_0=1$ and $a_j=-a_{j-1}/[2j(2l-2j+1)]$ cancels consecutive coefficients in $\Delta H$, and the final $\Delta^{\lfloor l/2\rfloor+1}P$ vanishes by degree, so $H$ is harmonic and $P-H$ is divisible by $r^2$; recursion gives the decomposition. For homogeneous harmonic $H_l,H_m$ the Green identity on the ball ([[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]) gives $0=\int_{S^2}(H_l\partial_nH_m-H_m\partial_nH_l)=(m-l)\int_{S^2}H_lH_m$, whence orthogonality of distinct degrees; if a harmonic of degree $l$ equalled $r^2Q$, its orthogonality to all lower-degree harmonics would force $\int_{S^2}H_l^2=0$, so $H_l=0$; the monomial count $\dim P_l=(l+1)(l+2)/2$ gives $\dim H_l=2l+1$, and restriction is injective by the same homogeneity argument. For density, continuous functions are dense in $L^2(S^2)$ by a finite smooth graph atlas with subordinate smooth cutoffs, pulling each localised function back, mollifying and using the $L^2$ translation and approximate-identity interfaces ([[lem-complex-translation-and-approximate-identity-interfaces]]); the restricted real polynomial algebra is unital and separates points, so Stone-Weierstrass ([[thm-real-stone-weierstrass-general]]) makes it uniformly dense in $C(S^2)$, and the homogeneous-degree decomposition puts every restriction in the finite span of spherical harmonics, giving $L^2$ density. Finite Gram-Schmidt ([[thm-gram-schmidt-orthonormalisation]]) applied to a fixed ordered monomial elimination basis of each $H_l$ produces the orthonormal bases without an undefined basis selection. For the addition theorem, $K_l(n,n')=\sum_mY_{lm}(n)Y_{lm}(n')$ is independent of the orthonormal basis and rotation-invariant, and for fixed $n'$ it is the unique (up to scale) rotation-invariant homogeneous harmonic polynomial of degree $l$, which is the coefficient $|y|^lP_l(n'\cdot y/|y|)$ of the convergent kernel of the zonal lemma ([[lem-em-convergent-legendre-kernel]]); evaluating the diagonal by integrating $K_l(n,n)$ gives $(2l+1)/(4\pi)$, completing the addition theorem. Countable Choice is inherited from the exact Statements of the Green/surface and Euclidean L2 approximate-identity interfaces. The fixed ordered finite monomial elimination lists and finite Gram–Schmidt provide one explicit basis in each degree, with no arbitrary basis choice or Dependent Choice. The solid zonal coefficient is harmonic by the finite t-derivative argument in the corrected kernel supplier. No unproved Cauchy bound is used. For the finite zonal uniqueness step rotate the pole to e3. An invariant homogeneous polynomial has the form $\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor l/2\rfloor}b_j z^{l-2j}(x^2+y^2)^j$: writing planar coordinates as x+iy and x-iy, rotation multiplies their monomial with exponents a,b by exp(i(a-b)theta); invariance for every theta forces a=b, by finite Fourier orthogonality on [0,2pi]. Harmonicity gives the explicit recurrence $4(j+1)^2b_{j+1}=-(l-2j)(l-2j-1)b_j$. Thus all coefficients are determined by b0, and the zonal harmonic space is one-dimensional. The generating solid coefficient has b0=P_l(1)=1, so it supplies the nonzero normalized generator. Rotation invariance of sphere measure is exactly [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], under AComega. Hence the addition argument invokes no undeclared zonal uniqueness theorem.

references.title: Sheldon Axler, Paul Bourdon, Wade Ramey, Harmonic Function Theory, 2nd edition, author-hosted full text
references.locator: Full260-page author PDF retrieved and relevant Chapter5 sections inspected: printed78-82 (orthogonal spherical decomposition),94-100 (zonal harmonic projection/addition/Poisson expansion). The source uses unit-mass sphere measure; formulas here adapt to mass4pi. The every-derivative harmonic-tail argument and exact library Choice bookkeeping are explicitly supplied locally, not claimed as a verbatim source theorem.

items.title: The spherical mean identity behind the wave equation
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]), carried by the cited sphere, parameter, polar and divergence suppliers. Let $c>0$, let $f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ (unbounded $f$ is allowed), and define the spherical mean

$$M_rf(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{S^2}f(x+rn)\,d\Omega(n),\qquad r\ge0,$$

with the outward sphere measure of total area $4\pi$ ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]). Then $r\mapsto M_rf(x)$ is smooth for $r\ge0$ and satisfies the Euler-Poisson-Darboux identity

$$\partial_r^2M_rf(x)+\frac2r\partial_rM_rf(x)=\Delta M_rf(x)\qquad(r>0),$$

and the function $H_f(x,t)=t\,M_{ct}f(x)$, $t\ge0$, satisfies

$$\partial_t^2H_f=c^2\Delta H_f,\qquad H_f(x,0)=0,\qquad\partial_tH_f(x,0)=f(x).$$

All identities are local and need no decay of $f$, since every integration set is compact. This is the pure spherical-mean identity; it makes no claim about finite-domain boundary data or about general rough data.
items.strategy:
Differentiating the compact sphere integral in the parameter $r$ is justified by the parameter-integral lemma ([[lem-em-parameter-integrals]], including its surface-measure form). One gets $\partial_rM_rf(x)=(4\pi)^{-1}\int_{S^2}n\cdot
abla f(x+rn)\,d\Omega$, and the divergence theorem on $B_r(x)$ ([[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], applied to the $C^1$ field $
abla f$ and using the Euclidean Laplacian, [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]) gives $4\pi r^2\partial_rM_rf(x)=\int_{B_r(x)}\Delta f(y)\,dy$. Differentiating this last integral in $r$ (radial derivative of a ball integral; one-variable fundamental theorem, [[thm-ftc-first-part]]) gives $\partial_r(r^2\partial_rM_rf)=r^2M_r(\Delta f)=r^2\Delta M_rf$, where the second equality uses linearity and the parameter statement to move $\Delta$ through the mean; dividing by $r^2$ gives the Euler-Poisson-Darboux identity. Twice differentiating $H_f(x,t)=tM_{ct}f(x)$ with the algebra of derivatives and the chain rule factor $c$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives $\partial_t^2H_f=2c\partial_rM+c^2t\partial_r^2M=c^2t\Delta M=c^2\Delta H_f$ for $t>0$, using the identity just proved; at $t=0$ one has $M_0f=f$ and $\partial_rM_0f=(4\pi)^{-1}
abla f\cdot\int_{S^2}n\,d\Omega=0$ by reflection symmetry, so $H_f(x,0)=0$ and $\partial_tH_f(x,0)=f(x)$; the defining compact integral is smooth in signed $r$ as well, so the equation extends to $t=0$.

items.title: Ball Poisson series: interior convergence, boundary data and the Poisson kernel
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $f\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega)$ with harmonic coefficients $f_{lm}$ in an orthonormal basis of the spherical-harmonic lemma ([[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]]), and for $0\le r<1$ set $u(rn)=\sum_{l,m}r^lf_{lm}Y_{lm}(n)$ (the $l=0$ term being the constant value at $r=0$). Then the series and all its derivatives converge uniformly on every closed smaller ball, $u$ is harmonic there ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]), $u(r\,\cdot)\to f$ in $L^2(S^2)$ as $r\uparrow1$, and $u$ is the unique harmonic function on the unit ball with $\sup_{r<1}\|u(r\,\cdot)\|_{L^2}<\infty$ and $L^2$ boundary limit $f$. For continuous $f$ the same function is $$u(rn)=\int_{S^2}\frac{1-r^2}{4\pi|rn-n'|^3}f(n')\,d\Omega(n'),$$ it extends continuously to the closed ball with boundary value $f$, and the kernel is positive of total mass one. This is the stated ball boundary branch; generic smooth-domain classical regularity remains a separate obligation.
items.strategy:
Fix the canonical real spherical-harmonic basis of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]]. Its complete orthonormality gives norm convergence and Parseval directly: the finite orthogonal projection S_N has ||f-S_N||2 no larger than ||f-v||2 for every finite-span v in its subspace, by finite Pythagoras; density therefore makes this error vanish. No arbitrary sequence of approximants is selected. The addition identity gives sum_m|Y_lm(n)|²=(2l+1)/(4pi). Finite and then countable Cauchy-Schwarz gives the absolute series tail bound $\|f\|_2[\sum_{l>N}r_0^{2l}(2l+1)/(4\pi)]^{1/2}$ on r<=r0<1. The terms r^lY_lm are actual homogeneous harmonic polynomials, including their smooth values at0. On a smaller ball use harmonic partial-sum differences on fixed-radius balls inside an intermediate smaller ball; the exact [[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]] converts the uniform tail bound into a uniform bound for every derivative. Uniform derivative limits are identified by the finite-coordinate FTC [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], yielding a smooth harmonic limit.

Orthogonality gives $\|u(r\cdot)\|_2^2=\sum_{l,m}r^{2l}|f_{lm}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$ and $\|u(r\cdot)-f\|_2^2=\sum_{l,m}(1-r^l)^2|f_{lm}|^2$. The latter tends to0 by [[thm-dominated-convergence]] on the countable coefficient index set with counting measure and summable bound4sum|f_lm|².

The corrected generating kernel and addition identity sum the Poisson series as $P_r(n,n')=(1-r²)/(4\pi|rn-n'|³)$: apply (1+2r partial_r) to the scalar generating function, justified on every r<=r0<1 by its derived power series. Positivity is explicit and integration in nprime leaves only the constant harmonic, so the total mass is1. For continuous f, integrating the uniformly convergent kernel series gives precisely u. The actual [[thm-dirichlet-problem-on-a-ball-by-the-poisson-integral]] (n3, Countable Choice) proves its continuous extension and the classical uniqueness for continuous data.

For general L2-boundary uniqueness, let v be any smooth harmonic function on the unit ball with the stated radial norm bound and L2 limit f. For0<r<s<1, apply the same published continuous Dirichlet theorem on radius-s ball to the continuous actual data v(s n). Scale x=s z and sphere surface measure by s²; the resulting unit angular Poisson kernel is P_(r/s). Expanding that kernel and using orthogonality gives $v_{lm}(r)=(r/s)^l v_{lm}(s)$. The L2 boundary limit implies $v_{lm}(s)\to f_{lm}$ by Cauchy-Schwarz as s tends1. Thus $v_{lm}(r)=r^l f_{lm}$ for every degree and every fixed r>0. Completeness gives v(r dot)=u(r dot) in L2, and continuity on that sphere makes equality pointwise; equality at0 follows by continuity. This proves the full uniqueness branch without invoking an undeclared polar-Laplacian or radial ODE theorem. Countable Choice is inherited by the actual harmonic, finite-surface and L2 approximation suppliers, with no additional Dependent Choice or full Choice use.

references.title: Sheldon Axler, Paul Bourdon, Wade Ramey, Harmonic Function Theory, 2nd edition, author-hosted full text
references.locator: Full260-page author PDF retrieved and relevant Chapter5 sections inspected: printed78-82 (orthogonal spherical decomposition),94-100 (zonal harmonic projection/addition/Poisson expansion). The source uses unit-mass sphere measure; formulas here adapt to mass4pi. The every-derivative harmonic-tail argument and exact library Choice bookkeeping are explicitly supplied locally, not claimed as a verbatim source theorem.

items.title: Exact Helmholtz boundary representation with actual traces
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded C-infinity domain of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let k>0 and x in Omega, and use the outgoing kernel $G_k$ of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]. A sufficient classical specialization is that u and f extend smoothly to an open neighbourhood of the closed domain and $(-\Delta-k^2)u=f$ there. More generally, retain the justified weaker classical-trace branch: u is C2 inside Omega, u and all first derivatives extend continuously to its closure, f=(-Delta-k²)u belongs to L1(Omega), and the equation holds inside. The boundary values and normal derivative in the formula below are these actual continuous traces. Then
$$u(x)=\int_\Omega G_k(x-y)f(y)\,dy+\int_{\partial\Omega}\bigl[G_k(x-y)\partial_nu(y)-u(y)\partial_{n_y}G_k(x-y)\bigr]dS_y,$$
with n the outward domain normal; both integrals are absolutely convergent. Merely being smooth on the OPEN domain without these trace/integrability data is insufficient.

For an exterior D=R3 minus closure of a bounded smooth obstacle, retain the exterior counterpart with actual inner boundary traces: suppose u is C2 on D with u and first derivatives continuous to its compact boundary, solves (-Delta-k²)u=f there, f is locally continuous and $\int_D|G_k(x-y)f(y)|dy$ is finite at the observation x, and the prescribed outgoing condition gives, uniformly on spheres at infinity, $u(y)=O(|y|^{-1})$ and $\partial_ru(y)-iku(y)=o(|y|^{-1})$. Then the same formula holds with volume D and its obstacle boundary, with n outward from D (pointing into the obstacle). Compactly supported L1 sources with the displayed local regularity are a sufficient source subclass. For the smooth-trace modal outgoing specialization beyond a source-containing sphere of radius $R_0>0$, retain the declared full Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for this sufficient branch. Write the smooth angular trace as $g(n)=u(R_0n)$, use the real unit-sphere harmonics of [[lem-em-spherical-harmonic-basis-and-addition]], set $c_{lm}=\int_{S^2}g(n)Y_{lm}(n)d\Omega(n)$, and define the outgoing modal class outside that sphere by
$$u(rn)=\sum_{l=0}^\infty\sum_{m=1}^{2l+1}c_{lm}\,\frac{h_l(kr)}{h_l(kR_0)}Y_{lm}(n),\qquad r\ge R_0,$$
where $h_l$ are exactly the earlier explicit functions of [[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]]. The proof below establishes smooth convergence, the homogeneous exterior equation, the actual trace g, the uniform bound $\sup_{r\ge R_0,n\in S^2}r|u(rn)|<\infty$ and the uniform Sommerfeld residual $\sup_{n\in S^2}r|\partial_ru(rn)-iku(rn)|\to0$. Thus this existing smooth modal branch satisfies the prescribed far conditions without a later same-page supplier. Its full-Choice premise is retained; the earlier prescribed-outgoing branch remains under Countable Choice.

The Green formula uses the consistent actual pair of traces. Assigning both aperture values independently does not establish an exact boundary problem; a declared scalar aperture-source model remains a separate approximation. No weak boundary trace or normal trace for arbitrary rough data is asserted by mere interior smoothness.
items.strategy:
For the closure-smooth bounded specialization, apply [[cor-second-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] on Omega with a small ball about x removed. The k² terms cancel, the outgoing kernel's unit inner flux gives u(x), and its derivative-test term is O(delta); the source integral near x is finite since f is continuous there and G_k is locally integrable. This proves the stated signs.

For the weaker C2-interior/C1-closure trace branch, let S be the compact smooth boundary with its outward normal n. The exact [[thm-euclidean-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem]] under Countable Choice gives a normal tube with positive smooth radius; compactness gives a positive minimum. For sufficiently small t>0, $S_t=\{p-t n(p):p\in S\}$ lies inside Omega and bounds the inner domain Omega_t. In the normal graph charts the surface Jacobian and outward normals converge uniformly to those on S (the differential of p to p-tn(p) tends uniformly to the tangent identity). The one-sided graph convention makes this the actual inside collar; injectivity of the tube prevents overlap. For small t, x and a fixed ball about x lie in Omega_t. On each punctured Omega_t the ordinary Green theorem applies, since u is C2 on a neighbourhood of its compact closure. First remove the x-excision radius by the same local flux argument. Then take t down0: u and its gradient converge uniformly on S_t to their continuous actual traces, while G_k and its y-gradient are bounded and smooth on this collar away from x. The boundary integrals therefore converge to exactly the displayed trace integrals using the compact surface chart formula and the uniformly converging Jacobians. For the volume term, split off a small ball about x, where f is bounded and the kernel is integrable; on its complement G_k is bounded and f is L1. This gives an absolute integrable majorant, so [[thm-dominated-convergence]] on the increasing inner domains yields the full volume integral. This proves the weaker branch completely rather than assuming unspecified traces.

For the exterior branch, truncate by B_R and use the same inner-boundary trace limit and x-excision argument, with the outward obstacle normal pointing into the obstacle. For fixed observation x, on y=Rn the explicit kernel has $G_k(x-y)=O(R^{-1})$ and $\partial_R G_k(x-y)-ikG_k(x-y)=O(R^{-2})$, uniformly in n; these follow by differentiating the norm and $\partial_R|Rn-x|=1+O(R^{-2})$. In the outer Wronskian, write $G_k(\partial_Ru-iku)-u(\partial_RG_k-ikG_k)$: its supremum is o(R^-2)+O(R^-3), so multiplying by the sphere area O(R²) makes it tend to0. Absolute convergence of the stated volume integral then permits the limit R to infinity. The smooth-trace modal outgoing subclass has the explicit earlier-supplier proof below; its existing full-Choice sufficient premise is retained. Other prescribed uniform-outgoing data use only Countable Choice through Green, tubular and surface interfaces. No independent assignment of both boundary traces or unproved rough-trace Green theorem is used. The cited Green theorem has real inputs; apply it to the four real/imaginary component pairs and combine by complex bilinearity to obtain the displayed complex kernel identity, with no conjugation introduced.

Smooth angular coefficient estimate from finite angular calculus. For smooth w on S2 let $L_jw(n)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}w(Q_j(t)n)\right|_{t=0}$, where $Q_j(t)$ is the elementary coordinate rotation about e_j, and put $\Lambda=\sum_{j=1}^3L_j^2$. Its tangent velocity is $e_j\times n$ with [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Rotation invariance of surface measure is the exact earlier [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]. Differentiate the invariant integral of w(Q_j(t)n)v(Q_j(t)n) on the compact sphere: uniform difference quotients of its smooth integrand give $\int(L_jw)v=-\int w(L_jv)$, so Lambda is symmetric under the bilinear integral; for complex data apply the same finite identity to components. No polar-operator theorem is presumed. On an ambient smooth extension, direct coordinate differentiation gives
$$\sum_jL_j^2=|x|^2\Delta-(x\cdot\nabla)^2-x\cdot\nabla.$$
Each Y_lm is the restriction of a degree-l homogeneous harmonic polynomial by the earlier H2 supplier, so Euler's identity and this finite formula give $\Lambda Y_{lm}=-l(l+1)Y_{lm}$. Therefore, for l>=1 and any integer p>=1, repeated symmetry and [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] yield
$$[l(l+1)]^p c_{lm}=\int_{S^2}(-\Lambda)^pg\,Y_{lm}\,d\Omega,\qquad |c_{lm}|\le\frac{\|\Lambda^pg\|_2}{[l(l+1)]^p}.$$
The smooth g and all these angular derivatives are bounded on the compact sphere and have finite L2 norms. Treat l0 separately as its single finite constant coefficient. The addition diagonal of H2 gives $\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty\le\sqrt{(2l+1)/(4\pi)}$. With p2, the total weighted absolute sum
$$\sum_{l,m}(l+1+2kR_0)|c_{lm}|\,\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty<\infty$$
follows: for l>=1 its degree-l bound is a fixed constant times $(2l+1)(l+1+2kR_0)\sqrt{(2l+1)/(4\pi)}[l(l+1)]^{-2}=O(l^{-3/2})$. This is the actual summability argument for every smooth trace, not an unproved claim of coefficient decay.

Exact radial majorants. From the earlier Hankel proof, $F_l(z)=z^2|h_l(z)|^2=\sum_{j=0}^la_jz^{-2j}$ has a0=1 and positive a_j, so it is nonincreasing in z>0. Consequently, for $\phi_l(r)=h_l(kr)/h_l(kR_0)$,
$$|\phi_l(r)|\le R_0/r\quad(r\ge R_0).$$
The same earlier supplier's exact t_l bounds, applied with radius r, give $|k h_l'(kr)/h_l(kr)|\le(l+1)/r+k$, hence
$$r|\phi_l'(r)-ik\phi_l(r)|\le R_0[(l+1)/r+2k]\le l+1+2kR_0.$$
For every FIXED l the explicit finite outgoing polynomial gives $r(\phi_l'-ik\phi_l)\to0$ as r tends infinity. The weighted coefficient sum therefore bounds every residual tail uniformly for ALL r>=R0 and n on the sphere. Given epsilon, choose a finite degree cutoff making that tail smaller than epsilon/2; the finitely many remaining radial residuals tend to0 uniformly after multiplication by their fixed finite angular suprema. This finite-head/finite-tail argument proves the uniform Sommerfeld limit. Also $r|u(rn)|\le R_0\sum|c_{lm}|\|Y_{lm}\|_\infty$ uniformly, which proves exactly the amplitude bound used in the outer Green Wronskian. The first radial derivative series is uniformly convergent on r>=R0 since $|\phi_l'|\le[(l+1)/R_0+k]|\phi_l|$ and the same weighted sum dominates it; finite-coordinate FTC [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]] identifies that derivative with partial_r u.

Smooth modal realization and normalization. Rotational differentiation preserves the degree-l harmonic space. Skew symmetry gives $\sum_j\|L_jv\|_2^2=l(l+1)\|v\|_2^2$ in that finite space, so each successive angular derivative has norm at most [l(l+1)]^(1/2) times the preceding norm. Its pointwise norm is bounded by sqrt((2l+1)/(4pi)) times its L2 norm by finite basis Cauchy-Schwarz and the addition identity. The radial ODE of the earlier Hankel supplier, differentiated finitely many times, gives for every fixed q a bound $|\phi_l^{(q)}(r)|\le C_{q,k,R_0}(l+1)^{2q}/r$ on r>=R0: q0 is the radial-ratio bound, q1 is the logarithmic-derivative bound, and the equation plus derivatives of r^-1,r^-2 gives the induction. Thus every radial/angular derivative series is dominated by a finite power of l times the coefficient estimate with a sufficiently large p. It converges uniformly on each closed bounded exterior annulus; FTC identifies all derivatives. Cartesian derivatives there are finite combinations of radial and angular derivatives with smooth coefficients (from $\nabla=n\partial_r-r^{-1}n\times(L_1,L_2,L_3)$), so the series defines a smooth exterior field. The finite angular identity above gives the polar Laplacian formula on phi_l(r)Y_lm, and the radial ODE makes each term solve (Delta+k²)u0; termwise second derivatives prove the equation for the limit. At rR0 the absolute series has its L2 coefficients c_lm; completeness of H2 and continuity give its actual smooth trace g. If trace coefficients are recorded instead in the sphere-normalized basis $Y^{R_0}_{lm}(R_0n)=R_0^{-1}Y_{lm}(n)$, their coefficients are R0 c_lm, so the displayed expansion is identical after normalization. No weaker rough-trace claim or obstacle-boundary existence is inferred. All bounded Green, weaker C1-trace, exterior source and smooth-modal conclusions are preserved, with the same declared Choice strengths.

items.title: Fixed-endpoint variation of the relativistic particle functional
items.statement:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]) and fix a conversion constant $c>0$, let $[a,b]$ be a nondegenerate compact interval, let $X:[a,b]	o A$ be a $C^2$ future timelike curve ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]), and let $\mathcal A$ be a $C^2$ covector field on a neighbourhood of the image of $X$. An inertial frame is $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with future positively oriented $\eta$-orthonormal basis, and its chart sends $p$ to the unique coordinates of $p-o$ in that basis; in these coordinates $\eta_{\mu

On $[a,b]$, $C^2$ means continuous components and continuous first and second derivatives with their one-sided endpoint values; equations at endpoints use those same one-sided derivatives. For fixed-endpoint $C^2$ variations $h:[a,b]	o V$ with $h(a)=h(b)=0$ and for $m,c>0$ and real $q$ consider

$$S[X]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}\,ds+q\int_a^bA_\mu(X)\dot X^\mu\,ds .$$

Then for each such $h$ the curve $X+\varepsilon h$ remains future timelike for all sufficiently small $|\varepsilon|$, and stationarity of $S$ under all such variations is equivalent to

$$m rac{dU_

where $	au(s)=	au_0+c^{-1}\int_a^s\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}\,dr$ with arbitrary $	au_0\in\mathbb R$, and $U(s)=\dot X(s)/	au\prime(s)$ are the proper-time function and four-velocity ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]]); $dU/d	au=U\prime/	au\prime$ and $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). This is a calculation about the chosen functional; adopting it as a physical particle action is an additional model assumption, and it makes no existence claim for coupled singular particles and fields. The coefficient-localization proof below is one-dimensional and choice-free; it does not invoke an AC-qualified Lebesgue fundamental lemma.
items.strategy:
Fix an inertial coordinate frame. The continuous functions $-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)$ and $\dot X^0$ have strictly positive minima on the compact nondegenerate interval; $h,\dot h$ are bounded there ([[thm-extreme-value-metric]]). Continuity of the quadratic form therefore keeps both margins positive for sufficiently small signed $\varepsilon$. The compact image of $X$ also has a finite neighbourhood cover inside the given potential domain; by shrinking $|\varepsilon|$ and using bounded $h$, every $X+\varepsilon h$ remains in that domain. Thus each admitted perturbation remains a future timelike curve with the same endpoints. The square-root derivative is the positive-base power derivative [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with its agreement with the positive rational square root supplied by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. The two integrands and their $\varepsilon$ derivatives are continuous on one compact parameter rectangle, with the square-root argument bounded away from zero. Apply exactly the finite-interval Riemann theorem [[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle]]; no Lebesgue conversion or AC-qualified parameter theorem is used.

The product and chain rules give
$$\delta S=\int_a^b mU_

Here $	au'=\sqrt{-\eta(\dot X,\dot X)}/c>0$ and $U=\dot X/	au'$ by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. All factors in the integrations by parts are $C^1$ on the closed interval, with continuous integrable derivatives. [[thm-integration-by-parts]], or the product rule followed by [[thm-ftc-second-part]], gives zero endpoint terms because $h(a)=h(b)=0$. Hence
$$\delta S=\int_a^b C_

Each coefficient is continuous on $[a,b]$.

For completeness prove the exact coefficient implication without the AC-qualified field lemma. If $C_

Divide by the positive $	au'$ to obtain $m\,dU_
