items.title: Real plane-wave fields encoded by complex amplitudes
items.statement:
Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular
frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and
$y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself
([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex
derivative is also its real total derivative
([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]),
and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word
$(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$,
$\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$,
by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with
$b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite
word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a).
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
items.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition. The domain and the identity of the real fields are those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] read on the whole-space laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; the field notion, class and units are those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. The phase convention $\theta=k\cdot x-\omega t$ (decreasing in $t$) is fixed here and used by every later item of the page: it is the convention in which the amplitude equations hold with the signs written in the cited treatments. The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of $w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$, recorded because later items speak of a 'nonzero wave'. No field equation or physical interpretation is introduced. Joint smoothness is proved locally by every coordinate-word derivative, using the entire exponential, its real total derivative and the real chain rule.
items.physical_scope: Ideal whole-space classical plane-wave fields with wavevector $k\ne0$, angular frequency $\omega>0$, complex amplitudes in $\mathbb C^3$ and the SI units of the framework, defined on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. No source, boundary, decay, finite-energy or empirical content is asserted.

items.title: Source-free vacuum Maxwell fields satisfy the wave equation
items.statement:
Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and the Laplacian $\Delta$ of
[[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. Let $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be
jointly $C^2$ fields of [[def-em-fields]], let $(\rho,J)$ be the source fields
of [[def-em-sources]], and let $W\subseteq\Omega\times I$ be open with
$\rho=0$ and $J=0$ on $W$ (a source-free region). Then on $W$, componentwise,

$$\Delta E=c^{-2}\partial_t^2E,\qquad \Delta B=c^{-2}\partial_t^2B;$$

equivalently each of the six Cartesian components of $E$ and of $B$ satisfies
the scalar wave equation $c^{-2}\partial_t^2v=\Delta v$ of speed $c$ on $W$.

(a) [Hypotheses actually used] The derivation differentiates the Faraday and
Ampère equations in time, commutes the time derivative with
$\operatorname{curl}$ (Clairaut's theorem, available for jointly $C^2$ fields),
uses the curl-curl identity of [[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]], and
uses the two Gauss equations $\operatorname{div}E=0$,
$\operatorname{div}B=0$ on $W$. The two evolution equations alone are not
sufficient for the conclusion without the constraint equations.

(b) [One-directional] No converse is asserted. The two vector wave equations do
not imply the four source-free Maxwell equations: the constraints
$\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$ and the two curl relations are not
recovered, and solutions of the six uncoupled scalar wave equations need not
lie in a source-free smooth Maxwell branch. The correctly constrained
initial-value problem is a separate result on this page.

(c) [Scope] Only the smooth branch is covered. No decay, boundedness, compact
support, finite-energy or boundary hypothesis is imposed or needed; the
conclusion is local on $W$, asserts no value of any field or derivative at a
point of singular source support, and does not cover the weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. The result is conditional on the adopted postulates
and makes no empirical claim.
items.strategy: Use the two evolution equations of the smooth branch with $J=0$: from $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ and $\partial_tE=c^2\operatorname{curl}B$ (the Ampere equation with $J=0$, multiplied by $c^2$), differentiate once more in time to obtain $\partial_t^2E=c^2\operatorname{curl}(\partial_tB)=-c^2\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E$ and $\partial_t^2B=-\operatorname{curl}(\partial_tE)=-c^2\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}B$; commuting $\partial_t$ with $\operatorname{curl}$ on the jointly $C^2$ components is Clairaut's theorem [[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]]. The curl-curl identity of [[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]] gives $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E=\nabla\operatorname{div}E-\Delta E=-\Delta E$ and likewise for $B$, because $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$ on $W$. This is the display. The witness for the failed converse is the time-independent field $E(x)=(x_1,0,0)$, $B=0$: its components have vanishing second time derivatives and are affine in $x_1$, so both wave equations hold, while $\operatorname{div}E=1\ne0$ excludes any source-free Maxwell branch. Nothing else is used.
items.physical_scope: Conditional statement about source-free regions of the smooth branch of the adopted vacuum Maxwell postulate, for jointly $C^2$ fields on a named inertial chart with SI constants. Excluded: the weak branch, singular sources, regions with surface sources, any converse from wave equations to Maxwell, and any decay or finite-energy hypothesis. No empirical claim.

items.title: Dispersion, transversality and the two polarization conditions for plane-wave solutions
items.statement:
Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, and let $(E,B)$ be the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on the whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with the terminology and phase convention of that definition, the cross product and inner product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] extended to $\mathbb C^3$ componentwise, the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and $\hat k=k/|k|$. Then: (a) [Amplitude equations] $(E,B)$ satisfies the four smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $ho\equiv0$ and $J\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$ if and only if $$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot b=0,\qquad k	imes e=\omega b,\qquad k	imes b=- rac{\omega}{c^2}e .$$ (b) [Dispersion, nonzero waves, two polarisations] The amplitude equations admit a nonzero solution $(e,b)
e(0,0)$ if and only if $|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is $e=b=0$. On the dispersion relation both zero and nonzero solutions occur; a particular solution is nonzero exactly when its amplitudes are not both zero, in the sense of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]](c). If $|k|=\omega/c$, the solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with $e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k	imes e/\omega$: a complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every nonzero solution $e
e0$ and $b
e0$. (c) [Transversality, orthogonality, magnitude relation and the wave equation] For every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$: $k\cdot E(x,t)=k\cdot B(x,t)=0$, $E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=0$ and $B(x,t)=\hat k	imes E(x,t)/c$; in particular $|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$ solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of [[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$. (d) [Scope] The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see [[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and is conditional on the adopted postulate.
items.strategy:
Substitution: for the fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]], $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{Re}(i\,k\cdot e\,e^{i	heta})$, $\operatorname{curl}E=\operatorname{Re}(i\,k	imes e\,e^{i	heta})$ and $\partial_tE=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\,e\,e^{i	heta})$, with the analogous expressions for $B$; these derivative formulas are the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]) applied to the entire complex exponential ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]) with the real part carried along by real-linearity ([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). Since $k
e0$ and $(x,t)$ ranges over $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$, the phase $	heta$ attains every real value; hence a relation $\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i	heta})=0$ valid for all $(x,t)$ forces $w=0$ in $\mathbb C^3$, by evaluation at $	heta=0$ and $	heta=\pi/2$. Applying this to the four Maxwell equations and their differences gives (a) in both directions. (b) If $e
e0$: $k	imes e
e0$ because $e$ and $k$ are linearly independent (transversality), so $b=k	imes e/\omega
e0$; crossing $k	imes b=-(\omega/c^2)e$ with $k$ gives $k	imes(k	imes b)=k(k\cdot b)-|k|^2b$ on one side and $-(\omega/c^2)k	imes e=-(\omega^2/c^2)b$ on the other, hence $|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$ by $k\cdot b=0$. Conversely, if $|k|=\omega/c$ take any complex $e\perp k$ and put $b=k	imes e/\omega$; then $k\cdot b=0$ and $k	imes b=k	imes(k	imes e)/\omega=(k(k\cdot e)-|k|^2e)/\omega=-(\omega/c^2)e$. The vector triple-product identity is the coordinate expansion licensed by [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]] with [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. If $e=0$ then $k	imes e=\omega b$ forces $b=0$. (c) Transversality of $E,B$ is immediate from (a). For orthogonality write $e=a+id$, $b=A+iD$ with real $a,d,A,D$ and $A=k	imes a/\omega$, $D=k	imes d/\omega$; then $E\cdot B=(a\cdot A)\cos^2	heta-(a\cdot D+d\cdot A)\sin	heta\cos	heta+(d\cdot D)\sin^2	heta$ and the three coefficients vanish by orthogonality and determinant alternation ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]). The relation $B=\hat k	imes E/c$ and the magnitude relation follow from $b=\hat k	imes e/c$ componentwise. For the wave-equation clause, (a) puts $(E,B)$ in the source-free smooth branch of the postulate on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$, so [[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] applies to each component. No step uses more than the listed suppliers.

items.title: Polarization of a transverse plane wave: linear, circular and elliptical traces, and handedness
items.statement:
Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and $\omega>0$, let $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$,
and let $(E,B)$ be the plane-wave pair of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on
the whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with phase
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$. Suppose the amplitude conditions of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold, so that $k\cdot e=0$ and
$b=k\times e/\omega$. By that theorem, if the pair is nonzero then it also
satisfies the dispersion relation $|k|=\omega/c$, while the zero pair is
permitted for every $k\ne0$ and $\omega>0$, both on and off this dispersion
relation. This item classifies the polarization of that class of transverse
plane waves; it adds no field-theoretic content.

Write $e=a+id$ with the real vectors $a=\operatorname{Re}e$ and
$d=\operatorname{Im}e$ of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]],
applied componentwise in $\mathbb C^3$; since $k$ is real and $k\cdot e=0$, the
real and imaginary parts of this complex equation give
$\langle k,a\rangle=\langle k,d\rangle=0$. Put $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $|\cdot|$ and $\times$ be the inner product, norm
and cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Then:

(a) [Trace] At every fixed $x$ one has
$E(x,t)=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ with $\theta=\theta(x,t)$. The curve
$\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, $\gamma(\theta):=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$,
lies in the transverse plane
$k^\perp=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:\langle k,v\rangle=0\}$; it is the image of the unit
circle $S^1=\{(u_1,u_2)\in\mathbb R^2:u_1^2+u_2^2=1\}$ under the $\mathbb R$-linear
map $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$; it is $2\pi$-periodic in the phase parameter
$\theta$ and satisfies $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$, while the map
$t\mapsto E(x,t)$ has time period $T=2\pi/\omega$. The curve $\gamma$ is
called the **polarization trace** at $x$; it does not depend on $x$, so the
classification below is the same at every point.

(b) [Classification] Exactly one of the following three cases holds.

(i) **Linear polarization**: $\dim_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$.
When $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$, the trace is a nontrivial closed
segment in that span, traversed twice per period; when $a=d=0$, the trace is
the single point $\{0\}$ and $(E,B)$ is the zero wave.

(ii) **Circular polarization**: $|a|=|d|>0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=0$. The
trace is the circle of radius $|a|$ in $k^\perp$, and $|E(x,t)|=|a|$ for all
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(iii) **Elliptical (nondegenerate, noncircular) polarization**:
$\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$ and not (ii). Here a **nondegenerate ellipse centred at $0$** in a real plane $P$ means
the set $L(S^1)$ for a real-linear isomorphism $L:\mathbb R^2\to P$.
The trace is such an ellipse in $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$, and the
origin lies in the relative interior of the enclosed region
$L(\{u\in\mathbb R^2:|u|\le1\})$ in that plane. If in addition $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, the
parametrization is along principal axes and the semiaxis lengths are $|a|$ and
$|d|$; the general principal-axis computation is not asserted by this item.

(c) [Handedness] For $a,d\in k^\perp$, the cross product $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $a$ and to $d$
([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), hence parallel
to $k$; define the **helicity sign**
$H:=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle\in\mathbb R$, whose sign is taken in the
order of [[def-real-order]]. One has $H=0$ exactly in the linear case (i), and
$H\ne0$ otherwise. This library calls the polarization **right-handed** when
$H<0$ and **left-handed** when $H>0$. Geometrically, $H<0$ means that at fixed
$x$ the electric vector rotates clockwise as seen by an observer facing the
incoming wave (looking along $-\hat k$), and $H>0$ means counterclockwise;
here the screen orientation is fixed by any positive orthonormal triad
$(u,v,\hat k)$, with $u$ to the right and $v$ up for that observer.
Equivalently, $\langle E(x,t)\times\partial_tE(x,t),\hat k\rangle=\omega H$ for
every $(x,t)$. The names "right" and "left" handedness are conventional and
both conventions occur in the literature, so later statements in this library
use only the sign of $H$.

(d) [Status] This is a classification definition. It introduces the trace,
the three cases and the sign $H$, and asserts no field equation, no
propagation, energy or empirical content. The magnetic amplitude enters only
through the two amplitude conditions $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$
recalled above; the definition covers the zero wave, both on and off the
dispersion relation, and no non-plane or non-transverse field is classified.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The real vectors $a,d$ are well defined by the componentwise real and
imaginary parts of $e$; because $k$ is real, taking real and imaginary parts of
$k\cdot e=\sum_jk_j(a_j+id_j)$ gives $\langle k,a\rangle=0$ and
$\langle k,d\rangle=0$, so $a,d\in k^\perp$ and $\gamma$ takes values in
$k^\perp$. The trace formula in (a) is Euler's formula
$\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of [[thm-eulers-formula]] together with
the field arithmetic on the right-hand side of
$E=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a+id)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\bigr)
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)+i(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)\bigr)$
and the real-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$: the real part is
$a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$, while the imaginary part is not a field. Since
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$ and $\omega>0$, at fixed $x$ the map
$t\mapsto\theta$ is a bijection onto $\mathbb R$; hence the set traced by
$E(x,t)$ as $t$ varies is the full image $\gamma(\mathbb R)$, independently of
$x$, and $\gamma$ is $2\pi$-periodic with $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$
because $\cos$ and $\sin$ shift by a sign under $\theta\mapsto\theta+\pi$. The
time period is $T=2\pi/\omega$, the least positive $s$ with
$\theta(x,t+s)=\theta(x,t)-2\pi$ for all $(x,t)$; it is distinct from the
phase-parameter period $2\pi$ of $\gamma$.

For the classification, "exactly one of the three cases holds" is checked
case by case: if $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$ then (i); otherwise
$\dim=2$, and either $|a|=|d|>0$ with $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, which is (ii),
or not, which is (iii). In case (i) with $\dim=1$, write $d=\lambda a$ with
$a\ne0$ (or symmetrically $a=\mu d$); then
$\gamma(\theta)=(\cos\theta-\lambda\sin\theta)a$, whose image is the segment
$\{sa:|s|\le\sqrt{1+\lambda^2}\}$ in $\mathbb R a$, traversed once in each direction between successive extrema of the scalar
factor (each such phase interval has length $\pi$). In case (ii),
expanding with the bilinearity of the inner product
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) gives
$|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2-2u_1u_2\langle a,d\rangle=|a|^2$
whenever $|a|=|d|$, $\langle a,d\rangle=0$ and $u_1^2+u_2^2=1$, so the image
of the unit circle under $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is contained in the
circle of radius $|a|$ in the plane $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; conversely,
for every $v$ in that plane with $|v|=|a|$ the coordinates
$u_1=\langle v,a\rangle/|a|^2$ and $u_2=-\langle v,d\rangle/|d|^2$ satisfy
$u_1^2+u_2^2=1$ and $u_1a-u_2d=v$, because $a/|a|$ and $d/|d|$ are orthonormal
and $v=\langle v,a/|a|\rangle(a/|a|)+\langle v,d/|d|\rangle(d/|d|)$; hence the
trace is exactly that circle. In case (iii) the vectors $a,d$
are linearly independent, so $T:(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is a linear
isomorphism of $\mathbb R^2$ onto the two-dimensional plane
$\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; the image of the closed unit disk under $T$ is a
compact convex subset with nonempty interior in that plane, the image of the
open disk is its nonempty interior, and the image of the unit circle is its
boundary, so the trace is a nondegenerate ellipse centred at
$0=T(0)$ with the origin in the relative interior of that enclosed region.
The trace itself is its boundary and has empty interior in the plane. If moreover
$\langle a,d\rangle=0$, then along the principal axes $a,d$ the parametrization
$u_1a-u_2d$ has the stated axis lengths because the two summands are
orthogonal: $|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2$; no computation of
principal axes for general $a,d$ is used or claimed.

For (c), the cross product $a\times d$ is orthogonal to both factors and
alternating ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), and the real Gram identity
[[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]] says
$|a\times d|^2>0$ exactly when $a,d$ are linearly independent. Thus
$a\times d=0$ holds exactly when $a$ and $d$ are linearly dependent, that is,
in case (i); then $H=0$. Otherwise $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$, and
since $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\subseteq k^\perp$ are both two-dimensional,
they are equal; being orthogonal to $a$ and $d$, the vector $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $k^\perp$, whose orthogonal complement in $\mathbb R^3$ is the
line $\mathbb R k$, so $a\times d=\mu k$ for a real $\mu$ and
$H=\mu|k|\ne0$. For the rotation identity, differentiating
$E=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ along $t$ with $\partial_t\theta=-\omega$ gives
$\partial_tE=\omega(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)$, so
$E\times\partial_tE
=\omega(a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)\times(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)
=\omega\bigl((\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)a\times d
+\cos\theta\sin\theta(a\times a-d\times d)\bigr)=\omega\,a\times d$
by bilinearity and alternation, and taking the inner product with $\hat k$
gives the displayed identity. As a concrete check of the convention, take
$\hat k=e_3$ with the positive orthonormal screen triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, so
that $e_1$ points right and $e_2$ up for the observer looking along $-e_3$;
then $e=e_1-ie_2$ has $a=e_1$, $d=-e_2$,
$E(0,t)=\cos(\omega t)e_1-\sin(\omega t)e_2$ (clockwise), and
$H=\langle e_1\times(-e_2),e_3\rangle=-1<0$, consistently with the
right-handed naming. This fixes the sign convention of the cited treatment:
the source writes $E_0=\alpha-i\beta$ and calls the polarization right-handed
if and only if $\beta=\hat k\times\alpha$, which under $a=\alpha$,
$d=-\beta$ is $H=-|\alpha|^2<0$ in the circular case.

Finally, all amplitudes $e,b$ and vectors $k,a,d$ are constant and all
quantities above are computed from them by the operations of the cited items;
no limit, no integral and no field equation is used, and the definition is at
the level of classification only.
items.strategy: An explicit classification definition. The transverse conditions $k\cdot a=k\cdot d=0$ are the real and imaginary parts of $k\cdot e=0$ from [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]. The trace formula is the elementary rewriting $\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a+id)e^{i\theta}\bigr)=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ ([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]); closedness and the reflection symmetry are immediate from the circular functions of the encoding definition. In (b)(iii), independence of $a,d$ makes $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ injective, so the trace is a linearly embedded circle (an ellipse) around the origin: the origin lies in the relative interior of the image of the closed unit disk, whose boundary is the trace. In (c), $a\times d$ is orthogonal to $a$ and $d$ and hence parallel to $k$ ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), and the exact Gram positivity criterion of [[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]] gives zero cross product exactly in the dependent case, hence $H=0$ exactly in the linear case; the rotation identity follows by differentiating $E=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ with $\partial_t\theta=-\omega$, giving $E\times\partial_tE=\omega a\times d$. For example, $\hat k=e_3$ and $e=e_1-ie_2$ give $E(0,t)=\cos(\omega t)e_1-\sin(\omega t)e_2$, clockwise in the specified screen orientation. The naming convention is fixed as stated and matches the cited treatment under the dictionary $a=\alpha$, $d=-\beta$. The principal-axis caveat is recorded because the general diagonalisation is not part of this item's strategy. No field equation or physical claim is introduced.
items.physical_scope: Definition-level classification of the polarization of ideal transverse plane waves satisfying the amplitude conditions of the plane-wave Maxwell theorem, in a named inertial frame with SI units and a fixed nonzero wavevector. It fixes the phase convention, the trace, the linear, circular and elliptical cases and the sign of the helicity $H$. Excluded: partially polarized or stochastic light, finite pulses, material media, non-plane or non-transverse fields, and any empirical claim.

items.title: Constrained smooth vacuum Maxwell initial-value theory, finite-energy conservation and finite propagation
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
[[def-countable-choice]]), inherited from
[[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]]. Let $t_0<T$ be real, let
$E_0,B_0:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^\infty$ fields
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) on the whole-space laboratory
region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the
constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and assume the constraints
$$\operatorname{div}E_0=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B_0=0$$ on $\mathbb R^3$
([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Put
$\dot E_0:=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$ and
$\dot B_0:=-\operatorname{curl}E_0$. No decay, boundedness, compactness or
finite-energy hypothesis is imposed on the data. Then:

(a) [Existence and explicit representation] There are jointly $C^\infty$
fields $E,B:\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R^3$ (in the extension sense of
[[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]]) satisfying the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$,
$J\equiv0$ and the initial conditions $E(\cdot,t_0)=E_0$,
$B(\cdot,t_0)=B_0$, $\partial_tE(\cdot,t_0)=\dot E_0$,
$\partial_tB(\cdot,t_0)=\dot B_0$. Explicitly, each component $E_i$ is the
scalar solution $u$ of [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](a) with data
$(a,b)=(E_{0,i},\dot E_{0,i})$ and $h=0$, each $B_i$ that with
$(a,b)=(B_{0,i},\dot B_{0,i})$, in the spherical-mean representation
$u=\partial_sH_a+H_b$ of that theorem, the mean being that of
[[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]].

(b) [Uniqueness] Every pair of jointly $C^2$ fields on
$\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ (in the extension sense) satisfying the same four
equations with $\rho\equiv0$, $J\equiv0$ and $E'(\cdot,t_0)=E_0$,
$B'(\cdot,t_0)=B_0$ equals $(E,B)$; the time derivatives at $t_0$ are then
automatically $\dot E_0,\dot B_0$ by the Ampere and Faraday equations.

(c) [Finite propagation and domain of dependence] If second constrained data
$(E_0',B_0')$ agree with $(E_0,B_0)$ together with all curls on the closed ball
$\overline B_{c(t_*-t_0)}(x_*)$ — that is, $E_0=E_0'$, $B_0=B_0'$,
$\operatorname{curl}E_0=\operatorname{curl}E_0'$ and
$\operatorname{curl}B_0=\operatorname{curl}B_0'$ there — then the
corresponding solutions agree at $(x_*,t_*)$, for all $x_*\in\mathbb R^3$ and
$t_*\in[t_0,T]$. Consequently the value at $(x_*,t_*)$ is determined by the
Cauchy data on the closed backward cone
$K(x_*,t_*)=\{(y,v):t_0\le v\le t_*,\ |y-x_*|\le c(t_*-v)\}$ of
[[def-forward-and-backward-wave-cones-domain-of-dependence-and-influence]]. In
the causal geometry of the adopted affine Minkowski model this cone is the
intersection of the slab with the model's causal past of the event $(x_*,t_*)$ in the chart $x^0=ct$; by
the reachability objects of
[[def-sr-causal-reachability-in-affine-minkowski-space]] and the
straight-segment criterion and time monotonicity of
[[thm-sr-future-cone-and-flat-domain-of-dependence]], events in the slab outside it cannot
be joined to $(x_*,t_*)$ by a future causal path, so the constructed field
supplies no vacuum influence outside the model's causal cones; this
identification of the PDE cone with the model's causal cone is the modelling
statement of the item, not an additional empirical claim.

(d) [Compact support] If in addition $E_0$ and $B_0$ vanish off a compact set
$K\subset\mathbb R^3$, choose $\rho>0$ with $K\subseteq\overline B_\rho(0)$
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]); then for every $t\in[t_0,T]$ one has
$E(x,t)=B(x,t)=0$ whenever $|x|>\rho+c(t-t_0)$.

(e) [Finite-energy branch] Define
$u(x,t)=(\varepsilon_0|E(x,t)|^2+\mu_0^{-1}|B(x,t)|^2)/2$ and
$S=\mu_0^{-1}E\times B$ as in [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and define total
energy by the nonnegative ball exhaustion
$\mathcal E(t):=\sup_{R>0}\int_{B_R(0)}u(x,t)\,dx\in[0,\infty]$. If
$\mathcal E(t_0)<\infty$, then $\mathcal E(t)=\mathcal E(t_0)$ for every
$t\in[t_0,T]$. More locally, for every $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$, $r>0$ and
$t_0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\int_{B_r(x_0)}u(x,t)\,dx\le\int_{B_{r+c(t-s)}(x_0)}u(x,s)\,dx.$$
This is a branch for the same smooth constrained data with finite initial
energy; no existence result for nonsmooth finite-energy data is asserted.

(f) [Scope] This is the smooth whole-space vacuum branch with initially
constraint-satisfying data; general smooth non-decaying data may have infinite
total energy, and no boundary condition, inhomogeneous source, weak-branch
content or empirical claim is asserted. The result is conditional on the
adopted postulates and on $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the latter used through the
scalar theorem and the divergence and substitution suppliers in clause (e).
items.strategy: Set $\dot E_0=c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$, $\dot B_0=-\operatorname{curl}E_0$, and solve the six scalar Cauchy problems by [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](a) with data $(E_{0,i},\dot E_{0,i})$ and $(B_{0,i},\dot B_{0,i})$; the $C^\infty$ claim and the explicit representation through the spherical-mean family $H_\varphi=sM_{cs}\varphi$ are clause (a) of that theorem, whose mean is that of [[lem-em-spherical-mean-wave-identity]]. Put $R_i:=\partial_tE_i-c^2(\operatorname{curl}B)_i$ and $Q_i:=\partial_tB_i+(\operatorname{curl}E)_i$. Each is $C^\infty$ and solves the homogeneous scalar wave equation: differentiating the component wave equations and commuting derivatives ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]) gives $\partial_t^2R_i=c^2\Delta R_i$, $\partial_t^2Q_i=c^2\Delta Q_i$. Initially $R=Q=0$, and $\partial_tR_i(t_0)=c^2\Delta E_{0,i}+c^2(\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E_0)_i=c^2\nabla_i\operatorname{div}E_0=0$, $\partial_tQ_i(t_0)=c^2\nabla_i\operatorname{div}B_0=0$ by the curl-curl identity [[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]] and the constraints. The uniqueness clause [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](b) applied to the zero wave problem gives $R=Q=0$, i.e. the two evolution equations. The constructed fields are smooth and satisfy the evolution equations with $\operatorname{div}E(\cdot,t_0)=\operatorname{div}E_0=0$ and $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t_0)=0$, so the constraint propagation of [[pthm-em-gauss-constraint-propagation]](a) with $\rho=J=0$ gives $\operatorname{div}E\equiv\operatorname{div}B\equiv0$; all four Maxwell equations therefore hold. Uniqueness (b): any other $C^2$ solution has componentwise the same Cauchy data and, by [[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]], satisfies the homogeneous scalar wave equation, so [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](b) identifies it with the constructed field. Clause (c) applies [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](c) componentwise, whose hypothesis is agreement of both scalar data functions on the ball: $E_0$ and $c^2\operatorname{curl}B_0$ for the $E$ components, $B_0$ and $-\operatorname{curl}E_0$ for the $B$ components, exactly the stated hypothesis; the cone reformulation uses the backward-cone object and the causal reachability and future-causal-path conclusions of the two cited SR items as the model's geometric language. Clause (d) applies [[thm-em-wave-cauchy-kirchhoff]](d) to each component, whose data vanish off $K$ because $E_0,B_0$ and their curls do. For (e), the local source-free Poynting identity [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]](a) is $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=0$. The coordinate identity $|E\times B|^2=|E|^2|B|^2-(E\cdot B)^2$ (by expansion of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]) gives $|E\times B|\le|E||B|$. This and $2pq\le p^2+q^2$, applied to $p=\sqrt{\varepsilon_0}|E|$, $q=|B|/\sqrt{\mu_0}$, give $|S|\le cu$. For a positive $C^1$ radius $r(v)$ put $F(v)=\int_{B_{r(v)}(x_0)}u(x,v)\,dx$. To justify moving-ball differentiation, set $x=x_0+r(v)y$ in the integral using [[lem-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-borel-functions-via-radon-uniqueness]]; the result is $r(v)^3\int_{B_1}u(x_0+r(v)y,v)\,dy$. One may replace $B_1$ by its compact closure because its boundary is Lebesgue null by [[lem-unit-sphere-is-lebesgue-null]]; translated scaled spheres are likewise null by the substitution lemma. [[lem-em-parameter-integrals]] differentiates this fixed compact integral. The radius terms are $(r'/r)\int_{B_r}\operatorname{div}((x-x_0)u)\,dx$, which by [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]] equal $r'\int_{\partial B_r}u\,dS$; the time term, by the same divergence theorem and Poynting, is $-\int_{\partial B_r}S\cdot n\,dS$. Thus $F'(v)=-\int_{\partial B_{r(v)}}(S\cdot n-r'(v)u)\,dS$. Choosing $r(v)=r+c(t-v)$ gives $F'=-\int_{\partial B_{r(v)}}(S\cdot n+cu)\,dS\le0$ by $|S|\le cu$, and integrating gives the stated local estimate. Taking the supremum in $r$ yields $\mathcal E(t)\le\mathcal E(s)$. For the reverse inequality apply the same local argument to the smooth source-free pair $\widetilde E(x,v)=E(x,t-v)$, $\widetilde B(x,v)=-B(x,t-v)$ for $0\le v\le t-s$. Its Maxwell equations follow by direct differentiation, its energy is $u(x,t-v)$ and its flux is $-S(x,t-v)$, so $\mathcal E(s)\le\mathcal E(t)$. This proves equality and finite-energy preservation when initially finite. Applied to the difference of two smooth source-free Maxwell solutions (the equations subtract), the same local estimate yields an energy uniqueness proof: zero initial difference has zero energy on every later ball; its continuous nonnegative density is zero everywhere, so both difference fields vanish. This supplements the scalar uniqueness argument without restricting its arbitrary-growth conclusion. All ball closures are compact smooth domains and the integrands are smooth; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used through the divergence/substitution suppliers as well as the scalar theorem. The arbitrary-growth branch requires no decay or additional regularity. Apply Gauss propagation on the open slab and use endpoint continuity. The causal-past assertion concerns only the slab intersection. Signed substitutions use finite positive and negative parts.
items.physical_scope: Conditional whole-space smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell initial-value theory in a named inertial chart with SI constants: existence, uniqueness, finite propagation speed $c$, compact-support propagation and smooth finite-energy conservation for initially constraint-satisfying $C^\infty$ data of arbitrary growth. Excluded: nonsmooth and weak-branch data, sources, boundary conditions, finite-domain problems, nonsmooth finite-energy data, and any empirical claim. Smooth finite-energy initial data retain their total energy; arbitrary-growth data remain allowed. $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is declared and used through the scalar wave theorem and clause (e)'s divergence and substitution suppliers.

items.title: Period-averaged energy density, Poynting vector and momentum flux of a plane wave
items.statement:
Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ with $\omega=c|k|$, let
$e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$, and let $(E,B)$ be
the corresponding plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Let $u$ and
$S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and $g=S/c^2$, $\sigma$, $\Pi=-\sigma$ the
momentum density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Write $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|e|^2=e\cdot\overline e$, $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle f\rangle:=\frac1T\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ be the period average at fixed
$x$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$:

(a) [Averaged energy density] $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$,
independent of $x$ and of the starting time.

(b) [Averaged Poynting vector]
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$; hence
$\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$, and the period-averaged intensity
is $I:=|\langle S\rangle|=c\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2$.

(c) [Averaged momentum density, stress and momentum flux]
$\langle g\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2c}|e|^2\hat k$, and componentwise
$\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$, equivalently
$\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$; the period-averaged
momentum flux across a plane with unit normal $n$ is therefore
$\langle u\rangle(\hat k\cdot n)\hat k$, a pure flux along $\hat k$ with signed
coefficient $(I/c)(\hat k\cdot n)$ and magnitude $(I/c)|\hat k\cdot n|$. The
tensor identity holds for every complex transverse amplitude $e$, not only for
real or circular ones.

(d) [Balance reading] On the source-free region the local identities of
[[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]] hold for this
field; since $u,g,S,\sigma$ are $T$-periodic in $t$, the period averages of
their time derivatives vanish ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), so averaging the
identities gives $\operatorname{div}\langle S\rangle=0$ and
$\operatorname{div}\langle\sigma\rangle=0$ consistently (both averaged fields
are in fact constant), and the reading of $u,S,g,\Pi$ as energy and momentum
densities and fluxes is that of those two theorems.

(e) [Scope] These are exact identities for the ideal plane wave; $I$ is the
intensity used by the radiation-pressure thought experiment of the companion
page and in radiation-flux arguments. No detection statistics, no finite-beam
or finite-time realisation and no empirical claim is made, and the zero
amplitude gives the zero wave and zero total energy, whereas every nonzero
amplitude gives infinite total energy over $\mathbb R^3$.
items.strategy: Clause (a)-(c) are the compact-period calculation of [[lem-em-period-average]] applied componentwise: with $E=\operatorname{Re}(e\,e^{i\theta})$, $B=\operatorname{Re}(b\,e^{i\theta})$, $\theta=k\cdot x-\omega t$, the lemma gives $\langle E_iE_j\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})$, $\langle B_iB_j\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(b_i\overline{b_j})$ and $\langle(E\times B)_i\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}((e\times\overline b)_i)$; hence $\langle|E|^2\rangle=|e|^2/2$ and, using $b=k\times e/\omega$ and $|k|=\omega/c$, $\langle|B|^2\rangle=|b|^2/2=|e|^2/(2c^2)$. Substituting into $u$ and $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] and using $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\varepsilon_0$ gives (a) and (b), since $e\times\overline b=e\times(k\times\overline e)/\omega=k|e|^2/\omega$ by the cross-product identity of [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]] and $e\cdot k=0$. For (c), expand $\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=(\varepsilon_0/2)\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})-(\varepsilon_0/4)\delta_{ij}|e|^2+(1/(2\mu_0))\operatorname{Re}(b_i\overline{b_j})-(1/(4\mu_0))\delta_{ij}|b|^2$ and substitute $b_i\overline{b_j}=(k\times e)_i\overline{(k\times e)_j}/\omega^2$ together with the coordinate identity $(k\times e)_i\overline{(k\times e)_j}=|k|^2|e|^2\delta_{ij}-k_ik_j|e|^2-|k|^2\overline{e_i}e_j$ (a bilinear coordinate expansion of the cross product, again from the cited lemma); with $|k|^2/\omega^2=1/c^2$ and $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\varepsilon_0$ $\operatorname{Re}(\overline{e_i}e_j)=\operatorname{Re}(e_i\overline{e_j})$, so all terms combine to $-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$. Clause (d) averages the balance identities: for the $T$-periodic smooth quantities the mean of the time derivative is zero by the fundamental theorem ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), and the remaining flux terms are the averaged quantities just computed, which are constant and hence divergence-free. No other input is used. For the last scope assertion, $e=0$ implies $b=0$ and $u=0$. If $e\ne0$, write $e=a+id$, so $u=\varepsilon_0|a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta|^2$. Choose one coordinate $j$ with $k_j\ne0$ and put $P=2\pi/|k_j|$. At fixed other coordinates and time, integration in $x_j$ over any interval of length $P$ gives $\varepsilon_0P(|a|^2+|d|^2)/2=\varepsilon_0P|e|^2/2$: expand the square and integrate $\cos^2$, $\sin^2$ and $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ over a full period, using the fundamental theorem and $\partial_{x_j}\theta=k_j$. Thus for $R=NP$ with a positive integer $N$, every such section of $[-R,R]^3$ has integral $N\varepsilon_0P|e|^2$. The continuous density and all its sections are Riemann integrable by [[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]. [[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]] (applied successively, with coordinate reordering justified by the identical finite product-grid Darboux sums) yields $\int_{[-R,R]^3}u=(2R)^2N\varepsilon_0P|e|^2\to\infty$. Nonnegativity and monotonicity of the box integral ([[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]) give divergence along all $R\to\infty$, not only this sequence. No interchange of time and space averages or choice principle is used.
items.physical_scope: Exact period-average identities for an ideal whole-space plane-wave solution of the smooth source-free vacuum Maxwell branch, in a named inertial chart with SI constants: averaged energy density, Poynting flux, momentum density and Maxwell-stress/momentum-flux tensor, with the balance reading under the two balance theorems. Excluded: finite beams and pulses, sources, boundaries, material media, any ensemble or detection statistics, any nonzero finite-total-energy whole-space plane wave, and any empirical claim. The admitted zero amplitude has zero total energy.

items.title: Superposition intensity and the coherent interference cross term
items.statement:
Let $\omega>0$ and let $k_1,k_2\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ satisfy
$|k_1|=|k_2|=\omega/c$. For $j=1,2$ let $e_j\in\mathbb C^3$ with
$k_j\cdot e_j=0$, put $b_j=k_j\times e_j/\omega$ and let $(E_j,B_j)$ be the
plane-wave solutions of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] given by
[[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]. Let $a_1,a_2\in\mathbb R$ and put
$(E,B):=a_1(E_1,B_1)+a_2(E_2,B_2)$. Write
$\hat k_j=k_j/|k_j|$, $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|z|^2:=z\cdot\overline z=\sum_{\ell=1}^3|z_\ell|^2$ for $z\in\mathbb C^3$,
and $\langle f\rangle(x):=T^{-1}\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ componentwise.
Then:

(a) [Superposition] $(E,B)$ is a smooth source-free solution of the vacuum
Maxwell equations ([[pthm-em-linear-superposition]]), and at each fixed $x$ it
can be written with a single phase,
$$E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\alpha(x)\,e^{i(k_1\cdot x-\omega t)}),\qquad B(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\beta(x)\,e^{i(k_1\cdot x-\omega t)}),$$
where $\alpha(x):=a_1e_1+a_2e_2e^{i\delta(x)}$,
$\beta(x):=a_1b_1+a_2b_2e^{i\delta(x)}$ and
$\delta(x):=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x$; constant relative phases are absorbed in $e_2$.

(b) [Averaged energy density with the coherent cross term] For every $x$,
$$\langle u\rangle(x)=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{4}|\alpha(x)|^2+\frac{1}{4\mu_0}|\beta(x)|^2=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\bigl(a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2\bigr)+\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}\bigl(W(x)\bigr),$$
where
$W(x):=\bigl(e_1\cdot\overline e_2+(\hat k_1\times e_1)\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline e_2)\bigr)e^{-i\delta(x)}$.
The first two terms are the sum of the averaged energy densities of the two
waves ([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]); the third is the interference cross
term, which may remain nonzero after time averaging at fixed relative phase.

(c) [Averaged flux and momentum; equal wavevectors] (with $u$ the energy
density and $S$ the Poynting vector of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]])
$\langle S\rangle(x)=\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\alpha(x)\times\overline{\beta(x)}\bigr)$.
In particular, if $k_1=k_2=:k$ then the superposition is the single plane wave
with amplitude $a_1e_1+a_2e_2$, and
$\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2$,
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2\hat k$
([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]]).

(d) [No incoherent or statistical claim] The formulas are deterministic
identities for the specified coherent superposition; they are not an ensemble
average over phases, and no detection statistics, finite-sample visibility
estimate or empirical conclusion is drawn. The computation is a conditional
consequence of the adopted Maxwell postulate and does not by itself distinguish
classical from quantum descriptions of light.
items.strategy: Clause (a): $E_j,B_j$ are source-free smooth solutions of the vacuum Maxwell postulate by [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]](a); the superposition is again such a solution by [[pthm-em-linear-superposition]] (real coefficients). The single-phase rewriting uses $e^{i\theta_2}=e^{i\delta(x)}e^{i\theta_1}$ with $\theta_j=k_j\cdot x-\omega t$ and $\delta=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x$. Clauses (b),(c): at each fixed $x$ write $E=\operatorname{Re}(A e^{-i\omega t})$, $B=\operatorname{Re}(D e^{-i\omega t})$, with $A=\alpha(x)e^{ik_1\cdot x}$ and $D=\beta(x)e^{ik_1\cdot x}$; the common spatial phase cancels in averages and apply the componentwise averages of [[lem-em-period-average]], $\langle\operatorname{Re}(\alpha e^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(\beta e^{-i\omega t})\rangle=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\alpha\overline{\beta})$ and the cross-product version; substituting into $u$ and $S$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] and using $|k_j|=\omega/c$, $b_j=k_j\times e_j/\omega$ together with the identity $(k\times u)\cdot(k\times v)=|k|^2u\cdot v$ for $u,v\perp k$ (from [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]) gives the displayed cross term with $W$: expanding $|\alpha|^2$ gives $a_1^2|e_1|^2+a_2^2|e_2|^2+2a_1a_2\operatorname{Re}(e_1\cdot\overline e_2e^{-i\delta})$, and similarly for $\beta$. For $k_1=k_2$ the bracket reduces to $2e_1\cdot\overline e_2$ and the formulas reduce to the single-wave averages of [[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]] for the amplitude $a_1e_1+a_2e_2$. No ensemble or statistical averaging is performed, which is exactly the content of the scope clause (d).
items.physical_scope: Deterministic superposition identities for two same-frequency ideal plane-wave solutions of the smooth source-free vacuum Maxwell branch in a named inertial chart with SI constants: the averaged energy density of the coherent sum with its interference cross term, the averaged Poynting vector, and the equal-wavevector specialization. Excluded: ensembles or random phases, partially coherent and finite sources, detection or sampling statistics, any empirical conclusion, and any claim discriminating classical from quantum descriptions.

pages.title: Vacuum waves and polarization — Examples

items.title: Linear, circular and elliptical amplitude choices
items.statement:
Use the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and the SI conventions of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Fix $K>0$, put
$\omega:=cK$ and $k:=Ke_3$, so that $|k|=K=\omega/c$ and $\hat k=e_3$, and let
$E_0>0$ carry the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$. For each amplitude choice
below put $b:=k\times e/\omega$; then the amplitude conditions of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold and the corresponding fields
$(E,B)$ of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] are smooth source-free vacuum
Maxwell solutions on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, with
$\theta(x,t)=Kx_3-\omega t$.

(i) [Linear] $e:=E_0e_1$, $b=(E_0/c)e_2$. Here $a=E_0e_1$ and $d=0$, the
trace is the segment $[-E_0,E_0]e_1=\{se_1:-E_0\le s\le E_0\}$ traversed
twice per period, the polarization is linear and
$H=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle=0$; moreover
$E=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$, $B=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$ and $|B|=|E|/c$.

(ii) [Circular] $e:=E_0(e_1+ie_2)$, $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-ie_1)$. Here
$a=E_0e_1$ and $d=E_0e_2$, so $|a|=|d|=E_0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=0$: the
polarization is circular of radius $E_0$, with
$E=E_0(\cos\theta\,e_1-\sin\theta\,e_2)$,
$B=(E_0/c)(\sin\theta\,e_1+\cos\theta\,e_2)$, $|E|=E_0$ and $|B|=E_0/c$
everywhere, and $H=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle=E_0^2>0$, so this
polarization is left-handed in the convention of
[[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The reversed choice $e=E_0(e_1-ie_2)$
gives $H=-E_0^2<0$ and is right-handed.

(iii) [Elliptical] $e:=E_0(e_1+2ie_2)$. Here $a=E_0e_1$ and $d=2E_0e_2$ are
orthogonal with unequal lengths, so by clause (b)(iii) of
[[def-em-polarization-definition]] the trace is the axis-aligned ellipse
$E_0\cos\theta\,e_1-2E_0\sin\theta\,e_2$ with semiaxes $E_0$ and $2E_0$ along
$e_1$ and $e_2$; $|E|^2=E_0^2(\cos^2\theta+4\sin^2\theta)$ varies between
$E_0^2$ and $4E_0^2$; and $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-2ie_1)$, $H=2E_0^2>0$.

(iv) [Degenerate and edge cases] $e=0$ gives the zero wave, for which
$a=d=0$ and the trace is the single point $\{0\}$. For $e:=E_0(1+i)e_1$ one
has $a=d=E_0e_1$, so the polarization is linear with trace the segment
$[-\sqrt2E_0,\sqrt2E_0]e_1$ and $H=0$; the classification (b) of
[[def-em-polarization-definition]] covers this case without requiring $a$ and
$d$ to be orthogonal.

(v) [Verification and scope] In every case $b=k\times e/\omega$ with
$|k|=\omega/c$, so the amplitude equations hold and the fields are smooth
source-free solutions by [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]; the amplitudes and
the semiaxis lengths carry the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, and
$|B|=|E|/c$ holds pointwise. The examples assert no empirical realization and
no measured polarization.
items.strategy: Direct substitution: for each choice compute $a=\operatorname{Re}e$, $d=\operatorname{Im}e$, the trace $a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$, the helicity sign $H=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle$ with $\hat k=e_3$, and $b=k\times e/\omega$; then apply the classification clauses (b),(c) of [[def-em-polarization-definition]] and the amplitude conditions of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]](b). For (ii) the identity $|E|=E_0$ follows from $|a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta|^2=|a|^2\cos^2\theta+|d|^2\sin^2\theta$ when $\langle a,d\rangle=0$ and $|a|=|d|$. For (iv) the trace values are $E_0(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)$, whose range is $[-\sqrt2E_0,\sqrt2E_0]$. Nothing beyond the listed suppliers is used, and no physical interpretation is added.
items.physical_scope: Explicit ideal plane-wave amplitude choices on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ in a named inertial frame with SI units: linear, circular (both handedness signs), elliptical with orthogonal axes, the zero wave and one dependent-amplitude linear edge case. Excluded: partially polarized light, superposition with other waves, and any empirical or measurement claim.

items.title: A nonzero whole-space plane wave has infinite total energy
items.statement:
Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-energy and compact-source comparison branches (ii), (iii), as required by their measure and wave-Cauchy suppliers. The explicit plane-wave fields of (i) use no choice.

Fix $K>0$, $\omega:=cK$, $k:=Ke_3$, $E_0>0$
(unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$), the amplitude $e:=E_0e_1$ and
$b:=k\times e/\omega=(E_0/c)e_2$, and let $(E,B)$ be the corresponding
plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ with energy
density $u$ of [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]; write
$\theta(x,t)=Kx_3-\omega t$. Then:

(i) [Explicit density] $E=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$,
$B=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$ and
$u(x,t)=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2\theta(x,t)$, a nonnegative function vanishing
exactly on the nodal planes $\cos\theta=0$; the period average at every fixed
$x$ is $\langle u\rangle=\varepsilon_0E_0^2/2>0$, uniformly in $x$ and $t$
([[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]](a)).

(ii) [Unbounded box integrals] Fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and let
$R\ge(\omega|t|+\pi/4)/K$. On the sub-box
$Q_R:=[-R,R]^2\times[(\omega t-\pi/4)/K,\,(\omega t+\pi/4)/K]$ of the box
$[-R,R]^3$ one has $\cos^2\theta\ge1/2$, hence
$u\ge\varepsilon_0E_0^2/2$ there; both boxes are product boxes with finite
volume ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]), $u$ is continuous on
them and therefore Riemann integrable
([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]), and
monotonicity of the multidimensional Darboux integral
([[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]],
[[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]]) gives
$$\int_{[-R,R]^3}u(x,t)\,dx\;\ge\;\int_{Q_R}u(x,t)\,dx\;\ge\;\frac{\varepsilon_0E_0^2}{2}\,\mathrm{vol}(Q_R)\;=\;\frac{\pi\varepsilon_0E_0^2}{K}\,R^2\;\longrightarrow\;+\infty\quad(R\to\infty).$$
Consequently the box integrals have no finite limit as
$R\to\infty$: the ideal plane wave has infinite total energy in the
box-exhaustion sense, in contrast to the total energy of a single wave 'mode'
being finite on any bounded box.

(iii) [Contrast with compactly supported data] If instead the constrained data
of [[pthm-em-general-wave-ivp]] vanish off a compact set, then by clause (d) of
that theorem the fields have compact spatial support at each time, and the
instantaneous total energy is the integral of the continuous density $u$
over a bounding closed box containing its support, hence finite. So finite total energy is available for
compactly supported data, while the ideal plane wave of (i)-(ii) is not a
finite-energy configuration.

(iv) [Scope] The example is an exact computation for the ideal plane wave; it
reports no measurement, and "infinite total energy" means the divergence
statement (ii), not a claim about any laboratory field or finite beam.
items.strategy: For (i) use $k\times e=(Ke_3)\times(E_0e_1)=KE_0e_2$ and the definitions of $E,B,u$: $u=(\varepsilon_0/2)|E|^2+(1/(2\mu_0))|B|^2=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2\theta$ by $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\varepsilon_0$, and $\langle\cos^2\rangle=1/2$ is the real-amplitude case of [[lem-em-period-average]] (equivalently (a) of [[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]] with $|e|^2=E_0^2$). For (ii) the range condition on $R$ places $Q_R$ inside $[-R,R]^3$; on $Q_R$, $|Kx_3-\omega t|\le\pi/4$ gives $\cos^2\theta\ge1/2$, and the comparison of integrals is the elementary monotonicity of the multidimensional Darboux integral for continuous integrands over boxes, with $\mathrm{vol}(Q_R)=(2R)^2\cdot\pi/(2K)$ from [[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]. The bound is $\pi\varepsilon_0E_0^2R^2/K\to\infty$. Part (iii) quotes clause (d) of [[pthm-em-general-wave-ivp]] and the finite integral of its continuous density over a nondegenerate bounding closed box, with zero density outside. No empirical input is used.
items.physical_scope: An exact computation for one explicit ideal plane-wave configuration on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: the positivity and uniformity of the period-averaged energy density, the divergence of the box integrals, and the contrast with compactly supported finite-energy data. No measured quantity, no finite beam and no empirical claim.

items.title: Ideal absorber and ideal reflector momentum transfer (radiation pressure)
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
[[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis under which the fixed-volume clause
of the momentum balance is stated. Idealised setup: the vacuum region is
$\{x_3<0\}$ and a material body occupies $\{x_3>0\}$ with plane surface
$x_3=0$; an incident plane wave of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] with
$k=Ke_3$ ($K>0$, $\omega=cK$), $e=E_0e_1$ ($E_0>0$, unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$) and $b=(E_0/c)e_2$ propagates in the $+e_3$
direction. By [[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]] its period-averaged Poynting
flux is $\langle S\rangle=I\hat k$ with $I=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}E_0^2$, and
its period-averaged normal Maxwell stress is $\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle=-I/c$
([[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] for $\sigma$). All period-averaged
quantities below are independent of time. Let $A>0$ be the area (in
$\mathrm m^2$) of a finite rectangular surface patch, let
$F\in\mathbb R^3$ be its period-averaged force (in N), and let $p\in\mathbb R$
be the signed normal force per unit area (in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m^{-2}$).
The adopted boundary-force law below sets $F=A p e_3$; these are patch
quantities in the uniform infinite-plane model. Two idealised models of the surface:

(i) [Ideal absorber] Adopt (A1) no reflected vacuum field and a zero back-face
stress for an ideal absorption layer, and (A2) the force on each surface patch
is given by the pillbox limit of the momentum balance, i.e. its signed pressure is the difference
$\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle_{\mathrm{back}}-\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle$ of
the back-face and incident-side normal stresses, with the back-face stress set
to zero by (A1). This is an exterior boundary-force model: the incident vacuum
field is not asserted to extend by zero across a sharp interface as a global
Maxwell solution. A real absorption layer must supply a compatible
material-field solution; no such realization is claimed here. Applying
[[pthm-em-momentum-balance]](b) to a fixed box inside the vacuum region with
one face at $x_3=-\delta$ and period-averaging (the time derivative of the
averaged field momentum of a periodic configuration has zero mean,
[[thm-ftc-second-part]] applied to the periodic integrated momentum) shows
$\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle$ is constant in $x_3$ in the vacuum region, so
$\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle=-I/c$. Then the force per unit area is
$p=I/c$ and $F/A=(I/c)\,\hat k$: the wave pushes the absorber along its direction of
propagation with pressure $I/c$.

(ii) [Ideal reflector] Adopt instead (A1') the field on the material side
vanishes identically while the vacuum field is the sum of the incident wave and
the reflected plane wave with $k'=-k$, $e'=-e$ (so that the tangential
electric field vanishes on $x_3=0$; the sum is a source-free solution by
[[pthm-em-linear-superposition]]), together with the same boundary-force law
(A2) with zero material-side stress. Compute the averaged normal stress of the
standing wave directly: the real fields satisfy
$E=E_0[\cos(Kx_3-\omega t)-\cos(Kx_3+\omega t)]e_1=2E_0\sin(Kx_3)\sin(\omega t)e_1$
and $B=(2E_0/c)\cos(Kx_3)\cos(\omega t)e_2$, whose cross terms cancel
identically in $\sigma_{33}=-(\varepsilon_0/2)|E|^2-(1/(2\mu_0))|B|^2$; with
$\langle\sin^2\rangle=\langle\cos^2\rangle=1/2$ this gives
$\langle\sigma_{33}(0^-)\rangle=-\varepsilon_0E_0^2=-2I/c$ (the incident and
reflected waves contribute $-I/c$ each). Hence $p=2I/c$ and $F/A=(2I/c)\,\hat k$: twice the
absorbing pressure, because the momentum of the reflected wave is reversed.

(iii) [Status] The absorber back-face and reflector vanishing-field
idealisations (A1)/(A1') and the boundary-force law (A2) are adopted model
assumptions of this thought experiment, not derived material laws and not
observations; the deduction from them with the computed averaged stresses is
complete and conditional. The setup idealises an infinite plane beam at normal
incidence on an infinite plane surface; oblique incidence, finite beams, real
absorbers and any magnetisation/current response of a material require a
material model and are excluded. No measured pressure is reported and no
empirical or statistical claim is made.
items.strategy: Deduction from the stated idealisations. Incident wave data: $k\times e=KE_0e_2$, so the amplitudes satisfy [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]](b) and (c) of [[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]] gives $I=\varepsilon_0cE_0^2/2$ and $\langle\sigma_{33}\rangle=-I/c$ for a single monochromatic wave. In (i), the vacuum fields are the incident wave alone; the fixed-volume balance [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]](b) for a finite open box $(-R,R)^2\times(-L,-\delta)$, with $R>0$ and $0<\delta<L$, whose compact closure is inside the vacuum region (where the field is a smooth source-free solution and $f=0$) with $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and the period average gives the third-component balance $0=\langle\sigma_{33}(-\delta)\rangle-\langle\sigma_{33}(-L)\rangle$, after division by the transverse area $4R^2$. The lateral third-component stress fluxes vanish since $\sigma_{31}=\sigma_{32}=0$ for these transverse fields; alternatively opposite lateral faces cancel because the fields are independent of $x_1,x_2$. Thus the limiting exterior value at $0^-$ is $-I/c$; the force law (A2) then gives $p=I/c$ and $F/A=(I/c)e_3$. In (ii), the standing-wave fields are computed explicitly and averaged with [[lem-em-period-average]]; the cross terms cancel identically in $\sigma_{33}$ because $|E|^2$ and $(c^2)$-weighted $|B|^2$ have opposite cross terms for the two counterpropagating waves, leaving $-\varepsilon_0E_0^2=-2I/c$ at $0^-$, whence $p=2I/c$ and $F/A=(2I/c)e_3$ by (A2). The real-vector trig identities and the substitution $\cos A\pm\cos B$, $\sin A\pm\sin B$ are elementary; the averaged squares use $\langle\cos^2\rangle=\langle\sin^2\rangle=1/2$ from [[lem-em-period-average]]. The direction $\hat k$ is $e_3$, the propagation direction of the incident beam. No material law, absorbed or reflected amplitude, or observed force is derived.
items.physical_scope: Adopted idealisations of a plane beam at normal incidence on an infinite plane ideal absorber or ideal reflector, with the pillbox force law as an explicitly stated model assumption; the conclusion is the conditional pressure $I/c$ or $2I/c$ along the propagation direction. Excluded: oblique incidence, finite beams and pulses, real material response, radiation reaction, measurements, and any empirical claim; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is declared for the fixed-volume balance clause.

items.title: Ideal deterministic two-wave interference and its fringe geometry
items.statement:
Let $K>0$, $\omega:=cK$, let $\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ (half the angle between the
beams) and $\varphi\in\mathbb R$, and take the two plane waves of
[[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] with
$$k_1=K(\sin\alpha\,e_1+\cos\alpha\,e_3),\qquad k_2=K(-\sin\alpha\,e_1+\cos\alpha\,e_3),$$
$$e_1^{\mathrm{amp}}=E_0e_2,\qquad e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}=E_0e^{i\varphi}e_2,$$
where $E_0>0$ carries $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and both amplitudes are
polarized along $e_2$, perpendicular to both wavevectors; with
$b_j=k_j\times e_j^{\mathrm{amp}}/\omega$ and $|k_j|=\omega/c$ both pairs
satisfy the amplitude equations of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]], so the
superposition is a source-free smooth Maxwell solution
([[pthm-em-classical-interference]]). Write
$\delta(x):=(k_2-k_1)\cdot x=-2K\sin\alpha\,x_1$. Then:

(i) [Averaged energy density]
$\langle u\rangle(x)=\varepsilon_0E_0^2\bigl[1+\cos^2\alpha\,\cos(2K\sin\alpha\,x_1-\varphi)\bigr]$
for every $x$, by clause (b) of [[pthm-em-classical-interference]] with
$e_1^{\mathrm{amp}}\cdot\overline{e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}}=E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}$ and
$(\hat k_1\times e_1^{\mathrm{amp}})\cdot(\hat k_2\times\overline{e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}})=E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}\cos2\alpha$.

(ii) [Fringes and visibility] At fixed $x_2,x_3$ the averaged energy density is
periodic in $x_1$ with period $\pi/(K\sin\alpha)=\lambda/(2\sin\alpha)$, where
$\lambda=2\pi/K$; its maximum and minimum are
$\varepsilon_0E_0^2(1\pm\cos^2\alpha)$, so the visibility
$V:=\frac{\langle u\rangle_{\max}-\langle u\rangle_{\min}}{\langle u\rangle_{\max}+\langle u\rangle_{\min}}$
equals $\cos^2\alpha=\frac12(1+\hat k_1\cdot\hat k_2)$. In particular
$V\to1$ as $\alpha\downarrow0$ through crossing beams, and $V\to0$ as
$\alpha\to\pi/2$. At $\alpha=0$ with fixed relative phase the profile is
spatially constant: its spatial visibility is $0$ when its value is positive,
and the displayed ratio is undefined when the field vanishes.

(iii) [The promised copropagating amplitude law] For $k_1=k_2=k$ with $|k|=K$ and $k\cdot e_2=0$, retain the common linear
polarization $e_2$ and amplitudes $E_0e_2$, $E_0e^{i\Delta}e_2$ (so that the
sum is the single plane wave with vector amplitude $E_0(1+e^{i\Delta})e_2$),
$\langle u\rangle=\varepsilon_0E_0^2(1+\cos\Delta)=2\varepsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2(\Delta/2)\propto|1+e^{i\Delta}|^2$,
the form used in the double-slit discussion of the content model. Scanning
$\Delta$ gives phase-scan visibility $1$, distinct from spatial visibility at
fixed phase.

(iv) [Statistical qualifications] This is a deterministic prediction of the
classical wave model for the specified coherent two-wave preparation, at every
point of the ideal plane-wave field; a *measured* fringe pattern or detector
histogram would additionally require a declared measurement model (detector
response, finite bin width, background, integration time, sampling) and a
statistical analysis. The example reports no observation, no finite-sample
claim and no visibility estimate from data; in particular classical
electromagnetic waves interfere, so the prediction alone does not discriminate
between classical and quantum descriptions of light. All quantities are
idealized field quantities of the framework.
items.strategy: Specialise clause (b) of [[pthm-em-classical-interference]] to the stated amplitudes: $|e_j^{\mathrm{amp}}|^2=E_0^2$, $e_1^{\mathrm{amp}}\cdot\overline{e_2^{\mathrm{amp}}}=E_0^2e^{-i\varphi}$, and $\hat k_1\times e_2=\sin\alpha\,e_3-\cos\alpha\,e_1$, $\hat k_2\times e_2=-\sin\alpha\,e_3-\cos\alpha\,e_1$ give $(\hat k_1\times e_2)\cdot(\hat k_2\times e_2)=\cos2\alpha$ by the coordinate cross product [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; the formula (i) follows with $W=2E_0^2\cos^2\alpha\,e^{-i(\delta+\varphi)}$. Part (ii) reads off the period, maxima, minima and visibility from (i). Part (iii) is clause (c) of [[pthm-em-classical-interference]] with $|a_1e_1+a_2e_2|^2=2E_0^2(1+\cos\Delta)$. Part (iv) is a scope statement: the field-theoretic identities are exact for the specified preparation, and no statistical model or dataset is introduced. No additional supplier is used.
items.physical_scope: A deterministic interference computation for two explicit ideal coherent plane waves of equal frequency and amplitude in a named inertial frame with SI units: averaged energy density, fringe period, visibility and the copropagating amplitude law. Excluded: real sources and detectors, finite coherence and bandwidth, sampling and noise models, finite-sample statistics, and any empirical claim; no discrimination between classical and quantum descriptions is asserted.
