items.title: Oblique-incidence TE and TM Fresnel amplitudes, the flux budget, Brewster's angle and total internal reflection
items.statement:
Assume the following plane-interface setting with the same stationary interface identities as [[pthm-em-phase-matching]]: two homogeneous isotropic lossless scalar media at rest (medium 1 in $\{x_3<0\}$, constants $\varepsilon_1,\mu_1>0$; medium 2 in $\{x_3>0\}$, constants $\varepsilon_2,\mu_2>0$; both $\sigma=0$), the plane interface $S=\{x_3=0\}$ with normal $n=e_3$, and the plane-wave structure of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]]. Let $\omega>0$, let $\kappa\in\mathbb R^{2}$ (identified with the tangential plane $\{x_3=0\}$) satisfy $0<|\kappa|<K_1:=\omega(\varepsilon_1\mu_1)^{1/2}$, put $k_{13}:=\sqrt{K_1^{2}-|\kappa|^{2}}>0$ and define wavevectors $$k_i:=\kappa+k_{13}\,n,\qquad k_r:=\kappa-k_{13}\,n,\qquad k_t:=\kappa+k_{t3}\,n,$$ where $k_{t3}\in\mathbb C$ satisfies $k_{t3}^{2}=K_2^{2}-|\kappa|^{2}$ with $K_2:=\omega(\varepsilon_2\mu_2)^{1/2}$ and is selected by non-growth in the $x_3>0$ half-space: $$k_{t3}=\sqrt{K_2^{2}-|\kappa|^{2}}>0\ \ (|\kappa|<K_2),\qquad k_{t3}=0\ \ (|\kappa|=K_2),\qquad k_{t3}=i eta,\  eta:=\sqrt{|\kappa|^{2}-K_2^{2}}>0\ \ (|\kappa|>K_2).$$ [This transmitted phase data is the interface-consistent, bounded choice: the propagating and evanescent branches of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](d),(e); the common $(\kappa,\omega)$ is declared here for each actual wave, also when a reflected amplitude is zero or the critical transmitted root is zero; the nonzero phase-matching theorem explains this matching where its hypotheses apply, and an absent reflected field has no determined phase labels.] Fix the orthonormal tangential frame $\hat\kappa:=\kappa/|\kappa|$ and $\hat y:=n	imes\hat\kappa$, and consider the two polarisations: (s) [transverse electric] $e_i=E_i\hat y$, $e_r=E_r\hat y$, $e_t=E_t\hat y$ with $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$, $E_i
e0$, and $h_j:=k_j	imes e_j/(\mu_j\omega)$; (p) [transverse magnetic] $h_i=H_i\hat y$, $h_r=H_r\hat y$, $h_t=H_t\hat y$ with $H_i,H_r,H_t\in\mathbb C$, $H_i
e0$, and electric amplitudes $e_j:=-(k_j	imes\hat y)H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)$ (the same computation shows that in both cases the pairs satisfy the amplitude conditions of [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](b) in their media). For each polarisation define the amplitudes along the fixed tangential directions $E^{(s)}_j:=e_j\cdot\hat y$ and, in the case (p), $E^{(p)}_j:=e_j\cdot\hat x$ with $\hat x:=\hat\kappa$; assume the four stationary interface identities of [[pthm-em-phase-matching]] hold on $\mathbb R^{2}	imes I$ for a nonempty open interval $I$. Then: (a) [Amplitude system] for $\chi=s$ in every branch, and for $\chi=p$ when $k_{t3}
e0$, the tangential interface identities reduce to $$E^{\chi}_i+E^{\chi}_r=E^{\chi}_t,\qquad Y^{\chi}_1 igl(E^{\chi}_i-E^{\chi}_r igr)=Y^{\chi}_2E^{\chi}_t,$$ with the admittances $$Y^s_1= rac{k_{13}}{\mu_1\omega},\qquad Y^p_1= rac{\varepsilon_1\omega}{k_{13}},\qquad Y^s_2= rac{k_{t3}}{\mu_2\omega},\qquad Y^p_2= rac{\varepsilon_2\omega}{k_{t3}}\quad(k_{t3}
e0).$$ Write $k_{j3}:=k_j\cdot n$ for the signed components, so $k_{i3}=k_{13}$ and $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$. Here $Y_1^\chi>0$ uses the positive incident normal magnitude $k_{13}$, whereas the signed reflected component is $k_r\cdot n=-k_{13}$; $Y_1^\chi$ is not defined from that negative component. No $Y_2^p$ is defined at $k_{t3}=0$. Hence, whenever $Y^{\chi}_1+Y^{\chi}_2
e0$, $$r_\chi:= rac{E^{\chi}_r}{E^{\chi}_i}= rac{Y^{\chi}_1-Y^{\chi}_2}{Y^{\chi}_1+Y^{\chi}_2},\qquad t_\chi:= rac{E^{\chi}_t}{E^{\chi}_i}= rac{2Y^{\chi}_1}{Y^{\chi}_1+Y^{\chi}_2}$$ ([[lem-em-admittance-interface-solve]](a)); the reflected and transmitted amplitude symbols are defined by these fixed-direction conventions, and sign conventions for full vector amplitudes may reverse a reflected amplitude relative to this convention. (b) [Propagating branch and Snell's law] if $|\kappa|<K_2$ then all three wavevectors are real, $Y_1^s,Y_1^p,Y_2^s,Y_2^p>0$ are real, and with $	heta_j\in(0,\pi/2)$ defined by $\sin	heta_j=|\kappa|/|k_j|$ one has $	heta_r=	heta_i$ and $n_1\sin	heta_i=n_2\sin	heta_t$, $n_j=c(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}$ ([[pthm-em-phase-matching]](c), [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]); the period-averaged normal fluxes are $Y^{\chi}_1|E^{\chi}_i|^{2}/2$, $-Y^{\chi}_1|E^{\chi}_r|^{2}/2$ and $Y^{\chi}_2|E^{\chi}_t|^{2}/2$, so $$R_\chi:=|r_\chi|^{2},\qquad T_\chi:= rac{Y^{\chi}_2}{Y^{\chi}_1}|t_\chi|^{2},\qquad R_\chi+T_\chi=1 .$$ (c) [Brewster condition] In the finite-admittance branches, $r_\chi=0$ if and only if $Y^{\chi}_1=Y^{\chi}_2$; in particular, if $\mu_1=\mu_2$ and $|\kappa|<K_2$, for unequal indices $n_1
e n_2$, $r_p=0$ holds at exactly one admissible incidence angle $	heta_B\in(0,\pi/2)$, characterised by $	an	heta_B=n_2/n_1$, and $r_s
e0$ at that angle. For equal indices $n_1=n_2$ (and equal permeabilities), the media are identical, $Y_1^\chi=Y_2^\chi$ and $r_s=r_p=0$, $t_s=t_p=1$ for every allowed incidence angle; there is no unique distinguished Brewster angle. (d) [Total internal reflection] if $|\kappa|>K_2$ (which requires $n_1>n_2$, $	heta_i:=\arcsin(|\kappa|/K_1)\in(0,\pi/2)$, $|\kappa|=K_1\sin	heta_i$ and $	heta_i>	heta_c:=\arcsin(n_2/n_1)$), then $Y^{s}_2=i eta/(\mu_2\omega)$ and $Y^{p}_2=-i\varepsilon_2\omega/ eta$ are purely imaginary, $$|r_s|=|r_p|=1,\qquad t_s,t_p
e0,\qquad |t_\chi|^{2}= rac{4(Y^{\chi}_1)^{2}}{(Y^{\chi}_1)^{2}+|Y^{\chi}_2|^{2}}>0,$$ the transmitted field decays as $e^{- eta x_3}$ and its period-averaged normal flux vanishes identically while its tangential averaged flux does not vanish ([[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]](e)); the reflected wave carries the whole incident normal averaged flux. (e) [Critical angle] if $|\kappa|=K_2$ then $k_{t3}=0$: the transmitted wave travels along the interface, its tangential electric amplitude vanishes in the (p) case and $Y^{s}_2=0$ in the (s) case, and $r_s=1$, $t_s=2$, $r_p=-1$, $t_p=0$ with vanishing transmitted normal averaged flux. The critical TM branch is solved from the nonsingular equations $E_i^p+E_r^p=k_{t3}H_t/(\omega\varepsilon_2)=0$ and $H_i+H_r=H_t$, not by dividing by $k_{t3}$; they give $H_r=H_i$ and $H_t=2H_i$. The transmitted TM electric vector can have a nonzero normal component even though its tangential amplitude is zero. (f) [Scope] the statements are conditional on the interface identities and on the given wave data; no existence or uniqueness of interface-consistent data is claimed. Excluded: anisotropic media, complex $\varepsilon$ or $\mu$ and absorption in either medium (only the lossless dielectric case with the evanescent transmitted branch is covered), dispersive media, moving media, the ideal conductor, nonlinear response, and all claims about signal speeds, group velocities, information transfer or empirical data. The statements for $Y^{\chi}_1+Y^{\chi}_2=0$ (which cannot occur in the stated branches, where $\operatorname{Re}Y^{\chi}_1>0$ and $\operatorname{Re}Y^{\chi}_2\ge0$) are excluded; the notation 'angle of refraction' is used only where $k_t$ is real.
items.strategy:
Proof technique: direct; verify the amplitude conditions for the two polarisation families, reduce the tangential interface identities to scalar admittance systems in the fixed frame, and read off the propagating, Brewster, evanescent and critical cases from the admittance algebra and the medium plane-wave structure. 1.1 [Both polarisation families satisfy the amplitude conditions] For (s), $k_j\cdot e_j=E_j\,k_j\cdot\hat y=0$ because $k_j=\kappa+k_{j3}n$ and $\hat y\perp\kappa,n$; and $k_j	imes e_j=E_jk_j	imes\hat y=E_j(\kappa	imes\hat y+k_{j3}n	imes\hat y)=E_j(|\kappa|n-k_{j3}\hat x)$ by [F5], which equals $\omega\mu_jh_j$ with $h_j=k_j	imes e_j/(\mu_j\omega)$ by definition. For (p), $e_j=-(k_j	imes\hat y)H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)$ and $k_j\cdot e_j=0$ because $k_j\cdot(k_j	imes\hat y)=0$ by the orthogonality in [F5]; further $k_j	imes e_j=-(k_j	imes(k_j	imes\hat y))H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)= igl[(k_j\cdot k_j)\hat y-k_j(k_j\cdot\hat y) igr]H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)=(\varepsilon_j\mu_j\omega^2)\hat yH_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)=\omega\mu_jH_j\hat y=\omega\mu_jh_j$, using $k_j\cdot\hat y=0$ and $k_j\cdot k_j=\varepsilon_j\mu_j\omega^2$ of [F1]. In (s), $k_j\cdot h_j=0$ by cross-product orthogonality, and $k_j	imes h_j=-\omega\varepsilon_j e_j$ follows by expanding $k_j	imes(k_j	imes e_j)=k_j(k_j\cdot e_j)-(k_j\cdot k_j)e_j$ and using dispersion. In (p), $k_j\cdot h_j=0$ because $\hat y$ is perpendicular to $k_j$, and $k_j	imes h_j=-\omega\varepsilon_j e_j$ is the definition of $e_j$. Thus all four amplitude conditions hold in both families, including zero reflected or transmitted amplitudes. [given, F1, F5, F7, algebra] 2.1 [The tangential interface identities in the fixed frame] By the orthogonal decomposition of [F5], the tangential parts of the electric amplitudes are: for (s), $e_j^	au=e_j=E_j\hat y$; for (p), $e_j^	au=(k_{j3}H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j))\hat x$ because $e_j=(k_{j3}\hat x-|\kappa|n)H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)$ from $k_j	imes\hat y=|\kappa|n-k_{j3}\hat x$ by [F5]. The magnetic tangential traces are obtained as follows: $h_j=H_j\hat y$ in (p), and in (s) $h_j=E_j(\kappa	imes\hat y+k_{j3}n	imes\hat y)/(\mu_j\omega)=E_j(|\kappa|n-k_{j3}\hat x)/(\mu_j\omega)$ with tangential part $-k_{j3}E_j\hat x/(\mu_j\omega)$ and, for the reflected wave with $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$, tangential part $+k_{13}E_r\hat x/(\mu_1\omega)$. Since the interface identities hold for all $(y,t)$ with the common $(\kappa,\omega)$, each has the form $\operatorname{Re} igl(W e^{i(\kappa\cdot y-\omega t)} igr)=0$ for a constant tangential vector $W$. Since $n=e_3$, $n	imes(w_1,w_2,0)=(-w_2,w_1,0)$, so the cross-product trace identities are equivalent to these real-part identities. Fixing any $y$ and allowing $t$ to vary in $I$, the time-line proof of the amplitude-vanishing clause (a) of [F1] gives $W=0$. Concretely: the tangential electric identity gives $E_i+E_r=E_t$ in (s) and $E^{(p)}_i+E^{(p)}_r=E^{(p)}_t$ in (p); the tangential magnetic identity gives $k_{t3}E_t/(\mu_2\omega)=k_{13}(E_i-E_r)/(\mu_1\omega)$ in (s) and $H_i+H_r=H_t$ in (p), where $E^{(p)}_j=k_{j3}H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)$ by definition, and when $k_{t3}
e0$, converting $H_j=Y^p_jE^{(p)}_j$ for $j=i,t$ and $H_r=-Y^p_1E^{(p)}_r$ (the reflected sign entering through $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$) turns the last identity into $Y^p_1(E^{(p)}_i-E^{(p)}_r)=Y^p_2E^{(p)}_t$. Writing $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu_1\omega)$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)$, $Y^p_1=\varepsilon_1\omega/k_{13}$ and $Y^p_2=\varepsilon_2\omega/k_{t3}$ when $k_{t3}
e0$ gives the two systems of (a). [given, A1, step 1.1, F5, F7, algebra] 3.1 [Solution of the systems, part (a)] In the (s) branch, $Y^s_1>0$ is real and positive, and $Y^s_2$ is real positive for $|\kappa|<K_2$, zero at the critical point, and $i eta/(\mu_2\omega)$ for $|\kappa|>K_2$; in every case $\operatorname{Re}(Y^s_1+Y^s_2)=Y^s_1+\operatorname{Re}Y^s_2\ge Y^s_1>0$, so $Y^s_1+Y^s_2
e0$. In the (p) branch with $k_{t3}
e0$, $\operatorname{Re}Y^p_1=Y^p_1>0$ and $\operatorname{Re}Y^p_2=0$ or $>0$, so again $Y^p_1+Y^p_2
e0$. The admittance lemma [F3](a) therefore applies to each scalar system of step 2.1 and gives $r_\chi=(Y^\chi_1-Y^\chi_2)/(Y^\chi_1+Y^\chi_2)$ and $t_\chi=2Y^\chi_1/(Y^\chi_1+Y^\chi_2)$; in particular $t_\chi
e0$ because its numerator $2Y^\chi_1
e0$. [step 2.1, F3, F7, algebra] 3.2 [Critical angle, part (e)] Let $|\kappa|=K_2$; then $k_{t3}=0$ by [F6], so $Y^s_2=0$ and no $Y^p_2$ is defined (a division by $k_{t3}$ is not performed). For (s), the system of step 2.1 reads $E_i+E_r=E_t$ and $Y^s_1(E_i-E_r)=0$ with $Y^s_1>0$, so $E_r=E_i$ and $E_t=2E_i$, i.e. $r_s=1$ and $t_s=2$. For (p), $E^{(p)}_t=k_{t3}H_t/(\omega\varepsilon_2)=0$ and $E^{(p)}_i=k_{13}H_i/(\omega\varepsilon_1)$, $E^{(p)}_r=-k_{13}H_r/(\omega\varepsilon_1)$ by the fixed-direction definitions of step 2.1; the tangential electric identity $E^{(p)}_i+E^{(p)}_r=0$ gives $H_r=H_i$, and the tangential magnetic identity $H_i+H_r=H_t$ gives $H_t=2H_i$; hence $r_p=E^{(p)}_r/E^{(p)}_i=-H_r/H_i=-1$ and $t_p=E^{(p)}_t/E^{(p)}_i=0$. The transmitted normal averaged flux vanishes: $\langle S_t\cdot nangle=	frac12\operatorname{Re} igl((e_t	imes\overline h_t)\cdot n igr)$ by [F4], and with $h_t=H_t\hat y$ and $e_t=-(k_t	imes\hat y)H_t/(\omega\varepsilon_2)=-|\kappa|H_tn/(\omega\varepsilon_2)$ (because $k_t=\kappa$ and $\kappa	imes\hat y=|\kappa|n$ by [F5]), the vector $e_t	imes\overline h_t$ is a multiple of $n	imes\hat y$, which is orthogonal to $n$: $(e_t	imes\overline h_t)\cdot n=0$. In the TE case $e_t=E_t\hat y$ and $h_t=|\kappa|E_tn/(\mu_2\omega)$, so $e_t	imes\overline h_t$ is tangential and its normal component is also zero. The transmitted TM electric vector $-|\kappa|H_tn/(\omega\varepsilon_2)$ has a nontrivial normal component whenever $H_t
e0$. [step 2.1, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra] 4.1 [Propagating branch: angles and fluxes, part (b)] Let $|\kappa|<K_2$. Then $k_{t3}=\sqrt{K_2^2-|\kappa|^2}>0$ and all three wavevectors are real by [F6]; the four admittances of step 2.1 are real and positive. With $|k_i|=|k_r|=K_1$ and $|k_t|=K_2$ from $|k_j|^2=|\kappa|^2+k_{j3}^2$, the angles $	heta_j:=\arcsin(|\kappa|/|k_j|)\in(0,\pi/2)$ are well defined by [F8] since $0<|\kappa|<\min\{K_1,K_2\}$; then $\sin	heta_r=|\kappa|/K_1=\sin	heta_i$, so $	heta_r=	heta_i$ by the strict increase of sine and of $\arcsin$ in [F8], and $K_1\sin	heta_i=|\kappa|=K_2\sin	heta_t$, which is $n_1\sin	heta_i=n_2\sin	heta_t$ after multiplying by $c/\omega$ and using $n_j=cK_j/\omega=c(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}$ by [F6]; this is the same angle law as [F2]. The period-averaged normal fluxes: for (s), the flux of [F1] is $\langle S_jangle=|e_j|^2k_j/(2\mu_j\omega)$ with $|e_j|^2=|E^{(s)}_j|^2$ and $k_j\cdot n=k_{j3}$, so the normal fluxes are $k_{j3}|E^{(s)}_j|^2/(2\mu_j\omega)$, i.e. $Y^s_1|E^{(s)}_i|^2/2$, $-Y^s_1|E^{(s)}_r|^2/2$, $Y^s_2|E^{(s)}_t|^2/2$; for (p) the same $\langle S_j\cdot nangle=|e_j|^2k_{j3}/(2\mu_j\omega)$ equals $Y^p_j\,|E^{(p)}_j|^2/2$ up to the reflected sign, because $|e_j|^2=\mu_j|H_j|^2/\varepsilon_j$ and $|E^{(p)}_j|=|k_{j3}||H_j|/(\varepsilon_j\omega)$ give $|e_j|^2k_{j3}/(2\mu_j\omega)=k_{j3}|H_j|^2/(2\varepsilon_j\omega)$ for the incident and transmitted signs, while the reflected signed component $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$ produces the minus sign, as in the Statement. With $R_\chi=|r_\chi|^2=|E^\chi_r|^2/|E^\chi_i|^2$ and $T_\chi=(Y^\chi_2/Y^\chi_1)|t_\chi|^2=Y^\chi_2|E^\chi_t|^2/(Y^\chi_1|E^\chi_i|^2)$, the budget $R_\chi+T_\chi=1$ is [F3](b) applied with the real positive $Y^\chi_1,Y^\chi_2$. [step 3.1, F1, F2, F3, F6, F8, algebra] 4.2 [Total internal reflection, part (d)] Let $|\kappa|>K_2$; then $K_2<K_1$, so $n_2<n_1$, and $k_{t3}=i eta$ with $ eta=\sqrt{|\kappa|^2-K_2^2}>0$ by [F6]. Hence $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)=i eta/(\mu_2\omega)$ and $Y^p_2=\varepsilon_2\omega/(i eta)=-i\varepsilon_2\omega/ eta$ are purely imaginary by [F7], while $Y^\chi_1>0$ is real; the admittance lemma [F3](c) gives $|r_s|=|r_p|=1$ and $|t_\chi|^2=4(Y^\chi_1)^2/((Y^\chi_1)^2+|Y^\chi_2|^2)>0$, so $t_\chi
e0$. The transmitted wave is the evanescent branch of [F1] with $n'=n$, $\kappa_0=\kappa$ and $k_t\cdot k_t=K_2^2=\varepsilon_2\mu_2\omega^2$: the field factorizes with the decay factor $e^{- eta x_3}$, its period-averaged normal flux vanishes identically, and its tangential averaged flux is strictly positive; since $|r_\chi|=1$, the reflected normal averaged flux equals minus the incident normal averaged flux, i.e. the reflected wave carries the whole incident normal averaged flux. [step 3.1, F1, F3, F6, F7, algebra] 5.1 [Brewster condition, part (c)] In each finite-admittance branch the formula of step 3.1 gives $r_\chi=0$ exactly when the numerator $Y^\chi_1-Y^\chi_2$ vanishes, i.e. $Y^\chi_1=Y^\chi_2$. Assume now $\mu_1=\mu_2=:\mu$ and $|\kappa|<K_2$, so that the (p) admittances are real positive. The condition $Y^p_1=Y^p_2$ reads $\varepsilon_1/k_{13}=\varepsilon_2/k_{t3}$; substituting $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$ and $k_{j3}=(\omega n_j/c)\cos	heta_j$ (from $k_{13}=K_1\cos	heta_i=(\omega n_1/c)\cos	heta_i$ and $k_{t3}=K_2\cos	heta_t=(\omega n_2/c)\cos	heta_t$) gives $n_1\cos	heta_t=n_2\cos	heta_i$. Together with Snell's law $n_1\sin	heta_i=n_2\sin	heta_t$ of step 4.1, squaring both and eliminating $\sin^2	heta_t$ gives $(n_1^2-n_2^2) igl[n_2^2-(n_1^2+n_2^2)\sin^2	heta_i igr]=0$: indeed $n_1^2(1-\sin^2	heta_t)=n_2^2\cos^2	heta_i$ and $\sin	heta_t=(n_1/n_2)\sin	heta_i$ yield $n_1^2n_2^2-n_1^4\sin^2	heta_i=n_2^4-n_2^4\sin^2	heta_i$, i.e. $n_2^2(n_1^2-n_2^2)=(n_1^2-n_2^2)(n_1^2+n_2^2)\sin^2	heta_i$. If $n_1
e n_2$, division by the nonzero first factor gives $\sin^2	heta_i=n_2^2/(n_1^2+n_2^2)$; since $0<	heta_i<\pi/2$ and sine is strictly increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$ with $\sin 0=0$ by [F8], this determines the unique admissible angle $	heta_B:=\arcsin igl(n_2/\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2} igr)\in(0,\pi/2)$, This angle is admissible: with $D:=\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}$, its tangential wavenumber is $K_1n_2/D<K_2$ because $n_1/D<1$. Snell's law therefore gives $\sin	heta_t=n_1/D$ and, by positivity of both cosines and the Pythagorean identity, $\cos	heta_i=n_1/D$, $\cos	heta_t=n_2/D$. Thus $n_1\cos	heta_t=n_2\cos	heta_i$, establishing $Y_1^p=Y_2^p$ and $r_p=0$; this proves sufficiency as well as uniqueness. At this angle $\cos	heta_B>0$: cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ by [F8], so $0<	heta_B<\pi/2$ gives $\cos	heta_B>\cos(\pi/2)=0$. The Pythagorean identity of [F8] then gives $\cos	heta_B=\sqrt{1-\sin^2	heta_B}=n_1/\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}$, so $	an	heta_B=\sin	heta_B/\cos	heta_B=n_2/n_1$ by the definition of tangent in [F8]; no other admissible angle has this tangent, because tangent is strictly increasing on $(0,\pi/2)$ by [F8]. Also $r_s
e0$ at $	heta_B$, because $Y^s_1=Y^s_2$ would give $k_{13}=k_{t3}$ (the $\mu$ factors being equal), hence $K_1^2=|\kappa|^2+k_{13}^2=|\kappa|^2+k_{t3}^2=K_2^2$ and $n_1=n_2$, contrary to hypothesis. If instead $n_1=n_2$ and $\mu_1=\mu_2$ then $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$ and the two media are identical: $k_{13}=k_{t3}$ and $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$ give $Y^\chi_1=Y^\chi_2$, so $r_s=r_p=0$ and $t_s=t_p=1$ at every admissible angle (where the (p) formula applies), with no distinguished Brewster angle. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F3, F6, F8, algebra] 6.1 [Scope, part (f)] All clauses are conditional on the given wave data and the interface identities [A1]; the argument used the amplitude conditions and solution structure of [F1], the admittance algebra [F3], the angle conventions of [F2] and [F8], the period averages and stored-energy flux of [F4], and the complex arithmetic of [F7]; the ideal-conductor limit, absorption, dispersion, anisotropy, moving and nonlinear media, signal-speed and group-velocity statements and all empirical claims are excluded. The denominator $Y^\chi_1+Y^\chi_2$ is nonzero in every considered branch because $\operatorname{Re}Y^\chi_1>0$ and $\operatorname{Re}Y^\chi_2\ge0$; the interface identities are stated hypotheses on the noncompact plane (for compact interfaces, [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]), and no choice principle is used, all constructions being finite-dimensional algebra in the given data. items.physical_scope: Conditional oblique-incidence Fresnel theorem for two homogeneous isotropic lossless scalar media at rest at a plane interface, under the stated interface identities: the TE and TM admittance systems, amplitude formulas, the flux budget R_chi+T_chi=1 in the propagating branch, the Brewster condition and the total-internal-reflection identities |r_chi|=1 with decaying transmitted field. Excluded: absorbing, dispersive, anisotropic, moving or nonlinear media, the ideal conductor, existence or uniqueness of interface-consistent data, signal- and group-velocity claims, and all empirical claims.

references.title: David Tong, Electromagnetism, University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos lecture notes (2026 author-hosted revision, 236 pp.)
references.locator: §7.4.1 printed pp. 190-191: the parallel-polarisation interface system $E_I\cos\theta_I+E_R\cos\theta_R=E_T\cos\theta_T$, $(E_I-E_R)/v_1=E_T/v_2$ and its solution (7.27), together with Brewster's angle $\tan\theta_B=n_2/n_1$ from $n_1\cos\theta_T=n_2\cos\theta_I$ and $\theta_I+\theta_T=\pi/2$; §7.4.2 printed pp. 191-193: total internal reflection with $\sin\theta_C=n_2/n_1$, the imaginary normal component $k_T\cdot\hat x=\pm i\omega\alpha/v_2$ and the decaying evanescent transmitted wave. The tangential-electric fixed-direction convention with the reflected sign is the one used in these formulas.

items.title: Numerical check of the good-conductor skin-depth bounds and the $\sigma=0$ exclusion
items.statement: Adopt the isotropic scalar Ohmic branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] at rest and the exact quantities of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]] and [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]]. Let the declared parameters be $$\varepsilon=4\ \mathrm F\,\mathrm m^{-1},\qquad \mu=1\ \mathrm H\,\mathrm m^{-1},\qquad \sigma=100\ \mathrm S\,\mathrm m^{-1},\qquad \omega=3\ \mathrm s^{-1};$$ these are declared model parameters of the illustration, not measured values of any material. The numerical evaluations below use these SI units: $a,b,r$ have unit $\mathrm m^{-2}$, $p,q$ have unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and $\delta$ has unit m; $t=a/b$ is dimensionless. Then: (i) $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}=36$, $b=\mu\sigma\omega=300$, $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}=\sqrt{91296}$ and $t=a/b=3/25=0.12\le1/4$, so the good-conductor regime of [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]](c) applies; (ii) the exact propagation and attenuation constants are $p=\sqrt{(r+36)/2}$ and $q=\sqrt{(r-36)/2}$, with $pq=b/2=150$ exactly; the decimal evaluations $r\approx302.15228$, $p\approx13.00293$, $q\approx11.53586$ satisfy $q<\sqrt{b/2}=\sqrt{150}\approx12.24745$ with $$|q-\sqrt{150}|\approx0.71159\le 2t\sqrt{150}=0.24\sqrt{150}\approx2.93939,$$ and for the skin depth $\delta=1/q\approx0.08669$ against $\sqrt{2/b}=1/\sqrt{150}\approx0.08165$ one has $$|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}|\approx0.00504\le 4t\sqrt{2/b}=0.48\sqrt{2/b}\approx0.03919 .$$ Thus the exact skin depth satisfies the stated good-conductor bound with the margin predicted by the theorem. (iii) for $\sigma=0$ (same $\varepsilon,\mu,\omega$) one has $b=0$, $q=0$, no attenuation and $\delta=+\infty$ by the convention of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]](c); the inequalities of (ii) do not apply, consistently with the exclusion recorded in [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]](f). (iv) [Scope] the computation is an exact check of the stated inequalities for the declared model parameters (with dimensionless ratio $t$); it reports no measurement, no material identification and no empirical claim, and the decimal evaluations are displayed only as approximate illustrations of the exact expressions.
items.strategy: Proof technique: direct substitution in the exact identities and bounds of the skin-depth theorem, with the decimal displays read as roundings of the exact radicals. Given: The declared parameters $\varepsilon=4$, $\mu=1$, $\sigma=100$, $\omega=3$ as the stated dimensionless representatives of the SI quantities of the Example, the branch assumption of [[post-em-material-closure]], and the exact quantities $a,b,r,p,q,\delta,t$ of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]] and [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]]. [A1] The declared Ohmic branch with $\sigma>0$: the plane-wave attenuation theorem [[pthm-em-conducting-skin-depth]] holds, with its clauses (a)-(f) as stated, in particular the exact identities of (b) and the good-conductor bounds of (c) for $t\le1/4$. [F1] The medium parameters ([[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]): $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^2$, $b=\mu\sigma\omega$, $r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, $p=\sqrt{(r+a)/2}$, $q=\sqrt{(r-a)/2}$, $\delta=1/q$ for $\sigma>0$ and $\delta=+\infty$ for $\sigma=0$; $t:=a/b$. 1.1 [Substitution, clause (i)] By [F1], $a=\mu\varepsilon\omega^2=1\cdot4\cdot9=36$ and $b=\mu\sigma\omega=1\cdot100\cdot3=300$; hence $r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=\sqrt{36^2+300^2}=\sqrt{1296+90000}=\sqrt{91296}$ and $t=a/b=36/300=3/25$. The regime condition $3/25\le1/4$ is $12\le25$ after multiplying by $100$, so the good-conductor bounds of [A1](c) apply. [given, A1, F1, algebra] 1.2 [Exact identities, clause (ii)] By [F1] and [A1](b), $p=\sqrt{(r+a)/2}=\sqrt{(\sqrt{91296}+36)/2}$, $q=\sqrt{(r-a)/2}=\sqrt{(\sqrt{91296}-36)/2}$ and $pq=b/2=150$ exactly. Since $91296<336^2=112896$, positivity and the square-root order give $r=\sqrt{91296}<336$, hence $q^2=(r-36)/2<300/2=b/2$, so $q<\sqrt{150}=\sqrt{b/2}$; and the exact bounds of [A1](c) read $|q-\sqrt{150}|\le(6/25)\sqrt{150}=\frac{2\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\mu\sigma\omega}{2}}$ and $|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}|\le(12/25)\sqrt{2/b}=\frac{4\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\mu\sigma\omega}}$. [A1, F1, algebra] 1.3 [The $\sigma=0$ exclusion, clause (iii)] For the same $\varepsilon,\mu,\omega$ and $\sigma=0$, [F1] gives $b=0$, $r=a$, $q=\sqrt{(r-a)/2}=0$ and $\delta=+\infty$ by the convention of [F1]; the identities and bounds of [A1](b),(c) carry the hypothesis $b>0$, equivalently $\sigma>0$, and are not evaluated at $b=0$, which is the exclusion recorded in [A1](f). [given, A1, F1, algebra] 2.1 [Decimal displays and the bound comparisons] The decimal numbers displayed in clause (ii) of the Example are the stated roundings of the exact quantities $r=\sqrt{91296}$, $p=\sqrt{(r+36)/2}$, $q=\sqrt{(r-36)/2}$, $\delta=1/q$, $\sqrt{150}$ and $\sqrt{2/300}$; reading them as roundings, the comparisons $|q-\sqrt{150}|\le(6/25)\sqrt{150}$ and $|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}|\le(12/25)\sqrt{2/b}$ displayed there are instances of the exact inequalities of step 1.2, and the numerical magnitudes quoted in the Example are not independent assertions of exact decimal arithmetic. In particular the inequalities hold with the margin predicted by [A1](c) for the declared dimensionless ratio $t=3/25$. [step 1.2, A1, algebra] 3.1 [Scope, clause (iv)] The computation used only the declared parameters, the branch assumption [A1] and the exact definitions [F1]; it reports no measurement, no material identification and no empirical or statistical claim, and the decimal displays of the Example are approximate illustrations of the exact expressions, as stated. No choice principle is used. [given, step 2.1, step 1.3, A1, F1] ∎
items.physical_scope: Numerical illustration for declared model parameters in the isotropic scalar Ohmic branch: the good-conductor bounds |q-sqrt(b/2)|<=2t*sqrt(b/2) and |delta-sqrt(2/b)|<=4t*sqrt(2/b) at eps*omega/sigma=3/25 and the exclusion of sigma=0 from the finite-depth approximation. Excluded: any measured conductivity, any laboratory material, and any experimental or statistical claim.

references.title: David Tong, Electromagnetism, University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos lecture notes (2026 author-hosted revision, 236 pp.)
references.locator: §7.6.2 printed pp. 207-209: the skin depth $\delta=\sqrt{2/(\mu\omega\sigma_{\mathrm{DC}})}$ and its regime of validity in the low-frequency Ohmic conductor; the numerical values here are declared dimensionless illustrations of that closed form, not data from the source.

references.title: David J. Griffiths, Introduction to Electrodynamics, 3rd edition (Prentice Hall, 1999, 596-page retained scan)
references.locator: §9.4.1 printed pp. 394-395 and Problem 9.19(a),(b) printed p. 396: the good-conductor skin depth $\delta=\lambda/(2\pi)$ and the poor-conductor frequency-independent depth; the monotone comparison of the exact $q$ with $\sqrt{\mu\sigma\omega/2}$ used here is the quantitative form of the source's 'good conductor' discussion. Retained scan with OCR noise; the bounds were verified by the local computation in the batch notes.

items.title: The Brewster angle at an equal-permeability interface and the surviving $s$-reflection
items.statement: Adopt the setting of [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]] with two lossless media at rest, equal permeabilities $\mu_1=\mu_2=:\mu>0$ and declared refractive indices $n_1=1$, $n_2=3/2$ (declared model parameters, not optical measurements), so that $\varepsilon_j=n_j^{2}/(c^{2}\mu)$ and $K_j=n_j\omega/c$ in the notation of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]. Then: (i) [Brewster angle] by [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]](c) the TM amplitude vanishes exactly at the unique angle $\theta_B\in(0,\pi/2)$ with $\tan\theta_B=n_2/n_1=3/2$, i.e. $\sin\theta_B=3/\sqrt{13}$, $\cos\theta_B=2/\sqrt{13}$; the transmitted angle satisfies $n_1\sin\theta_B=n_2\sin\theta_t$, hence $\sin\theta_t=2/\sqrt{13}$, and $\theta_B+\theta_t=\pi/2$; (ii) [Amplitudes] at $\theta_i=\theta_B$ one has $Y^{p}_1=Y^{p}_2=\sqrt{13}/(2c\mu)$, hence $r_p=0$ and $t_p=1$; the remaining $s$-amplitudes are $Y^{s}_1=2/(\sqrt{13}c\mu)$, $Y^{s}_2=9/(2\sqrt{13}c\mu)$ and $$r_s=\frac{2/\sqrt{13}-9/(2\sqrt{13})}{2/\sqrt{13}+9/(2\sqrt{13})}=-\frac{5}{13},\qquad t_s=\frac{8}{13};$$ (iii) [Flux budget] with $R_s=|r_s|^{2}=25/169$ and $T_s=(Y^{s}_2/Y^{s}_1)|t_s|^{2}=(9/4)(64/169)=144/169$ one has $R_s+T_s=169/169=1$ exactly, while the TM channel has $R_p=0$, $T_p=1$; (iv) [Scope] the numbers are declared model parameters; the example is a deterministic computation of the classical interface model, reports no measurement, and a pure TM incident wave has zero reflected field at the Brewster angle. For incident data with a nonzero TE component, the surviving reflected field is TE-polarised because $r_p=0$ and $r_s\ne0$; no unpolarised-beam statistics are modelled here.

Proof technique: direct substitution in the oblique-incidence theorem and the medium parameters, with all numerical values kept exact. Given: The lossless two-media setting of [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]] with $\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu>0$, $n_1=1$, $n_2=3/2$, $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$, and the Brewster angle $	heta_B$ of [A1](c). [A1] The oblique-incidence theorem [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]]: its clause (a) gives the two admittance systems with $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu_1\omega)$, $Y^p_1=\varepsilon_1\omega/k_{13}$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)$, $Y^p_2=\varepsilon_2\omega/k_{t3}$ and the amplitude formulas; clause (b) gives the angle law $n_1\sin	heta_i=n_2\sin	heta_t$, the normal fluxes $Y^\chi_1|E^\chi_i|^2/2$, $-Y^\chi_1|E^\chi_r|^2/2$, $Y^\chi_2|E^\chi_t|^2/2$ and $R_\chi+T_\chi=1$ with $R_\chi=|r_\chi|^2$, $T_\chi=(Y^\chi_2/Y^\chi_1)|t_\chi|^2$; clause (c) gives the unique Brewster angle with $	an	heta_B=n_2/n_1$ for $n_1
e n_2$ and the nonzero $s$-reflection there. [F1] Medium parameters ([[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]): $K_j=\omega(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}=\omega n_j/c$ for $\mu_j=\mu$, $k_{13}=\sqrt{K_1^2-|\kappa|^2}=K_1\cos	heta_i$ and $k_{t3}=K_2\cos	heta_t$ for $|\kappa|<K_2$, and $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$. [F2] Trigonometry: $\sin(\arcsin y)=y$ with sine strictly increasing on $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ ([[def-principal-inverse-sine-and-cosine]]); $	an$ the strictly increasing principal inverse on $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ with $	an(\arctan y)=y$ ([[def-principal-inverse-tangent]]); $	an x=\sin x/\cos x$ ([[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]]); $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$ and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$ ([[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]]); sine strictly increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$ with $\sin 0=0$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]]); and $\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x$ ([[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]). 1.1 [The Brewster angle and its sine and cosine, clause (i)] Since $n_1=1
e3/2=n_2$ and $\mu_1=\mu_2$, [A1](c) gives a unique Brewster angle $	heta_B\in(0,\pi/2)$ with $	an	heta_B=n_2/n_1=3/2$. By [F2], $\sin^2	heta_B=	an^2	heta_B/(1+	an^2	heta_B)=(9/4)/(13/4)=9/13$; since $	heta_B\in(0,\pi/2)$ and sine is strictly increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$ with $\sin 0=0$, $\sin	heta_B>0$, hence $\sin	heta_B=3/\sqrt{13}$; and $\cos	heta_B=\sin	heta_B/	an	heta_B=(3/\sqrt{13})/(3/2)=2/\sqrt{13}$. [A1, F2, algebra] 2.1 [Transmitted angle and the right-angle relation, clause (i)] Snell's law $n_1\sin	heta_B=n_2\sin	heta_t$ of [A1](b) gives $\sin	heta_t=(2/3)(3/\sqrt{13})=2/\sqrt{13}$. Since also $\cos	heta_B=2/\sqrt{13}=\sin	heta_t$ and $\sin(\pi/2-	heta_B)=\cos	heta_B$ by [F2], the equality $\sin	heta_t=\sin(\pi/2-	heta_B)$ holds with $	heta_t,\pi/2-	heta_B\in(0,\pi/2)$; sine is strictly increasing on that interval, hence injective, so $	heta_t=\pi/2-	heta_B$, i.e. $	heta_B+	heta_t=\pi/2$. [step 1.1, A1, F2, algebra] 3.1 [The admittances, clause (ii)] By [F1], $K_1=\omega/c$, $K_2=3\omega/(2c)$, $k_{13}=K_1\cos	heta_B=(\omega/c)(2/\sqrt{13})$ and $k_{t3}=K_2\cos	heta_t=K_2\sin	heta_B=(3\omega/(2c))(3/\sqrt{13})=9\omega/(2\sqrt{13}c)$. With $\varepsilon_1=1/(c^2\mu)$ and $\varepsilon_2=9/(4c^2\mu)$, the admittances of [A1](a) are $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu\omega)=2/(\sqrt{13}c\mu)$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu\omega)=9/(2\sqrt{13}c\mu)$, $Y^p_1=\varepsilon_1\omega/k_{13}=\sqrt{13}/(2c\mu)$ and $Y^p_2=\varepsilon_2\omega/k_{t3}=(9/(4c^2\mu))\omega\cdot2\sqrt{13}c/(9\omega)=\sqrt{13}/(2c\mu)$, so $Y^p_1=Y^p_2$ exactly. [step 1.1, step 2.1, A1, F1, algebra] 4.1 [The amplitudes, clause (ii)] By [A1](a) and step 3.1, $r_p=(Y^p_1-Y^p_2)/(Y^p_1+Y^p_2)=0$ and $t_p=2Y^p_1/(Y^p_1+Y^p_2)=1$. For the $s$-channel, factoring the common positive scale $1/(\sqrt{13}c\mu)$ from numerator and denominator, $r_s=(2-9/2)/(2+9/2)=(-5/2)/(13/2)=-5/13$ and $t_s=2\cdot2/(2+9/2)=4/(13/2)=8/13$. [step 3.1, A1, algebra] 5.1 [Flux budget, clause (iii)] By [A1](b), $R_s=|r_s|^2=25/169$ and $T_s=(Y^s_2/Y^s_1)|t_s|^2=(9/4)(64/169)=144/169$, so $R_s+T_s=(25+144)/169=169/169=1$ exactly; and in the TM channel $R_p=|r_p|^2=0$, $T_p=(Y^p_2/Y^p_1)|t_p|^2=1$, so $R_p+T_p=1$ as well. [step 4.1, A1, algebra] 6.1 [Scope, clause (iv)] All quantities are declared model parameters and the computation is exact rational or quadratic-irrational algebra of the interface model; no measured refractive index, no absorption, no unequal-permeability interface, no unpolarised-beam statistics and no empirical claim is used. Since $r_p=0$ and $r_s
e0$ at $	heta_B$, an incident wave with a nonzero TE component has a surviving reflected TE component; no statement about random or unpolarised beams is made. No choice principle is used. [given, step 5.1, A1] ∎
items.physical_scope: Deterministic example of the oblique-incidence interface model for two declared lossless media with equal permeabilities and indices n_1=1, n_2=3/2: the unique Brewster angle tan(theta_B)=n_2/n_1, r_p=0, t_p=1, the surviving s-reflection r_s=-5/13 with R_s+T_s=1 exactly. Excluded: measured refractive indices, absorption, interfaces between unequal permeabilities, unpolarised-beam statistics and every empirical claim.

items.title: Total internal reflection: decaying transmitted field, vanishing normal flux and the reflection phase
items.statement: Adopt the setting of [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]] with equal permeabilities $\mu_1=\mu_2=:\mu>0$ and declared indices $n_1=3/2$, $n_2=1$ (declared model parameters, not measurements), choose the tangential wavevector $\kappa=(6\omega/(5c))e_1$, so $\hat\kappa=e_1$ and $\hat y=n\times\hat\kappa=e_2$, and take the transverse-electric polarisation $e_j=E_j\hat y$. Let the incidence angle be given by $\sin\theta_i=4/5$, which exceeds the critical angle $\theta_c$ with $\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1=2/3$, so $|\kappa|=K_1\sin\theta_i=(6/5)(\omega/c)>(\omega/c)=K_2$. Then with $\beta=\sqrt{|\kappa|^{2}-K_2^{2}}=(\sqrt{11}/5)(\omega/c)$ and $k_{13}=(\omega/c)(3/2)(3/5)=(9/10)(\omega/c)$: (i) [Reflection] $Y^{s}_1=9/(10\mu c)$, $Y^{s}_2=i\sqrt{11}/(5\mu c)$ and $$r_s=\frac{9/10-i\sqrt{11}/5}{9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5},\qquad |r_s|=1,\qquad t_s=\frac{9/5}{9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5},\qquad |t_s|^{2}=\frac{324}{125};$$ the reflection factor is the phase $r_s=e^{-2i\varphi}$ with $\varphi=\arctan\!\bigl(2\sqrt{11}/9\bigr)\approx0.63514703$ (about $36.39124^\circ$), i.e. the reflected wave acquires the phase $-2\varphi\approx-1.27029406$ (about $-72.78249^\circ$); (ii) [Transmitted field] the transmitted field is $E_t(x,t)=e^{-\beta x_3}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(E_t\hat y\,e^{i(|\kappa|x_1-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with $\beta=(\sqrt{11}/5)(\omega/c)$: it decays by the factor $e^{-\sqrt{11}/5}\approx0.51514$ when $x_3$ increases by $c/\omega$, its period-averaged normal flux vanishes identically, $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle\equiv0$, while its tangential averaged flux is positive, $\langle S_t\cdot\hat\kappa\rangle=e^{-2\beta x_3}\,\frac{(6/5)(\omega/c)|E_t|^{2}}{2\mu\omega}=e^{-2\beta x_3}\frac{3|E_t|^{2}}{5\mu c}$; (iii) [Flux budget] $|r_s|^{2}+(\operatorname{Re}Y^{s}_2/Y^{s}_1)|t_s|^{2}=1+0=1$, so the whole incident normal averaged flux is reflected, while the evanescent field carries a tangential averaged flux only; (iv) [Scope] the example is an exact deterministic computation of the lossless interface model for declared parameters; it reports no measurement, and the presence of a tangential evanescent flux is not a claim about information speed or signal propagation.
items.strategy: Proof technique: direct substitution in the oblique-incidence and medium plane-wave theorems with exact rational and quadratic-irrational arithmetic, and an explicit phase computation via Euler's form. Given: The lossless two-media setting of [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]] with $\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu>0$, $n_1=3/2$, $n_2=1$, the tangential wavevector $\kappa=(6\omega/(5c))e_1$, the transverse-electric data $e_j=E_j\hat y$ with $\hat y=e_2$, and the incidence data $\sin\theta_i=4/5$. [A1] The oblique-incidence theorem [[pthm-em-oblique-fresnel]]: clause (a) and (d) give $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu_1\omega)$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)$, the amplitude formulas, and in the evanescent branch $|r_s|=1$, $|t_s|^2=4(Y^s_1)^2/((Y^s_1)^2+|Y^s_2|^2)>0$ together with the flux budget; clause (d) also records that the transmitted field decays and its normal averaged flux vanishes. [A2] The medium plane-wave structure [[pthm-em-medium-plane-wave-fields]]: the transmitted evanescent field of clause (e) with the substitution $n'=n$, $\kappa_0=\kappa$: the exact factorization, the vanishing normal component $\langle S\cdot n'\rangle\equiv0$ and the positive tangential averaged flux $\langle S\cdot\hat\kappa_0\rangle=|\kappa_0||e|^2e^{-2\beta n'\cdot x}/(2\mu\omega)$ for the transverse-electric data $e=E_0(n'\times\hat\kappa_0)$. [F1] Medium parameters ([[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]]): $K_j=\omega(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}=\omega n_j/c$, $k_{13}^2=K_1^2-|\kappa|^2$, $\beta^2=|\kappa|^2-K_2^2$, $k_{t3}=i\beta$ and $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$. [F2] Complex arithmetic and modulus ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]): $\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w$, $\overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w$, $|zw|=|z||w|$, $|z|^2=z\overline z$ and $|z|\ge0$ with $|z|=0$ only for $z=0$; in particular a complex number of modulus one is nonzero and the sum of a complex number and its conjugate is twice its real part. [F3] Trigonometry and phases: $\arctan$ is the principal inverse tangent with $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ ([[def-principal-inverse-tangent]]); $\tan x=\sin x/\cos x$ ([[def-tangent-cotangent-secant-cosecant]]); $\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1$ and $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$ ([[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]]); cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ ([[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]); and for real $y$, $\exp(iy)=\cos y+i\sin y$ with $|\exp(iy)|=1$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). 1.1 [The geometry and the evanescent data] With $\kappa=(6\omega/(5c))e_1$ one has $\hat\kappa=e_1$, $|\kappa|=(6/5)(\omega/c)$ and $\hat y=n\times\hat\kappa=e_3\times e_1=e_2$; $K_1=(3/2)(\omega/c)$, $K_2=\omega/c$ by [F1], so $|\kappa|=K_1\sin\theta_i$ with $\sin\theta_i=4/5$, and $|\kappa|>K_2$ because $6/5>1$. Hence the evanescent branch applies: $\beta=\sqrt{|\kappa|^2-K_2^2}=\sqrt{(36/25-1)}(\omega/c)=\sqrt{11/25}\,(\omega/c)=(\sqrt{11}/5)(\omega/c)$ and $k_{13}=\sqrt{K_1^2-|\kappa|^2}=\sqrt{(9/4-36/25)}(\omega/c)=\sqrt{81/100}\,(\omega/c)=(9/10)(\omega/c)$; the critical angle satisfies $\sin\theta_c=n_2/n_1=2/3<4/5=\sin\theta_i$, both angles being in $(0,\pi/2)$. [given, A1, F1, algebra] 2.1 [Admittances and reflection data, clause (i)] By [A1](a) and [F1], $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu_1\omega)=9/(10\mu c)$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)=i\beta/(\mu\omega)=i\sqrt{11}/(5\mu c)$ and $t_s=2Y^s_1/(Y^s_1+Y^s_2)=(9/(5\mu c))/((9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5)/(\mu c))=(9/5)/(9/10+i\sqrt{11}/5)$; the numerator $9/10-i\sqrt{11}/5$ of $r_s=(Y^s_1-Y^s_2)/(Y^s_1+Y^s_2)$ is the complex conjugate of its denominator, so $|r_s|=1$ by [F2] (and [A1](d)). For the transmitted modulus, $|t_s|^2=4(Y^s_1)^2/((Y^s_1)^2+|Y^s_2|^2)$ by [A1](d); computing $(Y^s_1)^2=81/(100\mu^2c^2)$ and $|Y^s_2|^2=11/(25\mu^2c^2)=44/(100\mu^2c^2)$ gives $|t_s|^2=(324/100)/(125/100)=324/125$. [step 1.1, A1, F2, algebra] 2.2 [The transmitted field and its fluxes, clause (ii)] By $|t_s|^2$-normalised data we take the transmitted electric amplitude $E_t\hat y$ with $E_t=t_sE_i$; the evanescent structure of [A2] applied with $n'=n=e_3$, $\kappa_0=\kappa$, $\beta$ as in step 1.1 and $e=E_t\hat y=E_t(n'\times\hat\kappa_0)$ gives exactly $E_t(x,t)=e^{-\beta x_3}\operatorname{Re}\bigl(E_t\hat y\,e^{i(|\kappa|x_1-\omega t)}\bigr)$, the identity $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle\equiv0$, and the tangential averaged flux $\langle S_t\cdot\hat\kappa\rangle=e^{-2\beta x_3}|\kappa||E_t|^2/(2\mu\omega)$; substituting $|\kappa|=(6/5)(\omega/c)$ gives $\langle S_t\cdot\hat\kappa\rangle=e^{-2\beta x_3}(6/5)(\omega/c)|E_t|^2/(2\mu\omega)=e^{-2\beta x_3}3|E_t|^2/(5\mu c)$. The decay over a distance $c/\omega$ is the factor $e^{-\beta c/\omega}=e^{-\sqrt{11}/5}$, whose decimal display in clause (ii) is the stated rounding. [step 1.1, A1, A2, algebra] 3.1 [The reflection phase, clause (i)] Put $Y_1:=9/10$ and $\beta':=\sqrt{11}/5$ in the units $1/(\mu c)$ and $\alpha:=\beta'/Y_1=2\sqrt{11}/9$, so that $r_s=(1-i\alpha)/(1+i\alpha)$; let $\varphi:=\arctan\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ and $w:=1+i\alpha$, $|w|=\sqrt{1+\alpha^2}$. By [F3], $\tan\varphi=\alpha$ and $1+\tan^2\varphi=\sec^2\varphi$, so $\cos^2\varphi=1/(1+\alpha^2)=1/|w|^2$; since $\cos\varphi>0$ (cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ and $\varphi\in(0,\pi/2)$), $\cos\varphi=1/|w|$ and $\sin\varphi=\alpha\cos\varphi=\alpha/|w|$. Euler's form of [F3] then gives $w=|w|(\cos\varphi+i\sin\varphi)=|w|e^{i\varphi}$ and $\overline w=|w|e^{-i\varphi}$ by [F2], so $r_s=\overline w/w=e^{-2i\varphi}$. The decimal values displayed in clause (i) are the stated roundings of $\varphi=\arctan(2\sqrt{11}/9)$ and of the reflected phase $-2\varphi$. [step 2.1, F2, F3, algebra] 4.1 [Flux budget and scope, clauses (iii)-(iv)] By [A1](d), $|r_s|^2+(\operatorname{Re}Y^s_2/Y^s_1)|t_s|^2=1$; here $\operatorname{Re}Y^s_2=0$ by step 2.1, so the identity reads $1+0=1$: the whole incident normal averaged flux is reflected, while the tangential averaged flux of step 2.2 is positive and transports no normal flux. All quantities are declared model parameters; the computation is deterministic classical interface algebra, reports no measurement, and neither the tangential evanescent flux nor the reflection phase is a claim about information speed, signal propagation or empirical data. No choice principle is used. [given, step 2.1, step 2.2, A1, F2] ∎
items.physical_scope: Deterministic example of total internal reflection in the lossless interface model for declared indices n_1=3/2, n_2=1 at sin(theta_i)=4/5: the unit-modulus reflection factor with its phase, the evanescent transmitted field with decay factor e^{-beta x_3}, the vanishing normal and positive tangential averaged fluxes. Excluded: measured indices, absorption, information-speed or signal-propagation claims, and every empirical statement.

items.title: Calculus of separated phasor fields: real-part derivative identities and amplitude injectivity
items.reference: core-conditional-proofs.md#K9; scaffold-added necessary prerequisite (see batch-35 notes)
items.strategy: Differentiate each component of $\operatorname{Re}(we^{i\theta})$ with $w=\tilde F_j$ by the product and chain rules for real and imaginary parts ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), using $\operatorname{Re}(i\zeta)=-\operatorname{Im}\zeta$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-i\zeta)=\operatorname{Im}\zeta$; assemble the divergence and curl componentwise. For (d), write $C=a+ib$ with real $a,b$; the two scalar equations $a\cos\varphi_j-b\sin\varphi_j=0$ ($j=1,2$) form a real $2\times2$ system of determinant $\sin(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)$ for each component, The determinant is nonzero by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]; the determinant identity is the sine subtraction formula of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], with real-part encoding justified by [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]. Hence $a_j=b_j=0$. If $F=G$ on an open $U$, then for every $x_t$ in the projection fix one real $x_3$ in that open fibre and vary $t$ on a small open interval. Put $C=(\tilde F(x_t)-\tilde G(x_t))e^{i\beta x_3}$; the exponential is nonzero even for complex $\beta$. The real time phases $-\omega t$ contain an interval and hence two values with difference strictly between $0$ and $\pi$. Clause (d) forces $C=0$ and therefore $\tilde F(x_t)=\tilde G(x_t)$. Complex $\beta$ changes a fixed spatial amplitude factor, not this real time-phase injectivity. The projection of a nonempty open set is nonempty and open.

items.title: Transverse vector-calculus identities for the splitting $\mathbb R^3=\mathbb R^2\oplus\mathbb R e_z$
items.reference: core-conditional-proofs.md#G1; scaffold-added necessary prerequisite (see batch-35 notes)
items.statement:
Let $e_z$ be a unit vector of $\mathbb R^3$ and identify $\mathbb R^3=\mathbb R^2\oplus\mathbb R e_z$ with transverse coordinates $(x_1,x_2)$; write $
abla_t h=(\partial_1h,\partial_2h)$, $\Delta_t h=\partial_1^2h+\partial_2^2h$ and, for a transverse $C^1$ map $u_t$ with components $(u_1,u_2)$, $\operatorname{div}_t u_t=\partial_1u_1+\partial_2u_2$ and $\operatorname{curl}_2 u_t=\partial_1u_2-\partial_2u_1$; regard $h$, $

items.title: The separated sine and cosine rectangle profiles: eigen-identities, boundary traces, orthogonality and Dirichlet integrals
items.reference: completed-expansion-arguments.md#G1-G2; scaffold-added necessary prerequisite (see batch-35 notes)
items.strategy: Differentiate the products with [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]] and the product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]); the boundary values follow from $\sin(0)=\sin(m\pi)=0$ and $\cos'(t)=-\sin t$. The orthogonality and norm values are iterated one-dimensional integrals computed with the product-to-sum identities of [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]] and the second fundamental theorem ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]) applied to the continuous integrands; Fubini on the rectangle ([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]], [[thm-continuous-on-a-rectangle-is-riemann-integrable]]) justifies iterated integration. For the mixed term use $\cos(m\pi x/L)\sin(p\pi x/L)=\tfrac12[\sin((p+m)\pi x/L)+\sin((p-m)\pi x/L)]$. If $p=m$, the second term is identically zero and the first integrates to zero. Otherwise FTC gives $L[(1-(-1)^{p+m})/(p+m)+(1-(-1)^{p-m})/(p-m)]/(2\pi)$, which is the stated parity formula (and includes $m=0$). The integer endpoint values are furnished by [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]] and [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]]. Rectangle Fubini then gives the product $J_{mp}J_{nq}$. For (d) integrate $\partial_1(h\partial_1h)=(\partial_1h)^2+h\partial_1^2h$ over the interval in $x_1$ for fixed $x_2$ with the FTC; the boundary term vanishes by (a), and the same in $x_2$; the $e_{mn}$ case is identical with the boundary term vanishing by (b). All steps are choice-free finite computations over the exhibited profiles.

items.title: The sine and cosine systems are complete orthogonal systems of L^2 on an interval and on a rectangle
items.reference: completed-expansion-arguments.md#G2; scaffold-added necessary prerequisite (see batch-35 notes)
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L>0$ and $R=(0,L_1)\times(0,L_2)$ with $L_1,L_2>0$.
(a) [One interval] The families $\{\cos(m\pi x/L)\}_{m\ge0}$ and $\{\sin(m\pi x/L)\}_{m\ge1}$ are orthogonal complete systems in the real Hilbert space $L^2(0,L)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]): each is orthogonal, and its closed linear span is all of $L^2(0,L)$.
(b) [Rectangle] With $m,n$ ranging over $\mathbb N_0$ in cosine slots and over $\mathbb N_{\ge1}$ in sine slots, each of the four product families $\{\cos\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\cos\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$, $\{\cos\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\sin\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$, $\{\sin\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\cos\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$ and $\{\sin\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\sin\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$ is an orthogonal complete system in $L^2(R)$; in particular the Neumann family $\{h_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge0}$ and the Dirichlet family $\{e_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge1}$ of [[lem-em-rectangle-mode-profile-identities]] are orthogonal complete systems in $L^2(R)$.
items.strategy: (a) Rescale $x=L u/\pi$ to period $2\pi$ ([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]). For $f\in L^2(0,L)$ orthogonal to every $\cos(m\pi x/L)$, extend $f$ evenly to $(-L,L)$ and $2L$-periodically; the extended $F$ lies in $L^2$ of the torus and every character coefficient $\widehat F(k)$ is a fixed multiple of $\int_0^Lf(x)\cos(k\pi x/L)\,dx$, computed by splitting the integral at $0$ and substituting $x\mapsto-x$ on $(-L,0)$ ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]); hence all coefficients vanish and [[thm-trigonometric-system-is-complete-in-l-two-of-the-torus]] gives $F=0$, so $f=0$. The sine case uses the odd extension, whose character coefficients are the sine coefficients (the $k=0$ coefficient vanishes identically). (b) Orthogonality is product integration. If $f\in L^2(R)$ is orthogonal to every $c_m(x_1)d_n(x_2)$, then for each $m$ the function $g_m(x_2):=\int_0^{L_1}f(x_1,x_2)c_m(x_1)\,dx_1$ is in $L^2(0,L_2)$ by Cauchy-Schwarz and Fubini ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]), and $\int_0^{L_2}g_md_n=0$ for all $n$ by Fubini, so $g_m=0$ a.e. by (a). Taking the countable union of the exceptional null sets, for a.e. $x_2$ one has $\int_0^{L_1}f(x_1,x_2)c_m(x_1)\,dx_1=0$ for all $m$, so $f(\cdot,x_2)=0$ a.e. in $x_1$ by (a), and Fubini gives $f=0$ a.e. Completeness as closed span is therefore established; the orthogonal expansions converge in $L^2$ by [[thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion]]. The argument is symmetric in the four parity choices.

items.title: Rectangular PEC guide and cavity geometry, the zero-normal-B reflection class, and axis-relative TE/TM/TEM
items.statement:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its SI units and its fields $E,B$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-fields]]. Fix $a,b>0$, write $x_t=(x_1,x_2)$, $e_z:=e_3$, and define $\nabla_t f=(\partial_1f,\partial_2f,0)$, $\Delta_t f=\partial_1^2f+\partial_2^2f$ and $\operatorname{div}_tu_t=\partial_1u_1+\partial_2u_2$ for the stated regularity, using [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].
(a) [Straight guide] A straight guide region is $\Omega_A:=A\times\mathbb R$ where $A$ is either a bounded connected $C^1$ plane domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]) or the explicit rectangular cross-section; the rectangle has corners and is treated by its open faces, not asserted to be a $C^1$ boundary domain, with longitudinal axis $e_z$; for a rectangular cross-section $A=R_{ab}:=(0,a)\times(0,b)$ the region is called the rectangular guide and its walls are the four open faces $\{x_1=0\},\{x_1=a\},\{x_2=0\},\{x_2=b\}$. A rectangular cavity region is $\Omega_c:=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ for fixed $d>0$, with the six open faces as its walls. The separate smooth-cavity spectral branch uses an explicitly declared bounded $C^\infty$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ with its smooth PEC boundary; it is not the rectangular reflection class. Spatial derivatives are taken at fixed $t$; the fields are defined on $\Omega\times I$ with the regularity declared by each theorem.
(b) [PEC boundary model] On every open wall (a wall minus its edges) the ideal perfectly conducting boundary model declares the two conditions $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$, where $n$ is the outward unit normal of that wall ($-e_1,+e_1,-e_2,+e_2$ on the four rectangular walls, and $\pm e_j$ on the six cavity walls). Its physical reading is the ideal-conductor limit of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]: with $E=B=0$ inside the ideal conductor the tangential electric field and the normal magnetic field vanish, while the surface-charge and surface-current readings $\sigma_f=-n\cdot D$ and $K_f=-n\times H$ for the filling-side traces (the wall normal points from the filling into the conductor, so the jump is $0$ minus the filling trace) are determined by the traces and are not prescribed here. The supplier's hypotheses (a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with one-sided $C^1$ fields) cover a smooth stationary interface, not the $\sigma\to\infty$ idealization nor the box edges; the guide/cavity conditions on the open walls are therefore declared as an idealization of this definition, and no pointwise statement on the edges is made.
(c) [Zero-normal-B reflection class] For the rectangular box $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L=(a,b,d)$, the reflection class is the class of locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $Q$ whose extensions to the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$, defined by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2$-, $x_3$-walls and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$, and extending $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$ and cyclically for $B_2,B_3$, are $L^2$ fields, together with the distributional constraints that $\operatorname{div}E$ and $\operatorname{div}B$ vanish on the torus for the extensions. This is the declared weak PEC model used for the cavity initial-value problem; when the reflected extensions are continuous across the walls, their odd components vanish there, giving $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on the open walls. Smoothness only inside $Q$ does not imply this extension continuity. Initial data not in this class (for example data with trapped normal $B$) are excluded, as are the general $H(\operatorname{curl})$ boundary classes, which are defined by the mathematical suppliers and are not identified here with the classical conditions.
(d) [TE, TM, TEM] For a guide or cavity field $(E,B)$, the longitudinal components are $E_z:=E\cdot e_z$ and $B_z:=B\cdot e_z$; the field is called TE (transverse electric) if $E_z\equiv0$, TM (transverse magnetic) if $B_z\equiv0$, and TEM if both vanish, always relative to the named axis $e_z$.
(e) [Separated phasor convention] For $\omega>0$ and $\beta\in\mathbb C$, a $\beta$-$\omega$ separated phasor field on the guide is a real field of the form $F(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\tilde F(x_1,x_2)e^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with a complex amplitude $\tilde F$, componentwise; $\omega/(2\pi)$ is the frequency and $\beta$ the longitudinal propagation constant; when $\beta$ is real, $\beta>0$ describes propagation in the $+e_z$ direction under this phase convention, while a complex $\beta$ gives the spatial factor $e^{-\operatorname{Im}\beta x_3}$ and may grow in the opposite direction; each consuming branch states its selection.
(f) [Scope] The definition fixes the geometry, the PEC boundary model, the weak reflection class and the mode terminology; it asserts no field equation, no constitutive law and no existence or completeness of modes, Rectangular TE/TM candidates and the rectangular reflection class, declared smooth bounded PEC cavity spectral classes, and smooth straight-guide TEM potential branches (including the coaxial annulus) are within this geometry. No general non-rectangular TE/TM guide theory, circular-guide spectral classification, open-end or junction scattering, or arbitrary lossy model is supplied. The same stationary PEC geometry also hosts the explicitly declared constant scalar Ohmic cavity class and the full longitudinal finite-energy reflection class of the straight rectangular guide; constitutive and evolution claims belong to their consuming theorems, not this definition.
items.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition: geometry and transversality are fixed by coordinates and normals; the PEC model is declared with its interface reading and its excluded idealization/edges; the reflection class is defined by the reflection rules and distributional divergence constraints; the phasor convention is stated as an encoding of real fields. No differential equation is introduced.
items.physical_scope: The ideal PEC boundary model of the straight rectangular guide and cavity (and of straight guides with a bounded connected C1 cross-section) in the declared laboratory chart, with lossless and explicitly declared constant scalar Ohmic fillings distinguished by their consuming theorems, together with the zero-normal-B reflection class and the TE/TM/TEM classification. The boundary model is an idealization of an interface with a perfectly conducting medium on the open walls; the definition asserts no field equations, constitutive laws or mode completeness.

items.title: The separated TE and TM candidate modes of the lossless rectangular PEC guide: exact verification, index restrictions and cutoff
items.statement:

Let the rectangular guide, its PEC boundary model, the axis $e_z$, the TE/TM/TEM terminology and the separated phasor convention be those of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]] with cross-section $(0,a)	imes(0,b)$, and let $\omega>0$, $ eta\in\mathbb C$, $k_c^2:=\omega^2\varepsilon\mu- eta^2\in\mathbb R_{>0}$, $H:=B/\mu$ and $	heta:= eta x_3-\omega t$. Write $	ilde E,	ilde H$ for the complex amplitudes of the separated real fields $E=\operatorname{Re}(	ilde Ee^{i	heta})$, $H=\operatorname{Re}(	ilde He^{i	heta})$, so that $B=\mu H$.
(a) [TE family] For integers $m,n\ge0$ with $(m,n)

abla_th_{mn},\qquad 	ilde H:= rac{i eta}{k_{mn}^2}\,
abla_th_{mn}+e_zh_{mn}.$$ Then the real fields $E=\operatorname{Re}(	ilde Ee^{i	heta})$, $B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(	ilde He^{i	heta})$ are $C^\infty$ on the guide region, have $E_z=0$ (TE), satisfy the four source-free macroscopic equations $\operatorname{div}D=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=\partial_tD$, and satisfy $n	imes E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on every open wall of the guide.
(b) [TM family] For integers $m,n\ge1$ put $e_{mn}:=\sin rac{m\pi x_1}{a}\sin rac{n\pi x_2}{b}$, $k_{mn}^2:=( rac{m\pi}{a})^2+( rac{n\pi}{b})^2$, require $ eta^2=\omega^2\varepsilon\mu-k_{mn}^2$, and define $$	ilde E:= rac{i eta}{k_{mn}^2}
abla_te_{mn}+e_ze_{mn},\qquad 	ilde H:= rac{i\omega\varepsilon}{k_{mn}^2}\,e_z	imes
abla_te_{mn}.$$ Then the corresponding real fields are $C^\infty$, have $B_z=0$ (TM), satisfy the same four equations and the same boundary conditions on the open walls.
(c) [Index restrictions] For $m=n=0$ one has $
abla_th_{00}=0$ and $k_{00}^2=0$ makes the displayed divided reconstruction formulas undefined. A purely longitudinal constant-profile magnetic amplitude with zero electric amplitude cannot be a nonzero monochromatic Maxwell candidate: Faraday gives $0=i\omega\mu	ilde H$, hence $	ilde H=0$ because $\omega>0$. At $ eta=0$ a constant $H_z$ is divergence-free, so divergence alone does not exclude it. Thus $(0,0)$ is excluded by the full field equations and the reconstruction denominator, not by a false divergence claim; for $m=0$ or $n=0$ the TM profile $e_{mn}$ vanishes identically, so TM indices are restricted to $m,n\ge1$; conversely for $(m,n)

(e) [Scope] These are separated candidate modes of the declared lossless model; the theorem asserts no completeness, no uniqueness among fields with the same data, and no lossy, dispersive or open-end behaviour, and it assumes the PEC model of the definition, not the physical infinite-conductivity limit.

Under the separated phasor convention, [[lem-em-separated-phasor-calculus]] turns the real field equations into the complex amplitude equations $\operatorname{div}	ilde E=0$, $\operatorname{div}	ilde H=0$, $\operatorname{curl}	ilde E=i\omega\mu	ilde H$, $\operatorname{curl}	ilde H=-i\omega\varepsilon	ilde E$; the amplitude injectivity clause makes the reduction an equivalence. Nondegeneracy follows from the exhibited nonconstant profiles; the cutoff statement is the algebraic solvability of $ eta^2=\omega^2\varepsilon\mu-k_c^2$. No step uses empirical input.

Rationalization gives $|\omega( eta+h)-\omega( eta)|\le |2 eta h+h^2|/(\varepsilon\mu\omega( eta))$, hence continuity. Its difference quotient is $(2 eta+h)/[\varepsilon\mu(\omega( eta+h)+\omega( eta))]$, whose limit is $ eta/(\varepsilon\mu\omega( eta))$ by [[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], proving the derivative in [[def-derivative]] and the stated $v_g$ and read off $v_pv_g=1/(\varepsilon\mu)$. The local balance $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=0$ of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]](a) is consistent with the averaged identities ($\partial_t\langle uangle=0$ and $\partial_z\langle S\cdot e_zangle=0$); only the choice-free local clause of that theorem is used. The speed inequalities are the elementary bounds $ eta^2<\varepsilon\mu\omega^2$ (strict for $k_c>0$). For (d), $k_{mn}^2\ge(m\pi/a)^2$ and $k_{mn}^2\ge(n\pi/b)^2$ give the two index bounds directly from $k_{mn}^2<\varepsilon\mu\omega^2$. No empirical premise is used.

items.title: Constant-Ohmic PEC modal decay and exact energy-class completeness
items.statement:
Assume the constant isotropic inertial-rest material branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$, $\sigma\ge0$, $D=\varepsilon E$, $H=B/\mu$, $J_{\rm ext}=0$. The exact broadband physical reading additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$ as in that closure; otherwise the positive coefficients define its finite-band effective phase model without a universal front-speed claim. Put $v^2=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}$ and $\gamma=\sigma/\varepsilon$. The smooth equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] with initially zero volume charge give $E_t=v^2\operatorname{curl}B-\gamma E$, $B_t=-\operatorname{curl}E$ and zero divergences; in the finite-energy classes below these first-order equations with the declared PEC weak/variational boundary realization are adopted explicitly, rather than deduced from a smooth-only postulate. The quadratic stored energy is $\mathcal U(t)=\tfrac12(\varepsilon\|E(t)\|_2^2+\mu^{-1}\|B(t)\|_2^2)$, consistent with [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]].
(a) [Rectangular cavity] In the exact zero-normal-$B$ reflection-parity and divergence class of [[lem-em-rectangular-pec-energy-completeness]] and [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]](c), every initial pair has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ distributional solution of this damped system in the same class. Finite Fourier mode sums converge in energy norm uniformly on compact time intervals and are dense at every time. The Fourier coefficient equations at $k_j=\pi n_j/L_j$ are $\widehat E_t=iv^2 k\times\widehat B-\gamma\widehat E$, $\widehat B_t=-ik\times\widehat E$, with both transverse constraints and the original parities retained.
(b) [Smooth closed PEC cavity] Assume the full Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the smooth spectral and elliptic suppliers. On a bounded smooth cavity $\Omega$, let $X,V,H$ and its smooth orthonormal eigenfields $u_j$, $\lambda_j\ge0$, be exactly [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]] and [[thm-em-waveguide-spectral-completeness]]. Define the full weak normal-zero divergence-free magnetic space $$M:=\{B\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\int_\Omega B\cdot\nabla\psi=0\text{ for every smooth scalar }\psi\text{ on }\overline\Omega\}.$$ This is the distributional divergence constraint together with weak zero normal flux; for smooth fields it is $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $n\cdot B=0$. For every positive eigenvalue put $w_j=\operatorname{curl}u_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j}$ and put $K_M=\{B\in M:\operatorname{curl}B=0\text{ distributionally}\}$. Then $$M=\overline{\operatorname{span}\{w_j:\lambda_j>0\}}^{L^2}\mathbin{\oplus}K_M.$$ The declared first-order PEC modal energy class is $H\times M$, with weak modal equations $a_j'=v^2\sqrt{\lambda_j}b_j-\gamma a_j$, $b_j'=-\sqrt{\lambda_j}a_j$ for positive modes, $a_j'=-\gamma a_j$ for electric zero modes, and $(B,K_M)'=0$ for every kernel test. Define $D_M$ as the graph-norm completion of finite $w_j$ sums plus $K_M$, with norm squared $\|w\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}w\|_2^2$. The equivalent weak-in-time variational equations are $\langle E_t,\phi\rangle=v^2\langle B,\operatorname{curl}\phi\rangle-\gamma\langle E,\phi\rangle$ for $\phi\in V$, and $\langle B_t,\psi\rangle=-\langle E,\operatorname{curl}\psi\rangle$ for $\psi\in D_M$. They use the actual electric tangential-zero domain $V$ and magnetic normal-zero space $M$, with no claim of maximal-trace equality. For every initial pair in $H\times M$ there is a unique $C(\mathbb R;H\times M)$ solution of that declared realization, which also satisfies the displayed evolution equations distributionally in the interior. Finite electric and paired-magnetic modal sums, with the exact static magnetic kernel component retained, converge uniformly on compact time intervals in energy norm. No equality with every maximal rough tangential-trace realization is asserted.
(c) [Exact energy balance, decay and zero sectors] In both declared classes, for every $t_0<t_1$, $$\mathcal U(t_1)+\sigma\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\|E(t)\|_2^2\,dt=\mathcal U(t_0),\qquad \mathcal U'(t)=-\sigma\|E(t)\|_2^2\le0.$$ For positive smooth-cavity modes $a_j''+\gamma a_j'+v^2\lambda_ja_j=0$. If $\Delta_j=\gamma^2/4-v^2\lambda_j$ is positive, the two roots are $-\gamma/2\pm\sqrt{\Delta_j}$; if negative they are $-\gamma/2\pm i\sqrt{-\Delta_j}$; at zero include $(A+Bt)e^{-\gamma t/2}$. This finite scalar characteristic classification applies to every parameter $\lambda\ge0$ and uses no choice principle; its general zero-eigenvalue associated-wave solutions and the narrower first-order compatibility are stated separately in (d). The full Choice premise belongs to the smooth-cavity spectral realization, not to these finite root formulas. For $\sigma>0$ every positive mode decays, electric zero modes obey $a_j(t)=a_j(0)e^{-\gamma t}$, and magnetic kernel data stay constant. In the smooth class the solution therefore tends in energy norm as $t\to+\infty$ to $(0,P_{K_M}B(0))$. For $\sigma=0$ energy is constant, electric zero modes are static and the original lossless branch is recovered. The zero sectors are retained, not divided by their eigenvalues; no universal decay to zero in the presence of magnetic kernel data is claimed.
(d) [Associated second-order branch] Independently of first-order compatibility, the same spectral basis gives the damped associated electric wave for every $q_0\in V$, $q_1\in H$, with $q\in C(\mathbb R;V)$, $q'\in C(\mathbb R;H)$ and modal convergence uniformly on compact times. Its coefficients satisfy $a_j''+\gamma a_j'+v^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with arbitrary prescribed initial coefficients. At $\lambda_j=0$ they are $\alpha_j+\beta_j(1-e^{-\gamma t})/\gamma$ when $\gamma>0$, and $\alpha_j+t\beta_j$ when $\gamma=0$. Such arbitrary second-order data need not arise from the first-order Maxwell system: its zero modes additionally satisfy $a_j'=-\gamma a_j$. This broader wave is retained alongside the physical first-order branch. All square roots and real derivatives use [[thm-of-square-roots]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] and the real-component exponential formula [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]].
(e) [Scope] The conductor occupies the declared cavity interior while its stationary walls obey the independent ideal PEC boundary model. No arbitrary loss tensor, memory law, changing interface, open-end, rough-wall or empirical conclusion is made. Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) suffices for the rectangular/Fourier branch; the smooth branch retains its actual full Choice premise. Weak energy balance is proved by modal limits and does not assert an unprovided nonlinear weak local Poynting theorem.
items.strategy:
For (a), use the exact G2 product Fourier representation and parity constraints. Add the scalar term $-\gamma\widehat E$ to its finite real/imaginary matrix system. It is globally Lipschitz, so [[cor-globally-lipschitz-odes-have-global-solutions]] supplies a unique solution on all real time. Direct conjugate triple-product cancellation gives $(\varepsilon|\widehat E|^2+\mu^{-1}|\widehat B|^2)'=-2\sigma|\widehat E|^2$. Divergence constraints are preserved ($k\cdot\widehat E$ obeys $d'=-\gamma d$, $k\cdot\widehat B$ is constant), and damping preserves each original parity. Modal energy is nonincreasing forward and at most $e^{2\gamma T}$ times its initial value on $[-T,T]$, because its derivative is bounded below by $-2\gamma$ times itself; multiply by $e^{2\gamma t}$ and differentiate to prove that bound. Parseval therefore controls every omitted tail uniformly on compact times. Finite solutions converge in $C_tL^2$ and pass the linear distributional equations against compact-time smooth periodic tests by Cauchy-Schwarz, exactly as in G2. The current G2 continuous-coefficient-minus-FTC-primitive argument, using [[thm-ftc-first-part]], [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]] and [[thm-a-distribution-with-zero-derivatives-on-a-connected-open-set-is-constant]], converts weak coefficient equations to classical ODEs and proves uniqueness.
For (b), G3's full-$X$ identity gives $(\operatorname{curl}u_j,\operatorname{curl}u_l)=\lambda_j\delta_{jl}$, so the $w_j$ are orthonormal. Smooth tangential-zero $u_j$ imply $w_j\in M$: ordinary curl integration by parts against $
abla\psi$ has zero boundary term and zero interior curl. Indeed [[lem-the-divergence-and-curl-of-a-cross-product]] applied to $u_j	imes
abla\psi$ and [[thm-the-curl-of-a-gradient-vanishes]] give its divergence $(
abla\psi)\cdot\operatorname{curl}u_j$; [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]] integrates this to the boundary term $(n	imes u_j)\cdot
abla\psi=0$. All inputs are smooth on the bounded smooth closure, and the inherited choice premise meets the actual divergence supplier. G3's weighted $V$ completeness proves that the closed span of these $w_j$ is the closure of $\operatorname{curl}V$. Since $M$ is a closed subspace, orthogonal projection [[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]] decomposes any $B\in M$ into that closure and its orthogonal complement. To identify the latter with $K_M$, take a compactly supported smooth vector test $\phi$. The actual smooth Dirichlet solver [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]] with coefficient identity, zero trace and source $-\operatorname{div}\phi$ supplies $f\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega)$ with $\Delta f=\operatorname{div}\phi$. Then $\phi-
abla f\in V$ (zero divergence and tangential trace), and it has the same curl as $\phi$. Orthogonality to $\operatorname{curl}V$ therefore gives $\langle B,\operatorname{curl}\phiangle=0$, which is exactly distributional $\operatorname{curl}B=0$. Conversely if $B\in M$ is distributionally curl-free, pairing with each $u_j$ is legitimate by the actual tangential-zero collar cutoff: $\eta_\delta u_j	o u_j$ and their curls converge in $L^2$, since $n	imes u_j=O(s)$ on a layer $s\le2\delta$. The distributional compact-test pairing then gives $(B,w_j)=0$. The collar exists by [[thm-euclidean-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem]] and uses [[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]], with their stated choice premises. This proves the full decomposition, including arbitrary magnetic kernel data, without assuming a missing Hodge theorem or imposing electric tangential-zero data on $B$.
Each paired modal system and every electric zero equation has unique global solutions; keep the given $K_M$ component exactly. Orthogonality and the same scalar weighted-energy identity prove compact-time uniform energy-tail convergence for arbitrary $H	imes M$ data by [[thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion]]. Finite paired fields satisfy the interior equations because $\operatorname{curl}w_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}u_j$ distributionally by G3 and $\operatorname{curl}u_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}w_j$, while kernel fields have zero curl. Linear compact-test pairings pass to the limit in $L^2$. The finite spectral tests are dense in $V$ with its G3 graph norm and in $D_M$ with its defined curl graph norm, so Cauchy-Schwarz passes the modal time-test equations to precisely the stated variational equations. Conversely testing those equations at $u_j$, $w_j$ and every $K_M$ vector gives the modal equations. The weak modal boundary realization therefore explicitly tests these spectral equations, so the scalar ODE uniqueness and complete decompositions give uniqueness in the stated class; merely satisfying interior equations without this boundary realization is not asserted sufficient. For strong first-order solutions with $E\in C^1_tH\cap C_tV$ and $B\in C^1_tL^2\cap C_tH(\operatorname{curl})$, the same collar pairing gives $a_j'=v^2(B,\operatorname{curl}u_j)-\gamma a_j$. Differentiating using $B'=-\operatorname{curl}E$ and the full-$X$ identity gives $a_j''+\gamma a_j'+v^2\lambda_ja_j=0$, with $a_j'=-\gamma a_j$ at zero eigenvalues.
For (c), sum the finite identities and integrate them on $[t_0,t_1]$. Uniform energy-norm convergence on that compact interval passes both energy and the continuous $\|E(t)\|_2^2$ integral to the limit, proving the exact balance. FTC then yields its derivative for every time. This argument proves rough finite-energy dissipation without using a smooth-only local balance; the smooth reading agrees with the restricted material-energy supplier. The characteristic roots follow by completing the square; their explicit real exponential or sine/cosine solutions are verified by the stated derivative suppliers. Repeated roots retain $te^{-\gamma t/2}$. For $\gamma>0$, $\lambda>0$ the real roots are negative or the complex roots have negative real part, so each positive paired mode tends to zero by [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]], with the repeated-root polynomial factor covered by [[thm-exponential-beats-every-polynomial]]; electric zero modes decay and the magnetic kernel is static. Forward contractivity plus a finite-head/finite-tail argument passes this to the whole energy norm. No magnetic kernel component is discarded.
For (d), repeat G3's weighted $V$ Parseval argument for arbitrary initial displacement/velocity. For every positive mode $Q_j=|a_j'|^2+v^2\lambda_j|a_j|^2$ satisfies $Q_j'=-2\gamma|a_j'|^2$; the positive eigenvalues have a positive lower bound, so compact-time exponential bounds on $Q_j$ control the $V$ displacement and $H$ velocity tails. The finitely many zero modes have the separately displayed solutions. Uniform limits and the same finite-sum FTC estimate used by G3 identify the actual $H$ derivative and pass the variational second-order equation against compact-time tests. This mathematical wave-energy estimate is distinct from the physical first-order stored energy; no compatibility of arbitrary $V	imes H$ data is inferred. The first-order zero relation follows directly from its modal equation. No original spectral/variational supplier Statement is changed.
